Whilst tilt relates to first order with flow-speed squared induced by mooring-line drag, considerable deviations from this relationship and larger tilt occur when the amplitude of relative vorticity attains values O(f), f the inertial frequency of planetary vorticity. The sign of relative vorticity is of no importance. Such larger-tilt events occur during most intense convection turbulence via warm-water slanting from above. During these events, variations in tilt-angle magnitude are as large as the average tilt O(0.1)degr, thereby reducing variational scales from 50 to 9.5 m. Thus, in a deep-sea environment where flow speeds are <0.07 m/s, O(0.01) m/s flow-speed variations provide important turbulent mixing, under conditions without deep dense-water formation.

items.title: Large-scale Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials in LAMMPS
items.summary: Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics (MCMD) simulations are widely used to study the properties of materials at the mesoscale. Simulations with hundreds of thousands of atoms usually rely on empirical potentials because MCMD with machine-learning interatomic potentials is impractical at this scale in existing implementations. Here, we introduce a hybrid MPI/OpenMP scheme for MCMD with Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) potentials in LAMMPS. Monte Carlo moves are evaluated from local energy changes and carried out in parallel over MPI ranks, while molecular dynamics is parallelized over OpenMP threads. At a fixed number of CPUs, the wall time of the Monte Carlo moves decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks. Larger simulation cells also reduce the statistical errors of free energy calculations because thermal fluctuations decrease with system size. We demonstrate the scheme by calculating free energies of the HCP and BCC phases in the strongly anharmonic Hf--Ti system and by simulating zirconium segregation in a nanocrystalline copper sample of 670,000 atoms. For Cu--Zr, an ACE potential and an empirical potential predict similar grain boundary compositions but different amounts of zirconium dissolved in the grains. The scheme makes MCMD simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials practical at the length scales of microstructure.

items.title: Out-of-training properties in frozen interatomic potential embeddings are decodable and ordered by physical scale
items.summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are trained on energies, forces and stresses, yet their frozen representations can predict other materials properties. We probe ORB-v3 and UMA-S across layers, read-outs and equivariant channels for nine properties of 154,875 Materials Project crystals. Both models outperform composition-only descriptors on all targets, including five outside their training objectives; errors in physical units help assess potential screening applications. Optimal depth varies by property, consistent with a physical-scale ordering. Random-weight controls reveal strongly property-dependent benefits of pretraining. UMA-S's rotation-invariant angular channels improve crystal-system classification, while higher scores from its full tensor disappear under rotation; matched-model controls do not isolate equivariance as the explanation. Accuracy varies across different probes, but nearest-neighbour prediction often approaches XGBoost performance, even though materials do not form distinct clusters according to their properties. We also test whether a linear predictor trained on one model's embeddings can predict properties using the other model's embeddings after a learned linear transformation. Predictive accuracy is largely preserved, despite differences in which atoms the two models place close together. These results guide the reuse of frozen MLIP representations for materials prediction.

items.title: Intransigence or compromise: concatenated opinion dynamics with voting feedback
items.summary: In this paper, we study opinion evolution in a sequence of Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) models, concatenated so that the final opinions of each model serve as the initial opinions of the next. Each FJ model is followed by a vote, and each agent becomes partially or fully stubborn in the next model, depending on how close its opinion is to the voting result. With the state-dependent switching of stubbornness, the dynamics are not guaranteed to be contractive. We show that, over any fixed strongly connected network, the opinions always converge. A sufficient condition on the initial opinions is proposed, under which consensus is reached exponentially fast. For the complete graph, we further show that, if the agents' stubbornness levels do not differ too much, an agent that is partially stubborn in one FJ model can never become fully stubborn in a subsequent one: once it has started compromising, it keeps doing so.

items.title: Reversal of dynamical backaction and cooling below the quantum backaction limit in Floquet-driven multimode optomechanical resonators
items.summary: Dynamical backaction describes how a driven cavity field responds with delay to mechanical motion, and can be used to cool that motion toward its quantum ground state or amplify it into self-oscillation. Control over this interaction underpins laser cooling, high-fidelity state preparation, quantum transduction, and phonon lasing. In conventional cavity optomechanics, both the sign and the magnitude of the optical damping are dictated by the laser detuning, and cooling is bounded by quantum backaction (QBA), the optomechanical analogue of the Doppler limit in cold atoms. We show, in theory and experiment, that dynamical backaction can be strongly enhanced in multimode optomechanical resonators driven by time-varying (Floquet) optical fields. A modulated drive couples a sideband-unresolved MHz mode to a sideband-resolved GHz mode through the shared cavity, replacing the QBA limit of the target mode by the occupancy of the auxiliary mode. Experimentally, we cool the MHz mode to $47 \pm 13$ phonons, about half its single-mode QBA limit and an order of magnitude below what single-tone backaction reaches at the same intracavity photon number. The character of the interaction can moreover be completely inverted at fixed laser detuning, turning cooling into amplification and vice versa, controlled solely by the modulation frequency. Floquet driving thus extends open-loop quantum control, which requires no measurement or feedback, to mechanical resonators outside the resolved-sideband regime.

items.title: Compact Dielectric Barrier Discharge Source for a Pulsed Supersonic Beam of Metastable Triplet H$_2$
items.summary: We present a compact dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) source for producing pulsed supersonic beams of metastable molecules, designed to mount directly onto existing gas valves without modification. Unlike plate or corona discharge sources, the DBD produces no static electric field in the expansion zone and relies on capacitively coupled microdischarges that are inherently self-limiting. Charge accumulation on the dielectric terminates each event within nanoseconds and locally suppresses re-ignition, so that successive microdischarges are distributed across the nozzle. Arc formation and the associated hot spots are thereby prevented, and the gas is excited uniformly over the duration of the pulse. The source requires only a single custom ceramic nozzle and a compact printed circuit board (PCB) carrying the drive electronics, mounted directly in front of the valve. The high-voltage pulses are generated in-vacuum on the PCB from a DC supply voltage. Complete design files, circuit schematics, fabrication details, and validated simulation files are provided to allow straightforward reproduction. The DBD is applied to produce H$_2$ in the metastable c$^3Π_u^-$ state. This state can be used as an intermediate step for state-selective preparation of H$_2^+$ molecular ions by pulsed field ionization of optically prepared molecular Rydberg states, without requiring vacuum-ultraviolet radiation. We characterize the source by time-of-flight and Resonance-Enhanced Multiphoton Ionization (REMPI) spectroscopy, obtaining an excitation fraction on the order of $10^{-8}$ into the metastable state. The dependence of the yield on stagnation pressure and discharge voltage is consistent with collisional quenching as the dominant pressure-dependent loss.

items.title: Electronic structure, phase stability, and transport properties of the AlTiVCr lightweight high-entropy alloy: A computational study
items.summary: We investigate the thermodynamics and phase stability of the AlTiVCr lightweight high-entropy alloy using a combination of ab initio electronic structure calculations, a concentration wave analysis, and atomistic Monte Carlo simulations. In alignment both with experimental data and with results obtained using other computational approaches, we predict a $\textrm{B2}$ (CsCl) chemical ordering emerging in this alloy at comparatively high temperatures, which is driven by Al and Ti moving to separate sublattices, while V and Cr express weaker site preferences. The impact of this $\textrm{B2}$ chemical ordering on the electronic transport properties of the alloy is investigated within a Kubo--Greenwood linear response framework and it is found that, counter-intuitively, the alloy's residual resistivity increases as the material transitions from the $\textrm{A2}$ (disordered bcc) phase to our predicted $\textrm{B2}$ (partially) ordered structure. Our results give fresh insight into the atomic-scale structure and consequent physical properties of this well-studied, technologically relevant material.

items.title: Evaluation of Performance of the p-stop fabrication process variations in ATLAS18 strip sensors, Pre- and Post-Irradiation
items.summary: The High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) requires the replacement of the ATLAS Inner Detector with a new all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk). Radiation-hard n-in-p micro-strip sensors were developed for use in the ITk. During quality control (QC) and quality assurance (QA) procedures performed on ATLAS18 production sensors and test chips, ATLAS ITk strip sensor institutes identified instances of low p-stop density in certain production batches. To investigate the origin of these issues and to try some technological improvements, two dedicated sample batches with four variations of the p-stop fabrication process were produced. These process types (1-4) were systematically evaluated to determine their effectiveness and uniformity. In total, 56 full-size sensors, along with numerous miniature sensors and test chips, were tested. A number of samples were used in the irradiation campaign reaching the maximum expected levels for the HL-LHC operation after 10 years - with neutrons up to 1.6E15 neq/cm2, and with gamma rays from a 60Co source up to 66 Mrad. The goal of this evaluation program is to assess the impact of of p-stop fabrication process variations on interstrip isolation performance and to provide feedback for future sensor development. This paper describes the applied test procedures and presents the corresponding results, which demonstrate good sensor performance for all investigated p-stop types. The findings confirm the reliability of the evaluated designs and identify specific advantages that can inform further optimization of strip sensor fabrication.

items.title: Design of nSPIRAL: a Neutron Spectrometric Position-Weighted Radial Array Long-Counter
items.summary: We present here the design of a neutron long counter intended to measure neutrons originating from radioactive decays or nuclear reactions. Like other similar detectors, it relies on a moderator (polyethylene) and $^{3}$He tubes. A novel feature of our design is the use of the weighting technique to achieve an efficiency that is virtually independent of the energy spectrum of the neutrons being measured; a property known as \textit{flat efficiency}. This approach offers two primary advantages: it yields a flatter efficiency response than conventional analysis methods, and it provides greater flexibility regarding the geometry of the long counter. The latter has enabled us to design the detector with almost every $^{3}$He tube positioned at a different distance from the neutron source, which allows us to perform not only neutron counting but also neutron spectroscopy.

items.title: Experimental Evidence of Elastic Instability in Viscoelastic Kolmogorov Flow
items.summary: Inertialess elastic instabilities can profoundly affect transport in complex-fluid flows, from mixing in microfluidic devices and displacement through porous media to polymer processing. While such instabilities are well understood in flows with curved streamlines, their origin in rectilinear flows like the prototypical Kolmogorov flow remains unresolved. Here, we report the first experimental evidence of the center-mode elastic instability, at vanishing inertia, in a confined quasi-two-dimensional viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow, driven by electromagnetic forcing. The instability is characterized by the emergence of "arrow-shaped" structures in the velocity field, which fluctuates chaotically as the forcing strength increases. We reproduce these observations in simulations of the Oldroyd-B model and trace the dynamics in the confined flow to the travelling arrowhead structures that emerge from the center-mode instability of unbounded Kolmogorov flow. Our work establishes a generic route to purely elastic instability in rectilinear flows, broadening the conditions under which elastic turbulence and enhanced mixing can arise.

items.title: Subwavelength confinement of optical and acoustic waves for enhancing Brillouin gain in a planar waveguide structure
items.summary: We propose a planar waveguide structure consisting of two layers separated by a gap that provides subwavelength confinement of optical and acoustic modes and a large overlap integral between them. This, in turn, leads to an increase in Brillouin gain. Using the structure of two Si$_3$N$_4$ layers with a subwavelength gap from SiO$_2$ as an example, we demonstrate that a hybridized transverse-magnetic (TM) optical mode exhibits strong field confinement in the SiO$_2$ gap. Simultaneously, a high-frequency acoustic mode can be confined in the same gap, providing a high spatial overlap between the optical and acoustic fields. This provides a high opto-acoustic interaction with a Brillouin gain up to $5$ W$^{-1}$m$^{-1}$. The proposed structure is compatible with planar photonic integration and offers a promising platform for compact, low-threshold Brillouin lasers and coherent phonon generation.

items.title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation
items.summary: The state space of a dynamical system can, under suitable conditions, be reconstructed from a single observational time-series through delay-coordinate embedding. However, reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse measurements remains a considerable challenge. Here, by combining deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity properties of unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation, we show that the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field can be reconstructed from observations collected at a {\it single} measurement location. We subsequently use these reconstructions to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics from point observations obtained in controlled water wave tank experiments, demonstrating excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field. Our results show that extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations and provide a framework that may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.

items.title: A Hierarchically Compressed Immittance Operator Formulation for Fast Statics-to-Full-Wave Electromagnetic Simulation with the Boundary Element Method
items.summary: The boundary element method allows the electromagnetic simulation of three-dimensional problems with a two-dimensional discretization, using a surface integral representation of Maxwell's equations. For applications involving broadband simulations or multiscale geometries, the well-known low-frequency breakdown of conventional integral equation formulations must be addressed, while ensuring that dielectric, semiconducting, and lossy metallic regions are modeled rigorously, including the skin effect. In this work, a new boundary element formulation based on an immittance operator is proposed, where the underlying integral equations are inherently valid from statics to the full-wave regime. To enable efficient matrix assembly and solution, a hierarchical matrix compression strategy is devised, leveraging fast direct factorization as an intermediate step, and fast matrix-vector products for the iterative solution of the final system of equations. The proposed formulation is capable of electrostatic, magnetostatic, quasistatic, and full-wave simulations of dielectrics, semiconductors, and lossy metals. Representative numerical examples drawn from a variety of applications demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method.

items.title: Observing Earth's ionospheric irregularities from the Moon
items.summary: Radio signals that propagate through the Earth's ionosphere carry information about possible irregular plasma structures. Such irregularities manifest themselves as amplitude signatures that depend on the propagation and observation geometry [1, 2]. Conventional ground and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) measurements sample these effects close to Earth. Here we present a systematic characterization of terrestrial ionospheric irregularities using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) amplitude observations from the lunar surface, at distances of approximately 356,000-398,000 km from Earth's surface [3]. Using nearly 93 h of 1-Hz lunar-surface observations of GPS L1/L5 and Galileo E1/E5a collected by the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE), we reconstruct the propagation and scanning geometry to characterize the spatiotemporal signatures of amplitude and phase fluctuations. At lunar distance, the Fresnel scale approaches its finite-source limit, extending the observations to a propagation regime beyond conventional near-Earth configurations. Detrended receiver-reported carrier-to-noise density ratios ($δC/N_0$) reveal pronounced polar amplitude fluctuations at both frequency bands, also visible in the original measurements. Within the regions and local times sampled, large fluctuations occur in about 30% of valid one-minute polar windows, compared with less than 5% in either the equatorial or mid-latitude band. These findings support using the lunar surface as a vantage point for studying Earth's polar ionospheric irregularities and testing how propagation and scanning relative to the magnetic field shape their amplitude signatures. Future lunar observations could extend this approach to long-term monitoring of Earth's ionospheric irregularities

items.title: Multipole Decomposition of Moving Sources
items.summary: Cartesian multipole moments are widely used to analyze and engineer radiation, but the usual relations for their radiated fields assume a wavevector-independent source frequency. For moving sources, Doppler shifts make the frequency depend on the wavevector, so the radiated fields predicted from the moments generally carry errors proportional to v/c. From charge conservation in the laboratory frame, we derive a multipole decomposition of moving sources that retains the usual moments but evaluates their contributions at Doppler-shifted wavenumbers and adds a convection-current term. Requiring no rest frame, it applies to moving matter and to excitation patterns in synthetic motion through media at rest, including superluminal ones. The decomposition also extends to nonuniform translation and to nonrigid patterns with curved spectral supports. Exact calculations for moving electric, magnetic, and toroidal dipoles confirm the decomposition and attribute the different radiation of a dipole in moving matter and in synthetic motion to the laboratory moments that each kind of motion induces. For an anapole, these moments decide whether it radiates. An anapole carried by uniformly moving matter remains nonradiating, whereas an excitation pattern with the same electric and toroidal dipoles radiates in synthetic motion. The decomposition thus makes multipolar analysis available for moving matter and for excitation patterns in synthetic motion, and it opens the way to designing their radiation.

items.title: Linear Electrostatic Instabilities Driven by Relativistic Non-Maxwellian Pair Beams
items.summary: We investigate how non-Maxwellian momentum distributions affect the linear growth of electrostatic instabilities driven by relativistic pair beams, motivated by the lack of a universally accepted analytical description of blazar-induced pair beams. Different beam distributions are used to describe relativistic pair beams in analytical studies and particle-in-cell simulations. A systematic comparison is therefore needed to determine how the beam distribution influences the instability growth rates. We formulate the relativistic electrostatic response in the weak-beam limit for an anisotropic $κ$-type distribution and compare the resulting growth rates with those obtained for Gaussian and Maxwell--Jüttner distributions. We require $κ>3/2$ for a finite root-mean-square momentum spread. For the parameters considered, the $κ$-type distributions yield higher maximum growth rates than the Gaussian distribution, even when their mean momenta and momentum spreads are the same. The fastest-growing modes correspond to parallel propagation for the $κ$ and Gaussian distributions, whereas the Maxwell--Jüttner distribution exhibits its maximum for oblique propagation for a mildly relativistic beam. An additional calculation for a highly relativistic pair beam with $κ=2$ finds an oblique maximum of the electrostatic growth rate. The beam momentum distribution influences the linear growth of electrostatic instabilities under the conditions investigated.

items.title: Reconfigurable Dysprosium Isotope Mixtures with Selectable Quantum Statistics
items.summary: Dipolar quantum mixtures offer new opportunities to explore many-body phenomena shaped by long-range anisotropic interactions, intercomponent coupling, and quantum statistics. Here we develop a reconfigurable platform for bosonic and fermionic dysprosium isotope mixtures using a single-isotope-like optical layout. We time-multiplex the 421-nm light to generate isotope-selective slow-atom fluxes, while spectrally engineered 626-nm light provides simultaneous common-path narrow-line cooling and trapping. By reconfiguring optical frequencies, we prepare seven isotope pairs spanning Bose--Bose, Bose--Fermi, and Fermi--Fermi combinations, with continuous population-balance control through the 421-nm dwell-time allocation. Systematic comparisons with sequence-matched single-isotope references, from magneto-optical-trap loading and compression to optical-dipole-trap transfer, reveal nearly single-isotope-like performance for most combinations. The larger deviations occur only for certain isotope pairs and preparation stages, with controlled measurements revealing optical sensitivities during loading and additional losses under high-density conditions. Our results make isotope composition and quantum statistics selectable within a strongly dipolar system while largely preserving single-isotope preparation simplicity and performance, opening new possibilities for exploring multicomponent dipolar quantum matter.

items.title: Bias Conditioning and Long-Range Electrostatics for Consistent Machine-Learning Potentials of Electrified Interfaces
items.summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) of electrified interfaces need the bias as input, but it is unclear whether a scalar electrode charge suffices and whether short-range models capture the non-local response. We add charge and field conditioning to short- and long-range MLIPs. State-of-the-art field-conditioned short-range models overpolarize thick water films nearly twofold and miss work-function shifts at stepped Pt. Our long-range model captures both, needs only the electrode charge at metals as input, and reproduces ab initio simulations of the Pt(111)--water interface.

items.title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications
items.summary: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability. This chapter explores the diverse applications of laser technology in energy applications. It begins with an overview of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, highlighting key experimental facilities and crucial laser parameters. The role of lasers in solar energy harvesting is examined, including photovoltaic cell optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted recycling of solar modules. The chapter further reviews recent developments into laser-based techniques for enhancing electrochemical performance through surface texturing at various scales. Advancements in lithium-ion battery technology are also discussed, focusing on next-generation materials, battery manufacturing processes, and the impact of laser techniques on performance, safety, and scalability. The chapter concludes with insights into future prospects for laser applications in sustainable energy solutions.

items.title: Intrinsic Berry Curvature on the Higher-order Poincare Sphere
items.summary: Higer-order geometric phase enable versatile spin-orbit manipulation of structured light . Con ventional theories describe this phase via a total-angular-momentum dependent Berry curvature . We develop an intrinsic theory restricted to the effective two-dimensional subspace, where the Berry curvature is independent of the topological charge of the light field . In our framework, the total-angular-momentum difference does not alter the effective monopole strength, whereas it controls the solid angle enclosed by the trajectory of the state evolution, insteadly. Our theory provides a different topological interpretation of geometric phase of the structured light, which unifies the underlying structures of generalized Poincare Spheres. Furthermore, it does not impose any specific form on the physical operation of the optical element, naturally encomoassing the case of previously reported experiment, and can be applied in arbitrary state evolutions in both classical structured light and quantum spin-orbit systems .

items.title: A physics-constrained emulator for time-discretised landslide runout modelling
items.summary: Numerical simulations of landslides are commonly used to forecast impact areas. Full physics-based models provide accurate predictions, but their computational expense can preclude their use for large parameter sweeps. To achieve efficient modelling for such cases, we developed a physics-constrained neural network to emulate full landslide runout in a time-discretised manner. This emulator is trained on over 200,000 samples, each consisting of a pair of landslide thicknesses and velocities on a given DEM with a fixed time interval. To constrain the model's physical consistency, we define physics-based loss functions based on mass conservation and the system's kinetic energy loss. The model demonstrates high fidelity across the test dataset, achieving root mean square errors of approximately 0.06 m for thickness and 0.11 m/s for velocity in single-step predictions. In autoregressive rollout, these errors evolved modestly to about 0.21 m and 0.09 m/s after 110 iterations, while greatly improving computational efficiency by more than 50 times.

items.title: Particle Identification Studies using a Highly Granular Crystal Electromagnetic Calorimeter
items.summary: A proposal for the Circular Electron Positron Collider electromagnetic calorimeter is a highly granular scintillating crystal design that uses silicon photomultipliers to measure physics signals from photons. The potential to develop particle identification methods using deep and traditional machine learning is explored. A contrastive machine learning technique was found to enable the separation of showering and 'punch-through' pions without explicit labels. A supervised particle identification method was then trained using the results, using both a graph neural network and a boosted decision tree to distinguish electron, showering hadron, and minimum-ionizing-particle-like events. The classifier achieved an area-under-the-receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.996 for both cases. A Shapley additive explanations analysis showed the boosted decision tree classifier matched expectations for each event type. The particle identification capability is then demonstrated on experimental data taken from the CERN Proton Synchrotron T9 beamline.

items.title: The relationship between junctional zone, smooth muscle tone and intra-uterine pressure
items.summary: The junctional zone is a thin low contrast region of the inner myometrium, visible on T2weighted MRI images. Investigators have long sought histologic particularities of this region. Here, we summarize evidence that this region's specific appearance is not due to a particular tissue composition, but is a reflection of underlying smooth muscle activity. Smooth muscle tone in the spirally fibered myometrium wrings out blood and interstitial fluids to create a static low-contrast T2 region around the myometrium, while phasic smooth muscle contractions create transient, propagative low-contrast waves. We show that the competition between centripetal inhibitory adrenergic innervation from the serosa and centrifugal excitatory hormonal gradients from the endometrium divides the uterus in a tonic inner-and a quiescent outer-region. Bridging MRI and manometry studies, we discuss the relation between smooth muscle activity and intra-uterine pressure. Dysregulation of nerve and/or hormonal activity can result in a thicker tonic smooth muscle layer, entailing a thicker junctional zone and high intrauterine pressures characteristic of dyscontractility in severe dysmenorrhea, endometriosis and adenomyosis.

items.title: Quantifying internal variability in large-ensemble climate data with the Wasserstein distance
items.summary: Estimating forced and internal variability in climate data is fundamental to detecting the climate change signal and assessing uncertainty in climate projections. We propose a metric that quantifies the relative magnitude of internal variability in single-model initial-condition large ensembles (SMILEs). We measure forced and internal variability by two 1-Wasserstein distances, a form of optimal transport cost. The proposed metric is the distance for internal variability divided by the sum of the two. Computing this ratio requires only sorting the samples and differencing the resulting quantiles, with no additional parameters. The metric reflects the entire distribution shape and applies to non-Gaussian variables, because the 1-Wasserstein distance measures the difference between any two probability distributions. We validate the metric with synthetic climate data from Gaussian, uniform, and lognormal distributions. Unlike the two existing metrics, the proposed metric gives stable estimates in the presence of outliers irrespective of the distribution shape, provided that the ensemble has about 40 members or more. We then apply the proposed and existing metrics to the 2 m air temperature and total precipitation of the Community Earth System Model Large Ensemble (CESM-LE) under two different forcing scenarios. All three metrics agree in the spatial pattern of the difference between the scenarios but not in amplitude. The amplitude of the difference is largest for the proposed metric, consistent with the synthetic-data result that this metric changes most rapidly when internal variability dominates. The 1-Wasserstein distance thus provides a simple and useful tool for analyzing large-ensemble datasets.

items.title: Transferable neural-network preconditioners for Wilson--Clover propagator inversions
items.summary: We investigate two single--layer neural-network architectures for accelerating four-dimensional Wilson--Clover propagator inversions on lattice ensembles in practical use; both transfer directly without retraining. The first is a gauge-covariant parallel transport convolution (PTC) network that directly reduces the number of generalized conjugate residual (GCR) solver iterations. The second is a CNN-like network used together with a multigrid-inspired algorithm. The two approaches can be combined to further reduce GCR iterations. PTC transfers without retraining across lattice volumes, lattice spacings, and pion masses while maintaining comparable acceleration, whereas the CNN-like network transfers directly from small- to large-volume ensembles with strong acceleration. A cost comparison accounting for both basis construction and solves shows that the proposed scheme is more advantageous for large-volume ensembles than for small-volume ones.

items.title: A Soft Sponge-Pillar Electrode Platform for Motion-Tolerant Ambulatory EEG and Sleep Monitoring
items.summary: Long-term wearable electrophysiological recording systems are essential for both clinical and real-world environments. While a wide range of wearable devices have been reported for electrocardiogram (ECG) and electromyogram (EMG) recording applications, most electroencephalography (EEG) measurements still require subjects to remain stationary while wearing rigid and uncomfortable equipment. Here, a soft and wearable sponge pillar EEG electrode is presented for long-term and motion-tolerant EEG recording. The electrode is composed of two layers of a carbon black (CB)-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composite, where a firmer solid base assists in bypassing hair, enabling stable access to the scalp, while a porous sponge tip ensures comfort, reliable contact, and low skin-electrode impedance. Fabricated via a sugar templating process without microfabrication steps, the microporous sponge structure offers low modulus and significantly enhances the contact area with the skin when loaded with conductive gel. This allows the electrode to achieve a lower contact impedance of $1.62 \times 10^{4}\,Ω$ at 10 Hz, outperforming conventional gelled electrodes while maintaining gel stability for over 18 hours. With the electrodes integrated into wearable form factors such as headbands, headphones, and baseball caps, EEG signal recording during motion have been demonstrated, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 16.46 dB. These features establish the sponge pillar electrode as a promising platform for next generation wearable EEG systems, enabling comfortable, stable, and prolonged brain signal acquisition on ambulatory subjects and in naturalistic environments.

items.title: Using an instrumented hammer to predict the lateral hinge fracture in high tibial osteotomy: A cadaveric study
items.summary: Open-wedge High-Tibial Osteotomy is the most commonly employed technique addressing varus knee osteoarthritis. During this procedure, the osteotome passes through cortical and trabecular bone. A common complication is lateral hinge fractures, which depends upon when the surgeon stops impacting the osteotome. The aim of the present study is to determine whether an instrumented hammer can be employed to detect (i) the bone type (cortical or trabecular) surrounding the osteotome tip and (ii) when bone is fractured by the osteotome. Seventeen lower-limb specimens were obtained from nine fresh human anatomical subjects. The osteotome was impacted using the instrumented hammer until rupture. Each impact signal was recorded and analyzed. An algorithm was developed to detect the transitions between cortical and trabecular bone and vice versa. Detection was based on the relative variation of $τ$ derived from the force signal as a function of time as the time difference between the second___and___first impact peaks. The values of $τ$ were significantly lower in cortical bone compared to trabecular bone. Considering the arrival of the osteotome tip in trabecular bone during a medial, a difference of less than 2 impacts between the surgeon and the algorithm was obtained for 71% of the cases. For the lateral osteotomy it was obtained in 81% of the cases. This cadaveric study demonstrated that the instrumented hammer could prevent impacts leading to hinge rupture, which suggests that future clinical trials are warranted.

items.title: Detecting the pterygomaxillary disjunction using an instrumented hammer: A cadaveric study
items.summary: Background: In many maxillofacial surgeries, the surgeon must perform a pterygomaxillary disjunction in order to separate the jaw from the skull. The disjunction is performed using an osteotome which is impacted with a hammer until its tip crosses through the pterygoid plates. To determine whether the disjunction has occurred and avoid complications, surgeons still rely on their proprioception. Methods: The aim of this study is to validate a vibroacoustic set-up constituted by an instrumented hammer equipped with a force sensor, aiming at detecting if the disjunction has occurred. To do so, fourteen osteotomies were performed in anatomical subject jaws. For each impact, the force signal was recorded and analyzed. A classification algorithm (Support Vector Machine method coupled with a cost matrix) was developed based on indicators extracted from the signal to determine whether the disjunction had occurred. Impacts were classified into two classes, one before and the other after the osteotome had crossed the pterygoid plates. To avoid undetected disjunctions a cost matrix was added to the algorithm. The coefficients from the matrix were chosen using by minimizing the Negative Likelihood Ratio. Findings: The algorithm was able to distinguish impacts before and after the disjunction with an accuracy of 96 %. Moreover, the instrumented hammer was able to detect the disjunction with a maximum delay of two impacts. Interpretation: These results pave the way for the development of a per-operative decision support system for the pterygomaxillary disjunction.

items.title: Multimodal assessment of the skin biomechanical properties during wound healing and hyaluronic acid response
items.summary: Various methods such as elastography or mechanical testing have been developed to quantify the mechanical properties of soft tissues, which are related to the tissue local pathophysiological conditions. This study is the first one to investigate the in vivo performances of the Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM) to characterize the biomechanical behavior of skin during physiological mechanisms. A murine model (12 Sprague-Dawley rats) was considered and various measurements of skin mechanical properties were conducted on different regions of interest over a 3-week period. The effects of wound healing after full-thickness excisional wound and an intradermal hyaluronic acid (HA) injection were monitored using IBAM, as well as two commercially available devices: Cutometer__ and MyotonPro__. The indicators $Δ$t (from IBAM), R0 and R5 (from Cutometer__) vary significantly as a function of wound healing time, which corresponds to a stiffening of healing tissue compared to healthy tissue. The indicator $Δ$t and S (from MyotonPro__) are significantly different when HA was injected compared to healthy tissue, which also corresponds to less stiff tissue. Additionally, both IBAM and Cutometer__ detect significant biomechanical variations in superficial soft tissue related to tissue growth in all measurement regions. This first in vivo use of IBAM shows that IBAM could assess significant variations related to wound healing or regeneration mechanisms following HA injection. This study paves the way for the development of a simple, low-cost and objective device. Future clinical studies or other animal models should be carried out to confirm these results.

items.title: A unified framework for net effects in signed social and ecological networks
items.summary: With improvements in data resolution and quality, researchers can now represent complex systems as signed, weighted, and directed networks. In this article, we introduce a framework for measuring net and indirect effects without simplifying these information-rich networks. It captures both direct and indirect interactions, the effect of the whole network on a node, and conversely, the effect of a node on the entire network, while accommodating the complexity of signed, weighted, and directed links. Our taxonomy unifies and extends existing approaches and measures from network science, computational social science, and ecological networks. We demonstrate its value in ecological systems, where net and indirect effects are critical yet difficult to quantify. Using generalized Lotka-Volterra dynamics, we find a strong correlation between negative net effects and species extinction. We further apply the framework to a real-world social network, where it identifies informative rankings that illuminate influence propagation and power dynamics.

items.title: Recovery of accidental bound states in the continuum in vertically asymmetric photonic lattices through radiation-source parity restoration
items.summary: Vertical asymmetry generally precludes accidental bound states in the continuum (BICs) in planar photonic lattices, yet the underlying physical mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we show that accidental-BIC formation is governed by the definite parity of the transverse radiation-source profile rather than by geometric vertical mirror symmetry. A semianalytical coupled-mode analysis shows that an accidental BIC occurs when the radiation overlap integral of a leaky Bloch mode vanishes. We decompose the overlap into contributions from the even- and odd-parity components of the transverse radiation-source profile. Complete radiation suppression requires both contributions to vanish simultaneously. In vertically symmetric lattices, the source profile has definite even or odd parity, causing one contribution to vanish identically. Thickness tuning can null the remaining contribution and produce an accidental BIC. In vertically asymmetric lattices, by contrast, both parity components are generally present. The waveguide dispersion forbids their simultaneous vanishing, thereby precluding an accidental BIC. Introducing a parity-restoring layer into a vertically asymmetric lattice restores definite parity to the transverse radiation-source profile, thereby enabling the formation of an accidental BIC. Finite-element simulations confirm the analytically predicted recovery of accidental BICs for both TE$_0$ and TE$_1$ Bloch modes.

items.title: How Elasticity and Chiral Damping Shape Domain-Wall Creep
items.summary: Asymmetric domain-wall expansion in the creep regime provides an experimentally accessible probe of the interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (iDMI) and, in principle, chiral damping. However, severe discrepancies with complementary measurement techniques and the lack of a model describing the full experimental phenomenology of the creep of chiral domain walls, limits the application of these measurements. Here, using a symmetry decomposition of the velocity curve, we derive an analytical model describing the coupled influence of domain-wall stiffness and chiral damping in the creep regime. Their interplay generates the antisymmetric distortion that shifts the velocity minimum away from the DMI field. Applied to Co-based magnetic multilayers, the model yields iDMI values consistent with BLS and flow-regime benchmarks and identifies the reasons for the longstanding discrepancy. The model provides insights for possible strategies to measure chiral damping via creep dynamics of domain walls.

items.title: Analog Resonant Recurrent Neural Networks via Metacircuits
items.summary: Physical neural networks offer a promising route to fast and energy-efficient edge intelligence by embedding computation in the intrinsic dynamics of materials and devices. However, processing temporal signals requires recurrent networks with memory, whose trained dynamics are hard to reproduce faithfully in physical systems. Here we present an analog resonant recurrent neural network (R$^2$NN) implemented as a metacircuit of coupled local resonators. A reformulated mechanical-electrical analogy based on frequency-dependent negative resistances maps a trained network one-to-one onto the metacircuit, with every trainable parameter realized as a resistance. Training tunes local resonances and global resistive couplings so that past responses persist as recurrent memory and interfere with incoming inputs, and the resulting impedance landscape routes different frequencies to distinct outputs. Exploiting this recurrent memory, the metacircuit solves a temporal-parity task whose output depends on the entire input history. Building on the learned frequency selectivity, stand-alone R$^2$NN systems classify raw tactile, acoustic and vibration signals in real time and directly drive downstream hardware. This work establishes engineered locally resonant dynamics as a physical substrate for recurrent neural computation and opens a route to compact, low-latency neural hardware for machine intelligence at the edge.

items.title: Highlighting Ukrainian Contributions to the Development of the Field of Particle Physics
items.summary: The contribution examines the role played by Ukrainian scientists, both in Ukraine and abroad, in the development of particle physics.

items.title: Role of flame localization in wavemaker regions on the suppression of combustion instability in turbulent partially-premixed methane flames
items.summary: The interaction between flame dynamics & hydrodynamic instabilities plays a fundamental role in determining the stability of swirl-stabilized combustors. In the present study, we investigate the hypothesis that spatial overlap between flame & wavemaker region is a necessary prerequisite for combustion stability in flows characterized by a wavemaker region. To test the hypothesis, a low-momentum secondary methane injection was introduced through circumferential holes located on the centerbody of a swirl-stabilized burner. The injection velocity was maintained below 5\% of bulk flow velocity to minimize momentum-induced modifications of flow field while selectively redistributing heat release. In addition, an equivalent amount of fuel was diverted from primary fuel supply to secondary injection ports, known as fuel-staging, to isolate the effects of flame relocation from those of the total fuel flow rate. The introduction of secondary injection produced a transition of the flame from M-shaped to V-shaped structure, while fuel-staging yielded a similar flame response, demonstrating that observed behavior results primarily from redistribution of heat release. Linear stability analysis revealed that wavemaker region remains near inlet of the combustion chamber. Moreover, flame root transitions from a lifted M-flame to attached V-flame and consistently stabilizes at radial position corresponding to the identified wavemaker region. The coincidence of flame attachment & wavemaker location under stable operating conditions provides strong experimental evidence that flame stabilization is governed by their spatial overlap rather than by a modification of the underlying hydrodynamic instability. The proposed framework provides new insight into the coupling between flame stabilization & hydrodynamic instability & offers practical guidance for the design of stable, low-emission combustion systems.

items.title: Radiation Effects on Breakdown Voltage and Quenching Resistance in SiPMs
items.summary: This study investigates the suitability of the Hamamatsu S13360 series as replacement photodetectors for the RICH upgrade II detector. I-V curves enabled a statistical analysis of breakdown voltage and quenching resistance before and after irradiation, quantifying the dependance of damage on neutron fluence and the mitigation effect of cooling. The results show that breakdown voltage degradation increases with fluence and becomes statistically significant only at high irradiation levels. Quenching resistance, by contrast, shows only a limited increase except at 6 x 10^13 neq/cm2, where substantial degradation appears. Both parameters exhibit a clear reduction in radiation-damage impact when operated at cryogenic temperatures.

items.title: Will it bend? Modelling hydrogel box hinges with a gel Lattice Spring Method
items.summary: Hydrogels are biocompatible smart materials comprised of a hydrophilic polymer network which can absorb a large volume of water (swelling). The changes in shape the gel undergoes as it swells or de-swells can be utilised in the design of actuators. This is of particular interest for many applications whereby hydrogel actuators would be combined into a complex origami-inspired structure which can fold and unfold according to application needs. In this paper, we therefore focus on one such actuator design, the bilayer hinge, which can induce bending (for potential use in a fold/unfold mechanism). We develop a model using the gel lattice spring method (gLSM) which can be used to simulate composite structures comprised of hydrogel and elastomer and compute the equilibrium bending angle of bilayer hinges for a range of geometries and material properties.

items.title: MolReps: Taking SELFIES, Making SMILES, Teaching LLMs
items.summary: The same molecule can be expressed in multiple, syntactically distinct representations, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize and relate these equivalent encodings. We introduce MolReps, a pipeline that generates 9,600 question-answer pairs across ten representations for conversion, normalization, and 2D structure recognition. Post-training on MolReps improves text-only and multimodal models, MolQwen3-4B-Instruct (MQ3-4B-I) and MolQwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (MQ3-VL-4B-I), from $4.01\%$ to $75.13\%$ and from $7.11\%$ to $73.14\%$ (InChIKey match) on the molecule-overlap test set, respectively. On the molecule-disjoint test set, post-training increased validity from $20.35\%$ to $58.12\%$ for MQ3-4B-I and from $17.19\%$ to $59.34\%$ for MQ3-VL-4B-I. However, InChIKey match remained low, decreasing from $3.86\%$ to $3.09\%$ and from $6.44\%$ to $2.29\%$, respectively. Furthermore, the resulting models achieve a relative $27.84\%$ improvement in average over their base model on MolRepBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating molecular property prediction. These results show the effectiveness of targeted post-training for enhancing molecular representation understanding and its potential to improve downstream molecular tasks.

items.title: Shape effects on the Shafranov shift of Solov'ev equilibria with prescribed boundaries
items.summary: The Shafranov shift, the outward displacement of the magnetic axis of a toroidal plasma, is known analytically for circular and elliptical cross-sections, whereas its dependence on shape in strongly shaped plasmas has not been studied systematically. Here the shift is analyzed for a wide range of prescribed boundaries, at fixed profiles or poloidal beta, using exact Solov'ev solutions of the Grad--Shafranov equation with the boundary imposed in a least-squares sense. For shaped boundaries the shift depends on the point from which it is measured, usually the geometric center, the midpoint of the radial extent of the boundary. Therefore, a straight-cylinder equilibrium with the same plasma shape is introduced as the zero-shift reference state, and the shift is measured from its magnetic axis. With this reference, some known features of the shift measured from the geometric center turn out to be effects of the reference point, whose error depends only on the boundary and can also make the shift negative. Three boundary parametrizations are used to analyze positive and negative triangularity, squareness from square to concave shapes, and non-convex star polygons of arbitrary symmetry order. At fixed poloidal beta the shift depends only weakly on triangularity: the larger shift of negative than of positive triangularity plasmas obtained with the geometric center is an effect of the reference point and nearly disappears with the cylindrical reference. Negative squareness and concavity, instead, reduce the shift itself: for concave plasma cross-sections it is almost half that of elliptical and D-shaped ones.

items.title: A Neural Physics Solver for Richards Equation
items.summary: A new approach to discretise and solve Richards equation based on the finite element method (FEM) is presented. The novelty of the approach, called the Neural Physics method, is that it expresses the discretisation as a convolution neural network (CNN) whose weights are predetermined by the integrals of the basis functions in the FEM. The Neural Physics method is physically consistent as it represents a discretisation of the governing equation and can run on CPUs, GPUs and the latest AI accelerators, resulting in an increase in computational speed. The Neural Physics method is demonstrated for two different discretisations of Richards equation, including a multigrid method that is realised through a U-Net architecture. The accuracy and speed of these methods is tested on a problem with a known analytical solution and compared to a standard FEM, and shows that the Neural Physics method is almost an order of magnitude faster than a comparable FEM. Finally, the Neural Physics method is applied to a real-world test case with integrated experimental data and simulates the infiltration of water through a rain garden. This new approach therefore provides a route to efficiently and accurately solve Richards equation for a wide array of hydrological applications.

items.title: Condensation-related expansion work of water vapor as a major pathway for kinetic energy generation in the lower atmosphere
items.summary: Earth's atmosphere operates a steam cycle: water evaporates from the surface, expands as vapor, condenses in colder air, and returns as precipitation. Yet its power and relationship to atmospheric mechanical power remain poorly quantified. Applying the Clausius--Clapeyron relation between saturated vapor expansion work and latent heat converted at Carnot efficiency to vertically distributed condensation, we derive the steam-engine power as a sum of the gravitational and condensation-related contributions, $W_v=W_g+W_c$; it is not the net power of a complete moist-air cycle. Using twelve years of GPM/DPR spectral latent-heating profiles and MERRA-2 fields, we estimate $W_v\simeq4.1$ W m$^{-2}$, with $W_c\simeq2.8$ W m$^{-2}$. Separately, we diagnose total atmospheric mechanical power $W=W_P+W_K\simeq4.3$ W m$^{-2}$, comprising gravitational power of precipitation $W_P\simeq1.1$ W m$^{-2}$ and kinetic energy generation $W_K\simeq3.2$ W m$^{-2}$, including $2.4$ W m$^{-2}$ below 500 hPa. Both correspondences $W_v\simeq W$ and $W_c\simeq W_K$ lie within 20--30\% uncertainty estimates. To explain these correspondences, we propose that $W_c$ generates the potential energy associated with surface pressure gradients. Cross-isobaric flow in the frictional lower atmosphere converts this energy into kinetic energy. In a horizontally isothermal atmosphere, this positive pressure work would be nearly cancelled by compression aloft. An idealized circulation illustrates how differential heating can offset compression, allowing nearly isobaric upper return flow. In the proposed mechanism, condensation-driven circulation unlocks this thermal compensation thus providing a major pathway for lower-atmospheric kinetic energy generation. We discuss how changes in the coupling between condensation and differential heating could test this proposed causal relationship.

items.title: Experimental observation of higher-harmonic generation of whistler waves in magnetized plasma of Large Volume Plasma Device
items.summary: We report the higher-harmonic generation of whistler waves using a loop antenna in the Large Volume Plasma Device (LVPD). The antenna is energized using a pulse-forming network (PFN), and the excited magnetic fluctuations are measured using a three-axis B-dot probe. Experiments are performed in a moderate-density ($n_e \sim 1-2 \times 10^{17}\ \text{m}^{-3}$), low-temperature ($T_e \sim 2-5\ \text{eV}$) argon plasma in a uniform axial magnetic field ($B_z \sim 6.2\ \text{G}$). A Helmholtz coil is employed to investigate the dependence of the wave response and propagation on the local magnetic-field configuration. A clear distinction between wave characteristics is observed in the absence and presence of plasma: in plasma, the excited wave shows a significant $δB_y$ component along with $δB_x$, indicating polarization. In addition to the fundamental frequency, distinct spectral peaks are observed at $300\ \text{kHz}$, $450\ \text{kHz}$, and $600\ \text{kHz}$. These harmonics indicate nonlinear wave-plasma interactions, and bicoherence analysis further provides evidence of nonlinear coupling between the observed frequency components. The spatial propagation of the wave was systematically diagnosed using a linear array of five identical B-dot probes. Spatial cross-correlation analysis reveals strong structural coherence during wave propagation, allowing the explicit experimental determination of the wave phase velocity ($V_{ph}$) and parallel wave number ($k_{\parallel}$) for the generated higher harmonics. The measured propagation is oblique at an angle of approximately $48^\circ$ with respect to the background magnetic field, and the experimental dispersion relation agrees with the cold-plasma oblique whistler dispersion relation within experimental uncertainty.

items.title: Communication-Efficient Hamiltonian Evaluation for Massively Parallel Tensor-Product Bitstring Selected Configuration Interaction
items.summary: Extreme-scale selected configuration interaction (SCI) requires coordinated Hamiltonian evaluation, distributed CI-vector storage, and interprocess communication on massively parallel computers. Our previous work [J. Chem. Phys. 164, 194103 (2026)] introduced the tensor-product bitstring selected configuration interaction (TBSCI) framework, combining on-the-fly Hamiltonian evaluation with fully distributed CI-vector storage and enabling parallel diagonalization of trillion-determinant spaces on up to 54,000 Fugaku nodes. Here, we introduce FLIP, a new Hamiltonian evaluation algorithm within TBSCI that reorganizes the CI-vector layout and excitation-link data to replace remote CI-coefficient transfers for $α$-electron double excitations with local coefficient access and link retrieval from nearby MPI ranks. In communication-intensive full configuration interaction (FCI) benchmarks on Fugaku, no exposed communication waiting time was recorded on the slowest process across all 32 measured Hamiltonian-vector multiplications. For N$_2$/cc-pVTZ with $2.62\times10^{12}$ determinants, the multiplication achieved 91.3% strong-scaling efficiency from 18,000 to 81,000 nodes (more than 3.8 million compute cores). We also obtained an FCI reference potential-energy curve for N$_2$/cc-pVTZ. At all six bond lengths, spin bitstrings selected by their collective weights in reference SCI wavefunctions yielded variational TBSCI energies within 0.1 m$E_h$ of FCI using fewer than 1% of the FCI determinants, demonstrating the compactness of the tensor-product bitstring representation. Finally, we discuss local construction of double-excitation links to substantially reduce communication volume and eliminate persistent storage of precomputed double-link tables for future second-order perturbation theory calculations with large external determinant spaces.

items.title: Parametrised-Quadratic Interface Reconstruction and Geometric Velocity Extension in the Volume-of-Fluid Framework
items.summary: A conservative Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) framework using local parametric-curve interface reconstruction (PI-VOF) is developed for geometric interface propagation on fixed Cartesian grids. While VOF methods achieve conservative and second-order accurate interface advection under prescribed velocity fields, normal-velocity-driven interface propagation requires the interfacial velocity to be extended to neighbouring staggered-grid locations. Existing studies on interface evolution employ auxiliary distance functions, kernel smoothers, or high-resolution VOF in multiple grids to compute propagation velocities and address first-order-accuracy limitations. In contrast, PI-VOF directly employs higher-order parametric interface geometry for local normal-velocity extension, aiming to achieve second-order accurate interface evolution on fixed Cartesian grids. The resulting velocity field is employed in conservative geometric advection using a directionally split Eulerian-implicit and Lagrangian-explicit (EI-LE) scheme, while the reconstructed interface provides the geometric information required for curvature evaluation and the ghost-fluid finite-difference discretisation of sharp interfacial Dirichlet conditions. Static reconstruction and reversible-vortex advection tests demonstrate higher-order interface geometry and approximately second-order transport convergence, with mass conservation to the chosen tolerance on refined grids. Prescribed normal-velocity and curvature-dependent propagation tests establish near second-order convergence. Coupled Stefan benchmarks involving capillarity and attachment kinetics demonstrate approximately second-order thermal convergence and decreasing interface errors under mesh refinement. The results establish a geometric formulation connecting conservative VOF transport, local normal-velocity extension, and sharp Stefan conditions for evolving interfaces.

items.title: Solubility and Diffusion of Hydrogen Isotopes and Helium in Molten FLiBe
items.summary: Tritium produced in molten 2LiF-BeF$_2$ (FLiBe) may dissolve as T$_2$ or as TF, which differ greatly in solubility. Permeation experiments give a solubility close to that of HF and a flux proportional to the square root of the T$_2$ pressure, which has usually been taken as evidence of dissociation. We have developed a fixed-charge classical potential for FLiBe containing atomic tritium, T$_2$, TF, the hydride ion T$^-$ and helium, fitted only to periodic DFT calculations for hydrogen. The nuclei are classical, so the solubilities apply to all hydrogen isotopes. The host reproduces the measured density and neutron structure factor but is too fluid close to the liquidus. The calculated solubilities of T$_2$ and TF agree with experiment, and neither molecule dissociates in the melt. Because TF is much more soluble, it holds most of the dissolved tritium unless the salt is strongly reducing, and at constant redox potential its concentration varies with the square root of the T$_2$ pressure, which accounts for the permeation results without dissociation. Helium does not change the solubility of T$_2$: a helium bubble in the melt takes up T$_2$ as its Henry constant predicts, while TF is enriched at the bubble surface. T$_2$ diffuses somewhat faster than measured, and TF and T$^-$ two to three times more slowly than T$_2$.

items.title: High-order Crank-Nicolson method via diagonal Padé factorization
items.summary: We present a numerical method to solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation at arbitrary order of accuracy in the time step, particularly well suited for tridiagonal Hamilton operators. The method is based on a factorization of the diagonal Padé approximants of the matrix exponential into products of linear factors, which preserves tridiagonal matrix structure at every time step and yields a propagator of order 2q in the time step at a cost of O(qN) operations. The propagator is exactly unitary by construction, and at lowest order q=1 it reduces to the standard Crank-Nicolson algorithm. We further extend the method to any Hamiltonian admitting a decomposition into a sum of tridiagonal or diagonal operators via high-order split-operator techniques (McLachlan, 2022), retaining O(qN) scaling at each time step. We also analytically show and numerically verify that the precision is dictated by the split-operator method. This covers a broad range of physically relevant cases, including higher-dimensional systems, higher-order spatial discretizations, and non-separable potentials.

items.title: Detecting False Self-Consistency in Density-Functional Calculations
items.summary: Density-functional calculations feed materials databases and machine-learning models, and are declared converged when energy changes and residuals fall below thresholds. We show that these criteria, and even the agreement of independent optimizers, can accept a state from which the energy still descends or whose Hamiltonian is inconsistent with the energy. A variational formulation of self-consistency in the space of Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians yields a descent probe that exposes lower states accessible from a returned solution, and a frozen-orbital Janak test detects such an inconsistency. Both apply to any code without modification. In VASP, a UO$_2$ PBE+$U$ calculation converges 1.46 eV above a lower state, and CoO and FeO converge as metals 0.8-0.9 eV above insulating states. In a census of 339 converged calculations on tungsten-free Materials Project structures, recomputed with a modified static protocol, 57 (16.8%) show energy decreases above the threshold, 49 without an initial energy rise exceeding the tolerance.

items.title: ThermoSight: From Appearance to Internal Thermofluid Fields via Physics-Guided Neural Reconstruction
items.summary: Most neural reconstruction methods focus on reproducing scene appearance, yet inferring physical states from visual observations is essential for machine understanding of the physical world. Reconstructing the internal temperature and soot fields of radiating thermofluids such as flames is challenging yet essential for improving energy efficiency and assessing heat exposure and fire spread. In flames, temperature and soot concentration jointly govern visible emission, and soot self-absorption alters the light that reaches each camera. With limited views, changes in the two fields can offset one another in the recorded RGB images, making temperature and soot difficult to disentangle. ThermoSight, a physics-guided neural framework for scientific imaging, jointly reconstructs continuous three-dimensional temperature and soot volume fraction fields from limited calibrated flame images without field-level ground truth during optimization. A differentiable spectral model links these fields to measured RGB through thermal emission, self-absorption, and calibrated camera responses. Temperature-dependent emission spectra and wavelength-dependent attenuation constrain shared fields across RGB channels, reducing temperature-soot ambiguity. Chromaticity consistency, observation-derived spatial constraints, and soot regularization complement intensity fitting. In a synthetic ablation, wavelength-resolved attenuation reduces temperature RMSE in the hot, sooty region from 234 to 112 K relative to a three-channel approximation, with nearly identical RGB PSNR (65.23 vs. 65.24 dB). Measured data yield coherent fields and competitive RGB reconstructions. These results demonstrate that physics-guided neural fields recover interpretable internal physical quantities beyond visually consistent appearance.

items.title: Size and shape of condensing steam jets and plumes
items.summary: Droplet-laden cloud dynamics emerge from coupled phase transitions and turbulent mixing. Combining experiments and mean-field theory, we establish scaling laws for steam-injected clouds in unsaturated air seeded with condensation nuclei. Depending on whether the cloud is confined to the initial momentum-dominated zone of the jet or extends into the buoyancy-dominated plume, two asymptotic regimes arise. In the momentum regime, cloud dimensions scale with the injector radius. In the buoyancy regime, size follows a $\dot{m}^{2/5}$ scaling, where $\dot{m}$ is the injected steam mass flow rate. Assuming interdroplet air remains humidity saturated, our mean-field analysis predicts cloud persistence governed by enthalpy and humidity mixing. These findings bridge microphysical processes and macroscale dynamics, offering a quantitative framework for atmospheric cloud evolution.

items.title: Directionality of low-energy electron recoils in the CYGNO experiment
items.summary: Electron-recoil directionality can help distinguish solar-neutrino interactions from backgrounds and, together with recoil-energy measurements and three-dimensional tracking, enable neutrino-energy spectroscopy. We study the reconstruction of the initial direction of low-energy electron recoils in the CYGNO optical time-projection chamber, focusing on the 50 L LIME prototype and its high-granularity scientific CMOS (sCMOS) readout. A dedicated algorithm identifies the interaction point from the asymmetry of the track light distribution and estimates the recoil direction from the early portion of the ionization trail, before multiple scattering erases most of the directional information. The method is characterized with a detailed Monte Carlo simulation of electron recoils and detector response. Samples spanning 15 keV to 70 keV are used to optimize the algorithm parameters by minimizing the width of the reconstructed-minus-true projected-angle distribution. The projected angular response is modeled by two Gaussian components that account for its dependence on track inclination. The narrower component, associated with favorable projections approximately parallel to the Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) plane, has a width that improves from about $20^\circ$ near 20 keV to about $12^\circ$ at 60 keV. We also quantify the fraction of events in the correctly reconstructed angular core and discuss the dominant limitations of a camera-only two-dimensional measurement.

items.title: iPINN for Broadband CARS Phase Retrieval: A Framework for Function Approximation and Inverse Modeling Problems in Nonlinear Spectroscopy
items.summary: Broadband coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (BCARS) records chemically specific vibrational spectra, but the measured signal mixes the resonant, Raman-like response of the sample with a non-resonant background that changes from one measurement to the next. Recovering the resonant response, known as phase retrieval, is an ill-posed inverse problem. We present iPINN, an inverse physics-informed neural network that predicts the positions, amplitudes, and widths of Lorentzian vibrational bands directly from a BCARS spectrum. A transformer network estimates these band parameters, and a differentiable analytical model of the resonant susceptibility rebuilds the Raman-like spectrum from them as a sum of physically defined bands. We train the network on simulated spectra in which the bands of each reference compound stay fixed while the shape and strength of the background and the noise vary. Training also encourages similar band predictions for the same compound across these variations. On a public benchmark of toluene and dimethyl sulfoxide spectra, the network reached a mean absolute error about one third of that of the best of five deep-learning baselines. Its error for dimethyl sulfoxide stayed nearly constant across three noise levels. We also used 28 spectra of seven solvents, recorded at four focal depths with different background strengths. For five of the seven solvents, the mean absolute error changed little with depth, while it varied more for the other two. These results indicate that this approach keeps phase retrieval stable for most of the tested solvents when the background changes.

items.title: Cavity Control of Emission Dynamics from Spin Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
items.summary: Optically addressable negatively charged boron vacancy ($\mathrm{V_B^-}$) defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are promising for quantum sensing at room temperature. The two-dimensional structure of hBN allows direct access to the local environment, enabling proximal sensing of target materials. However, its broadband emission and low quantum yield hinder efficient light-matter interaction, and the coupling of $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ optical dipoles to confined cavity fields remains poorly understood. In this study, we integrate $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defects with a tunable plano-concave microcavity, achieving three-dimensional optical confinement. This approach yields photoluminescence (PL) enhancement and cavity-modified optical decay dynamics, providing insights into the orientation of the $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect dipole. Time-resolved PL measurements identify a distinct fast decay component, suggesting a complex dipole geometry for the defects. Therefore, a tilted optical dipole model is considered to attribute the fast and slow decay components to in-plane and out-of-plane dipole contributions, respectively. Additionally, optically detected magnetic resonance and excitation-polarisation-dependent PL measurements provide further insights into local symmetry breaking and potential optical dipole configurations. These results highlight the role of optical dipole orientation in $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect-cavity coupling.

items.title: Scintillator-Based Event-Mode Neutron Imaging with Timepix4 Readout
items.summary: Scintillator-based event-mode neutron imaging is emerging as a powerful approach to neutron radiography. Unlike conventional integrating-mode neutron imaging, which accumulates scintillation light during an exposure, event reconstruction estimates neutron-event positions and arrival times from time-stamped optical responses. We investigated this approach using a self-developed Timepix4-based optical readout system, image-formation analysis, and beam experiments at the China Spallation Neutron Source under different scintillator and optical configurations. The analysis explains how event localization can reduce image blur associated with the spatial extent of individual scintillation responses. Under the same 0.35$\times$ optical configuration, event reconstruction improved the spatial resolution from 164.2 to 91.9 $μ$m at 10% modulation transfer function (MTF), while a 2.1$\times$ configuration with a $\mathrm{Gd_2O_2S:Tb}$ scintillator achieved 26.1 $μ$m at the same MTF threshold. Following event reconstruction and rejection of single-photon reconstructed events, the mean peak-normalized spectral response in the 6-8 angstrom out-of-band interval decreased by 85.4% relative to the raw-pixel wavelength-count spectrum, indicating reduced afterglow-related spectral background. Under the tested pulsed-beam conditions, the maximum instantaneous pixel-hit rate per pixel was approximately four times its time-averaged value, providing an experimental basis for assessing readout requirements at higher neutron flux. Conventional radiography resolved structural details, while energy-selective imaging enhanced the contrast between materials with similar broadband transmission and Bragg-edge imaging revealed crystallographic features in steel. These results demonstrate the imaging-quality benefits and capabilities of scintillator-based event-mode neutron imaging.

items.title: Reduced Density Matrices from Renormalization-Group Flows
items.summary: We reconstruct complete one- and two-body reduced density matrices (RDMs) by a single collective backward evolution along the in-medium similarity renormalization-group flow. Benchmarks show improved accuracy and physical consistency over conventional elementwise evolution. In neutron matter, two-body RDMs reveal spin-triplet dominance in interaction-dependent Fermi-sea depletion trends. Meanwhile, the forward-backward energy difference provides an internal diagnostic of many-body truncation errors, whose quantification remains challenging in nuclear $ab\ initio$ calculations.

items.title: High-quality intrinsic circular dichroism in silicon-based bound states in the continuum metasurfaces via strong coupling
items.summary: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) can significantly enhance spin-selective light-matter interactions. However, current BIC metasurfaces generally rely on single or multiple chiral BIC modes to enhance circular dichroism (CD), limiting their application in functional integrated devices. This paper proposes a method that utilizes the strong coupling effect in BIC metasurfaces to achieve intrinsic CD with both a high quality factor (Q-factor) and high efficiency. The metasurface is designed as a silicon-based cross-shaped nanohole array, which can simultaneously support a TM-like BIC mode and a TE-like guided-mode resonance (GMR) mode. By introducing under-etching to break the out-of-plane symmetry and tuning the in-plane asymmetry parameter, strong coupling between the quasi-BIC (QBIC) mode and the GMR mode can be induced, thereby achieving near-perfect intrinsic CD with a high Q-factor. In the strong-coupling region, the resonant wavelengths of the QBIC and GMR modes exhibit anti-crossing behavior, while the imaginary parts of the eigenfrequency cross; the corresponding Rabi splitting energy reaches a minimum of 3.16 meV, and the induced intrinsic CD achieves a maximum of 0.995 at a wavelength of 1653.9 nm, with a high Q-factor of 1083. The evolution of far-field polarization singularities shows that, under strong coupling, the Γ point corresponds to a left-handed circular polarization singularity (C-point). Furthermore, the strong-coupling-induced CD exhibits good robustness. Even under considerable variations in structural parameters, the high-Q and high-efficiency CD response is maintained. This method offers a novel design strategy for integrated chiral photonic devices and holds promise for applications in areas such as chiral sensing, chiral lasers, and nonlinear chiral optics.

items.title: Material Tailored Multispectral Magnetization via the Inverse Faraday Effect in Tunable Coaxial Nanoantenna
items.summary: All-optical control of magnetization via the Inverse Faraday Effect presents a transformative pathway for ultrafast high-density data storage and nanoscale spintronics. However, unlocking its full potential requires moving beyond traditional gold-centric, narrowband constraints. In this study, we present a comprehensive theoretical framework evaluating IFE-driven static magnetic field generation across a diverse library of plasmonic materials, including gold, silver, copper, aluminum, and titanium nitride. Using a dimensionally tunable coaxial nanoantenna, we map the optomagnetic response across the deep-ultraviolet to near-infrared spectrum. Our findings reveal highly distinct, material-dependent behaviors: aluminum uniquely sustains robust magnetization in the deep-UV, whereas silver, copper, and gold exhibit superior efficiency at longer wavelengths.
