Although second-order optimization offers enhanced robustness, explicitly constructing the full Hessian matrix is computationally prohibitive for large-scale systems. In this work, we bypass this bottleneck by introducing an analytical Hessian-vector product kernel designed for arbitrary compositions of linear maps. This two-pass algorithm leverages a recursive tangent-state propagation with a bounded virtual bond dimension to guarantee scalability. We demonstrate its use within a Riemannian trust-region method for quantum circuit compression. For time-evolution circuits with up to 17 layers, our method reproduces previous results in substantially fewer iterations, reducing wall-time by up to an order of magnitude. For deeper quantum circuits, incorporating second-order derivative information yields a better solution, reducing the final error to less than half that of the first-order result.

items.title: Radial Evolution of a Corotating Interaction Region from a High-Resolution MHD Simulation
items.summary: Corotating interaction regions (CIRs) are large-scale structures formed by fast--slow solar wind interaction, playing a crucial role in heliospheric dynamics and space weather. However, the evolution of individual CIRs and their full three-dimensional morphology remain poorly understood. We investigate the radial evolution of a single CIR using a high-resolution simulation combined with a backmapping method. The simulation reproduces the major plasma and magnetic signatures observed by Wind at 1~AU and by MAVEN and Tianwen-1 at $\sim$1.6~AU. The CIR exhibits a warped, shell-like spiral structure tilted relative to the heliospheric current sheet, consistent with theoretical predictions. During its developing stage, geometric changes are modest, and the radial scalings of velocity ($V_r \propto r^{0.02}$), density ($N \propto r^{-2.00}$), magnetic field ($B_{\rm total} \propto r^{-1.74}$), and temperature ($T \propto r^{-0.97}$) are comparable to those of the background solar wind. In the mature stage, the CIR drifts in longitude and expands toward high latitudes, while its longitudinal and latitudinal widths decrease with distance. The full-domain scalings change markedly to $V_r \propto r^{0.13}$, $N \propto r^{-1.91}$, $B_{\rm total} \propto r^{0.35}$, and $T \propto r^{-0.52}$, differing from both the background wind and the ecliptic-plane CIR. This study quantifies the radial evolution of a CIR from formation to maturity and highlights the importance of its three-dimensional structure in characterizing its morphology and dynamics.

items.title: High-power photoconductive THz emitters for fast parallel electro-optic detection
items.summary: The terahertz (THz) spectral region is highly attractive for imaging because it penetrates many optically opaque materials and can distinguish them by composition. THz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) is ideally suited for spectroscopic imaging, since it records the full electric-field waveform and thus broadband amplitude and phase information. Translating this capability into fast, wide-field imaging has remained a major challenge, largely because the low average power of conventional TDS sources forces a trade-off between acquisition speed, field of view and sensitivity. Here we demonstrate a fast hyperspectral THz camera based on parallel electro-optic sampling, driven by a large-area photoconductive emitter delivering a record-high 38.3 mW of average power at 400 kHz. A numerical model reproduces the measured emitter scaling and shows that, under 515 nm excitation, electron transfer into low-mobility satellite valleys delays radiation screening, allowing higher pump fluences before its effect dominates. The camera records the full THz waveform, with ~1.5 THz bandwidth, simultaneously at 145,000 pixels over a ~14.5 mm2 field of view at 2 Hz. These results establish high-average-power THz-TDS as a route to broadband, high-speed imaging, for inline material-resolved inspection and for spectroscopic imaging of irreversible, second-timescale processes such as hydration in biologically relevant systems.

items.title: Data-Driven Design Optimization of Streaming-Potential-Mediated Electrokinetic Transport of Viscoelastic Fluids in Microchannels
items.summary: Streaming-potential-mediated transport of viscoelastic fluids has attracted research attention owing to its applications in electrokinetic energy conversion and microfluidic transport. Existing analytical and semi-analytical models in published literature provide valuable physical insights, but require repeated numerical evaluations for exploring large design spaces and identifying the optimal operating conditions. In this work, a surrogate-assisted framework is developed for rapid design optimization of pressure-driven electrokinetic transport of simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluids in a slit microchannel. A high-fidelity numerical database is generated over a broad range of governing dimensionless parameters, which includes the zeta potential, the Debye parameter, the Dukhin number, and the viscoelastic parameter. A Neural Network surrogate model is subsequently trained to accurately approximate the nonlinear relationship between the governing parameters and the streaming potential, while the volumetric flow rate and hydroelectric energy conversion efficiency were calculated from closed form equation by using the streaming potential predicted by the surrogate. This is coupled with a multi-objective optimization strategy to identify operating conditions that simultaneously maximize energy conversion efficiency and volumetric flow rate. The proposed methodology can significantly accelerate parametric exploration compared with repeated numerical simulations across different parameters and provides practical design guidelines for electrokinetic microfluidic devices. The study demonstrates the potential of combining computational fluid mechanics with data-driven surrogate modeling for efficient engineering design and optimization.

items.title: Hydration-induced local diffusivity heterogeneity modulates aqueous $H_2+OH$ reaction kinetics
items.summary: At room temperature, a Kramers reaction rate calculated with homogeneous solvent friction exceeds the measured rate of the aqueous reaction $H_2 + OH -> H + H_2O$ by about an order of magnitude. We show that spatially correlated hydration-induced diffusivity fluctuations increase effective friction and suppress the predicted escape rate. Estimates based on hydration-shell properties bring the theoretical rate closer to experiment. The suppression weakens with increasing temperature, linking local solvent heterogeneity to activated aqueous reaction kinetics.

items.title: Food co-purchasing networks encode geographic disparities in cardiometabolic health
items.summary: Unhealthy diets are a major driver of cardiometabolic disease, yet the geospatial structure of dietary behavior and its links to population health remain poorly understood. While large-scale retail transaction data offer a unique view of population dietary behavior, conventional approaches reduce purchases to isolated items, not accounting for how foods are actually combined. Here, we analyze 51 million grocery receipts across 95 Danish municipalities using a statistically validated bipartite network framework to isolate co-purchases that product popularity alone cannot explain. We find that, although municipalities buy largely the same products, their co-purchasing networks reorganize along a continuous urban-to-peripheral gradient in how those products are combined. The network backbone can be resolved into modular dietary communities whose local cohesion allows us to predict cardiometabolic prescriptions, explaining a quarter to a half of the variance left after sociodemographic adjustment, beyond what product prevalence alone accounts for. Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) show no spatial gradient in prevalence and are located at the network periphery, where they share baskets with fresh foods but rarely form the combinations that hold the network together. Taken together, our findings show that geographic dietary differences are encoded not only in what people purchase, but in how foods are systematically combined within shopping baskets, offering a scalable network approach for population nutritional epidemiology.

items.title: Quantum Field Approach to Relativistic Turbulence
items.summary: The goal of this work is to apply quantum field theory methods to a typical relativistic hydrodynamic model. We shall take as representative model an Israel-Stewart framework, where the energy-momentum conservation laws for a conformal invariant fluid are supplemented by a Cattaneo-Maxwell equation for its viscous energy-momentum tensor. In these models the viscous energy-momentum tensor relaxes to its Landau-Lifshitz value on a finite time scale. We assume the parameters of the model depend on the speed of light $c$ in such a way that as $c\to\infty$ the fluid becomes an incompressible fluid obeying the Navier-Stokes equations. We show that because the relativistic model must be hyperbolic, each mode behaves as an overdamped oscillator with two decay constants, one of which diverges as $c\to\infty$. Thus for finite $c$ there are two basic patterns, one which contains only slowly decaying modes, and reproduces Kolmogorov turbulence when $c\to\infty$, and another made of fast decaying modes only. Each flow pattern is associated to definite relations among the velocity and viscous energy tensor correlators.

items.title: An implicit high-order flux reconstruction method with logarithmic variables for hypersonic flows in thermochemical nonequilibrium
items.summary: Simulating hypersonic flows in thermochemical nonequilibrium requires solving the Navier-Stokes equations for reacting, possibly ionised mixtures. Compact high-order computations of viscous two-temperature air flows on unstructured grids have not gone beyond P = 2. We present an implicit Flux Reconstruction (FR) method for such flows, built on three ingredients. First, the solver stores and updates the logarithms of the partial densities and temperatures, making every state admissible without a positivity limiter and, for ionised mixtures, imposing charge neutrality consistently with the implicit update. Second, shocks are captured by subcell order blending, extended to steady implicit computations on curved Gauss-Legendre meshes, with second-order subcell blending in subsonic regions and an automatic freeze of the blending near convergence. Third, a pseudo-transient Newton method with a physicality-limited update and automatic CFL control reaches steady state from the free stream with the same settings at every order. The design order is verified up to sixth order on a manufactured solution for five-species air with finite-rate chemistry and vibrational relaxation. Steady viscous solutions up to sixth order are obtained for five- and eleven-species air on the High Enthalpy shock tunnel Göttingen (HEG) cylinder and for eleven-species air on the RAM-C II vehicle. To our knowledge, this work gives the first design-order verification of a high-order method with finite-rate air chemistry and vibrational relaxation, and the first high-order finite-element-type computations of viscous eleven-species, two-temperature air. On the HEG cylinder, the stagnation-point heat flux is within 2% of finite-volume references and within 6% of the measurements, with a comparable number of degrees of freedom to second-order finite-volume computations but on meshes with 20 to 40 times fewer elements.

items.title: Parity nonconservation in hyperfine transitions of hydrogen-like muonic atoms
items.summary: We investigate parity nonconservation (PNC) in the $2s_{1/2}(F=0)\leftrightarrow 2s_{1/2}(F=1)$ hyperfine transition of hydrogenlike muonic $^{13}\mathrm{C}^{5+}$ and $^{15}\mathrm{N}^{6+}$. Finite-nuclear-size effects and the Uehling potential are incorporated directly into the Dirac equation, whereas the leading kinematic-recoil and Fermi--Breit hyperfine corrections to the energy levels are treated to first order in perturbation theory. The spin-independent PNC amplitude is evaluated using hyperfine-resolved energy denominators and is proportional to the weak charge $Q_W$. The spin-dependent amplitude is proportional to $κ=κ_a+κ_Z$, where $κ_a$ and $κ_Z$ denote the nuclear-anapole and direct neutral-current couplings, respectively. For absorption we obtain the PNC degree $\mathcal P_{\rm abs}(^{13}\mathrm{C})=-5.9\times10^{-8}Q_W +1.3\times10^{-5}κ$ and $\mathcal P_{\rm abs}(^{15}\mathrm{N})=-8.8\times10^{-9}Q_W -8.1\times10^{-6}κ$. Nuclear-structure calculations indicate that $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ has enhanced relative sensitivity to direct $Z^0$-boson exchange, whereas the spin-dependent interaction in $^{15}\mathrm{N}$ is expected to be dominated by the nuclear-anapole contribution. In an idealized cavity-polarimetry model, a column density of order $10^{15}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ is required; however, the production of metastable hydrogenlike muonic ions remains the principal experimental challenge.

items.title: Neural Surrogates for Tabulated Nuclear Equations of State in Core-Collapse Supernova Simulations
items.summary: Large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations rely on tabulated nuclear equations of state (EOSs), whose memory requirements can become a practical constraint in massively parallel calculations. We explore a compact alternative by replacing the tabulated thermodynamic mapping with a neural-network surrogate, using the Lattimer--Swesty EOS as a representative reference model. The surrogate directly predicts pressure, sound speed, and effective adiabatic index from $(\log ρ, \log e, Y_e)$ and accurately reconstructs the nonlinear thermodynamic structure of the EOS, including its behavior across phase-transition regions. It reproduces one-dimensional shock-tube solutions with hydrodynamic errors at the $\sim 10^{-3}$ level under different thermodynamic conditions and yields hydrostatic equilibrium configurations closely matching those obtained with the reference EOS. We find that smaller regression errors do not necessarily yield better hydrodynamic performance, demonstrating the importance of hydrodynamic validation in surrogate model selection. A compact network with only $\sim 10^4$ parameters retains this accuracy while reducing the memory required to store the EOS from $\sim 160$ MB to $\sim 100$ KB, corresponding to a reduction by a factor of $\sim 1500$. The surrogate also remains stable through collapse, bounce, shock formation, and post-bounce evolution in a one-dimensional adiabatic core-collapse calculation. These results demonstrate the potential of compact neural EOS surrogates for reducing memory requirements in large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations.

items.title: Modeling stellar convective transport with plumes : II. Transport Properties of Locally and Non-locally driven Convection
items.summary: We perform three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations of two idealized convection setups: a cooling-driven model (Model C) and an entropy-gradient-driven model (Model S). The two setups exhibit clear differences: while Model S develops large, relatively stationary eddies excited at depth, Model C is dominated near the surface by intermittent plume-like downflows that produce broad non-Gaussian velocity distributions and a turbulent energy flux that exceeds that in Model S by nearly an order of magnitude in the upper convection zone. Conventional gradient-diffusion (GD) closures reproduce the transport in Model S but significantly underestimate it in Model C, demonstrating that the plume-dominated transport realized in our cooling-driven setup cannot be reproduced by a local, gradient-based model. To address this, we introduce a Time-Space Double Averaging (TSDA) method that extracts coherent fluctuations, yielding a diagnostic variable $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}$ that peaks where the flux is largest. Building on this insight, we propose a modified GD closure in which the turbulent diffusivity is corrected by a plume-mediated term, achieving quantitative agreement with simulation results. Although the closure requires a calibrated model parameter and a careful choice of the averaging window, it provides a physically transparent framework that links coherent plume dynamics to mean-field transport and offers a pathway toward improved subgrid models for non-equilibrium stellar convection zones.

items.title: Porosification of the dielectric layer in alternating-current electroluminescence devices enables high-resolution tactile imaging
items.summary: Vision-based tactile sensing enables high-resolution contact perception, yet bulky optical architectures consume valuable space and constrain the functional design of dexterous robotic hands. Here we introduce a self-emissive tactile imaging strategy based on alternating-current electroluminescence (ACEL) devices, in which a compressible porous dielectric encodes contact pressure into spatial emission patterns without external illumination or discrete sensing pixels. We identify a nonlinear capacitance-dependent emission window that provides a basis for tunable pressure-to-light conversion. Pore-size engineering further suppresses local emission deficiencies, reducing spatial intensity variation by nearly ninefold and enabling faithful imaging of contact features down to 100 μm. The continuous electroluminescent interface also reproduces complex contact patterns without computational reconstruction of electrical fields. Direct lamination of the ACEL device onto a complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) image sensor is expected to enable compact contact imaging in an assembly less than 5 mm thick, substantially thinner than conventional vision-based tactile sensors. This approach could reduce the space required for high-resolution tactile imaging, offering greater design freedom for dexterous robotic hands.

items.title: Absence of binding for the helium anion
items.summary: We study the helium anion in the nonrelativistic Coulomb model with an infinitely massive nucleus and spin-$\frac12$ electrons. We prove the absence of binding, with $E^{\mathrm{F}}(3,2)=E^{\mathrm{F}}(2,2)$ and no three-electron ground state. A decomposition relative to the helium ground state and completion of the square reduce the problem to a one-dimensional variational inequality.

items.title: Data-driven non-contiguous photon-energy groups for fast multigroup radiation transport in line-dominated plasmas
items.summary: Radiation transport in line-dominated plasmas, such as extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light source plasma, laser-fusion hohlraums, and stellar interiors, needs too many photon-energy groups for accurate radiation-hydrodynamic simulations. Our data-driven method assigns the bins of an opacity table to $K$ non-contiguous groups with fixed spectral shapes that never couple. Existing multigroup codes can use it by replacing the opacity table.In a radiation-hydrodynamic code, 30 such groups replaced 151 conventional groups; the energy conversion efficiency from laser to EUV changed by less than 0.5\% in absolute value.

items.title: Exploring Energy Landscapes for Functional Materials: Ga vacancies in $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$
items.summary: Energy landscape exploration requires extensive energy and force evaluations, making efficient access to interatomic potentials an important practical challenge. We present a persistent socket interface that connects the landscape exploration tools in the GMIN, OPTIM, and PATHSAMPLE programs to potentials available through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). The persistent design keeps both the calculator and socket connection active throughout the search, avoiding repeated initialisation. We apply this framework to understand and predict the properties of Ga vacancies in $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ using two NequIP-based potentials, and construct kinetic transition networks describing complex vacancy configurations and migration pathways. Temperature-dependent analysis of the dominant paths reveals how the most probable migration sequence can change, with the mechanism governed by global properties of the network, rather than simply the highest energy barrier. Visualisation, mean first-passage times, and heat capacities enable us to connect the organisation of the landscape to relaxation time scales and thermodynamic observables. The interface extends energy landscape methods to ASE-compatible atomistic models, providing a general framework for combining global optimisation, transition state searches, kinetic network analysis, and thermodynamic characterisation with recent developments in machine-learned interatomic potentials.

items.title: Numerical Integration Instabilities in Likelihood Fits: Mechanisms and Remedies
items.summary: Numerical instabilities in the normalization of probability density functions can produce artificially lower negative log-likelihood (NLL) values than the true minimum of a likelihood fit, even when the resulting fit provides a poorer description of the data. Motivated by anomalously low NLL values found in non-converged fits associated with a recent CMS search for fully charmed tetraquark candidates, we use a pseudo-dataset generated from a likelihood model based on that analysis to investigate how numerical integration can yield unreliable normalization results, how these errors affect likelihood minimization, and how they can be addressed. We find that, even at fixed integration tolerance, the stopping decision of a numerical integrator can change with the fit parameters, introducing discontinuities in the normalization integrals that propagate to the likelihood surface. Such discontinuities can trap the minimizer at a numerical step and yield an artificially lower NLL. Tightening the integration tolerance mitigates these numerical discontinuities, while adaptive integration methods, such as Gauss--Kronrod quadrature, can also improve the numerical stability. A more severe failure occurs when the integration grid cannot adequately resolve a sharply localized contribution. In this case, the integrator may satisfy its estimated-error criterion despite substantially underestimating the normalization, allowing the minimizer to enter a region with an artificially low NLL. Tightening integration tolerances or using alternative adaptive integration methods does not necessarily resolve sharply localized contributions. We demonstrate that a suitable variable transformation can improve their numerical resolution, yielding more accurate normalization integrals and restoring fit convergence.

items.title: Tunable topological droplets on supercoiled DNA under tension
items.summary: DNA--protein co-condensation is an important regulatory mechanism for gene expression and repair. For straight DNA under constant stretching forces, co-condensation is ``all-or-nothing'': above a critical force, condensates are prevented from nucleating, while below it the entire molecule collapses into a droplet. Here we show by coarse-grained simulations and analytic theory that DNA supercoiling mechanically differentiates the condensation substrate: DNA plectonemes constitute force-insulated pockets on which condensates can nucleate even above the critical force. The size of the resulting droplets is tunable through the applied force and linking number. Surface tension drives the coarsening of multiple plectoneme-associated condensates into a single topological droplet. Magnetic tweezers experiments with spermine reproduce both the force-dependent collapse and the supercoiling-dependent condensation.

items.title: Study of Randomness in Quantum Random Number Generator using Bayesian Neural Networks
items.summary: We propose a Bayesian neural network (BNN) framework to quantify the intrinsic (aleatoric) uncertainty in a continuous-variable quantum random number generator (CV-QRNG). This provides a direct data-driven measure of the QRNG's randomness generation. The BNN is trained on raw homodyne voltage time-series data from a fiber-coupled vacuum-fluctuation QRNG (VFQRNG). For each voltage data segment, the network predicts a Gaussian distribution (mean and variance) for the next sample, and the ensemble-averaged predicted variance is used as a diagnostic of entropy-related behavior under assumptions of our quantum source model. Thus, the predicted variance serves as a BNN model-based monitor of the randomness-generation process. We validate that the BNN metric increases with the local-oscillator (LO) power, consistent with theoretical min-entropy (extractable randomness). We also show the metric is sensitive to practical imperfections, coarse-graining (simulating limited analog-to-digital converter (ADC) sampling) or reducing ADC bit depth causes a clear drop in predicted aleatoric uncertainty, consistent with the source min-entropic model. These results establish the BNN-based metric as a complementary, physically motivated diagnostic tool for QRNG characterization. Unlike conventional tests (e.g. autocorrelation) that miss hardware issues like low ADC resolution, our method provides a direct real-time monitor of the VFRNG performance. Therefore, this metric is useful for real-time monitoring of CV-QRNG conditions, including drifts and other imperfections.

items.title: Large-scale patterns of small-scale vorticity interactions foster moist convection during cyclogenesis
items.summary: Understanding the self-organization of small-scale moist convection at synoptic scales during tropical cyclogenesis is essential. We examine the role of vorticity interactions in dynamical organization of moist convection during cyclogenesis in the Bay of Bengal. Using time-varying complex networks, we encode local vorticity correlations between nodes (locations), only within a spatial proximity of sub-meso length scales. Links are established using short-time correlation of vorticity fluctuations. Spatial patches of high network connectivity depict regions of locally coherent vorticity dynamics. We find that various patches of high network connectivity arrange into extended structures forming identifiable large-scale patterns. Examining the co-evolution of moist thermodynamics parameters with local vorticity coherence, we discover a unique spatial correlation between the convective processes occurring at far away locations, owing to self-organization. We find that such spatial correlation are evident only for depressions that form cyclones, and not otherwise. We discover the physical mechanism of self-organization using modal analysis of network connectivity and vorticity budgets. In regions identified as most influential by the modal analysis, we find that vertical vorticity is enhanced locally as well as advected horizontally outwards to other locations. Such horizontal advection of vertical vorticity induces nonlocal interactions and couples small-scale convective processes across a large domain. We show that, vertical vorticity transported from regions of high convective potential help sustain strong updrafts and weaken convective inhibition in other regions. Thus, spatial interdependence is introduced between small-scale convective processes at different locations, thus explaining the self-organization of moist convection during cyclogenesis.

items.title: Yb/Sr optical clock comparison at 2.08E-18 uncertainty over a 1350-km fiber link
items.summary: Redefining the International system of Units (SI) second requires independent frequency-ratio measurements between clocks based on different laboratories, with an overall uncertainty below 5E-18, to validate individual clock evaluations through consistency checks. Reaching this uncertainty over long distances has remained challenging. So far, comparisons at this level have been achieved only a few times, between co-located clocks, and their results disagree markedly. Previous high-precision comparisons have therefore been limited to local or kilometre-scale links. Here we compare a ytterbium optical lattice clock in Wuhan with a strontium optical lattice clock in Shanghai over a phase-stabilized fiber link spanning 1350 km, and determine the Yb/Sr frequency ratio to be 1.207 507 039 343 337 716 0(26), with a Bayesian statistical uncertainty of 1.14E-18 and a total uncertainty of 2.18E-18. To our knowledge, this is the first intercity long distance frequency-ratio measurement, whose total uncertainty reaches the level required by the redefinition roadmap. The measured ratio exhibits a significant correlation with Earth tides and its response agree with the model within the statistical uncertainty. At intercity scale, this comparison demonstrates the capability of an optical-clock network for frequency comparison and Earths gravitational-potential sensing, a key step toward a wide-area optical-clock network.

items.title: A high-order ghost-point immersed boundary method with auxiliary differential equations for time-domain impedance walls
items.summary: This paper presents a method for performing time-domain simulations of a sound field interacting with a wall having a locally-reacting impedance. The linearized Euler equations are solved using a high-order finite difference method. To impose the impedance condition on a wall that is not aligned with the Cartesian grid, an immersed boundary method (IBM) is employed. It relies on a ghost-point approach with a normal-stencil-based reconstruction, where the impedance is accounted for via auxiliary differential equations (ADEs), which are integrated using the same Runge-Kutta scheme as the governing equations. The method is validated against semi-analytical solutions for a pressure pulse reflecting off a flat or cylindrical wall with an impedance corresponding to a mass-spring-damper system. The cylindrical case solution is derived in the appendix. The measured convergence order is approximately 4 for a flat wall and just slighlty smaller for a curved wall. Long-term stability is verified by the diffraction of a monopole by a cylinder.

items.title: Deriving the Continuous $β$-FPUT Model for Decayless Solar Coronal Oscillations Directly from Resistive MHD
items.summary: We present an analytical framework deriving the fluid-continuum $β$-Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou ($β$-FPUT) system directly from a third-order resistive magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) expansion to explain persistent, decayless transverse oscillations observed in solar coronal loops. For a continuous wave field propagating along a longitudinal magnetic field with cross-field density variations, a multi-scale expansion demonstrates that quadratic $\mathcal{O}(2)$ advective and Maxwell tension terms vanish identically due to out-of-plane polarization symmetry. Instead, the quadratic longitudinal ponderomotive force drives field-aligned density modulations that back-react on the primary transverse wave, yielding a cubic $\mathcal{O}(3)$ restoring force. In the long-wavelength limit, the governing equations reduce to a fluid-continuum Modified Korteweg-de Vries (mKdV) system where cross-field profile variation provides the non-linear dispersive mechanism. We prove that this internal fluid mechanism establishes stable, amplitude-dependent frequency self-focusing, which phase-locks adjacent elements and prevents phase-mixing wave attenuation without requiring external steady driving parameterizations. This framework enables macro-scale coronal seismology, providing closed-form expressions to invert observed decayless wave-packet durations to compute the unresolved cross-field density gradient scale length ($L_x$) and the internal volumetric filling factor ($f_V$) without relying on traditional emission measure or spectroscopic line-ratio diagnostics. Much like famous Enrico Fermi's historic use of macro-scale displacements to estimate complex atomic explosion yields, this framework establishes a paradigm where monitoring macroscopic oscillation durations empowers observers to extract fine-scale, otherwise unresolvable waveguide properties.

items.title: Predicting local electric field in Al$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$N p-i-n photodiodes using exciton Franz-Keldysh photocurrent spectroscopy
items.summary: In AlGaN p-i-n photodiodes, reverse bias redshifts and broadens the sub-bandgap photocurrent responsivity through the eXciton Franz-Keldysh (XFK) effect, and this spectral line shape encodes the local electric field inside the device. Fitting the photocurrent spectra of two such photodiodes, with 5% and 40% Al, to an XFK absorption model at each bias yields the local voltage, $V_l$, a single parameter that sets the line shape and uniquely determines the electric-field profile inside the device. In both devices, $V_l$ varies linearly with the applied bias ($R^2 = 0.994$ and $0.998$) but changes far more slowly than the bias itself, revealing a strong local reduction of the electric field that points to non-uniform electrostatics. The slopes show that only 12.4% of the applied bias in the 5% Al device, and 45.8% in the 40% Al device, drops across the junction at the probed location. Extrapolated to zero bias, $V_l$ gives built-in voltages of 3.39 and 4.29 V, within 0.02 V of the 3.41 and 4.28 V obtained from technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulation, which validates the extracted local voltages at equilibrium. These results extend sub-bandgap photocurrent spectroscopy to AlGaN devices as an optical probe of local electrostatics, relevant to ultraviolet photodetectors and high-voltage electronics.

items.title: Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction for Binary-Encoded Fourier Single-Pixel Imaging
items.summary: Digital micromirror devices enable high-speed Fourier single-pixel imaging (Fourier-SPI), but their binary modulation introduces quantization errors that degrade the reconstructed image quality. In particular, each binarized Fourier probe contains non-target Fourier components, thereby distorting the corresponding Fourier-domain measurement. This Letter presents a Fourier domain correction framework that characterizes these errors using the Fourier-domain response matrix of the decoded binary Fourier patterns. Accordingly, a response-matrix-based Fourier-SPI measurement model is established by partitioning the matrix into components associated with the sampled and unsampled frequencies, thereby decomposing the quantization error into sampled-frequency crosstalk and unsampled-frequency leakage. This model established a generalized correction framework, termed Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction (FCLC), alongside two simplified methods: Fourier Sampled-Frequency Crosstalk Correction (FSCC) and Fourier DC Crosstalk Correction (FDCC). FSCC is implemented via an inversion-free Richardson-type iteration, whereas FDCC admits a closed-form solution. Numerical simulations and experiments across multiple binary encoding strategies reveal that the proposed framework improves reconstruction fidelity without modifying the binary patterns or acquisition process.

items.title: RECOVAR: Representation Covariances on Deep Latent Spaces for Seismic Event Detection
items.summary: Modern deep learning methods have improved earthquake detection, but the most widely used approaches typically rely on supervised learning from large labeled waveform datasets. Constructing such datasets is time-consuming and introduces biases from existing catalogs, detection pipelines, and human review, which can limit cross-dataset generalization and sensitivity to underrepresented events. We present RECOVAR, an unsupervised method for seismic event detection that can be trained directly from raw waveforms without using event/noise labels. The method uses an ensemble of convolutional autoencoders and detects events by measuring temporal alignment in their compressed latent representations through a cross-covariance-based metric. The results suggest that RECOVAR can reach the performance of supervised detectors on public benchmark datasets, remain robust under cross-dataset scenarios, and stay effective on imbalanced continuous waveform data where event-containing windows make up less than $1\%$ of the training stream. The method can also complement supervised pipelines by acting as a filter improving precision in a multi-station setting. Because the detection principle makes no domain-specific assumptions, the approach may extend to signal-detection problems beyond seismology.

items.title: Femtosecond Free-Space Time-Frequency Transfer at km/s Relative Motion with Doppler Compensation
items.summary: A global optical clock network holds great promise for a wide range of applications, including international metrology--particularly the redefinition of the ``second''--as well as navigation, geoscience, and fundamental physics. Satellite-based high-precision time-frequency dissemination is essential for realizing such a network. Despite remarkable progress in ground-based free-space simulations over high-loss channels, the Doppler effect arising from satellite motion has remained an unsolved barrier. Here we demonstrate femtosecond two-way time-frequency transfer over a 113-km free-space link under simulated Doppler shifts of up to 1.55 km/s. To overcome the Doppler barrier, we first reproduce satellite-like Doppler shifts of up to 1.55 km/s on the ground by locking a frequency comb to a broadly tunable laser. We then correct the resulting disturbances with two complementary techniques: a dual-channel sampling architecture that compensates for optical dispersion and radio frequency (RF) nonlinearity while eliminating Nyquist dead zones, and an iterative interferogram reconstruction algorithm that removes Doppler-induced distortion. After correction, residual systematic errors are within $\pm10$ fs over the full 1.55 km/s range. Using simulated medium earth orbit (MEO) and geosynchronous orbit (GSO) satellite trajectories, we achieve fractional frequency instability of $3.9\times10^{-19}$ at 4,600 s and $3.6\times10^{-19}$ at 23,600 s, respectively. This extends the operational velocity range by nearly two orders of magnitude beyond previous free-space demonstrations, removing the last major technical barrier to a global femtosecond-precision satellite-based time-frequency link.

items.title: Raman optical activity and helicity-dependent phonon splitting in chiral CoSi
items.summary: Circularly polarized Raman scattering in solids provides access to two distinct phenomena: Raman optical activity (ROA), an intensity difference between circular polarization channels, and helicity-dependent frequency splitting of chiral phonons. We observe both in the chiral topological semimetal CoSi and show that they arise through two different symmetry channels, each rendering phonon components with opposite crystal angular momenta inequivalent. Doubly degenerate E phonons exhibit a large ROA, with an approximately fourfold intensity contrast between the two cross-circular channels. The sign of this ROA reverses between the front and back {111} surfaces, while its strong suppression on {110} supports the assignment to the axial electric toroidal octupole. By contrast, triply degenerate T phonons show helicity-dependent frequency splittings, whose mode-dependent signs are reproduced by the calculated dispersion of branches with opposite crystal angular momenta, thus identifying structural chirality as their source. First-principles calculations yield a pronounced E-mode intensity asymmetry in the resonant regime, reproduce the mode-dependent signs of the T-mode splittings, and account for their magnitudes within approximately 40%. These results establish circularly polarized Raman scattering as a symmetry- and angular-momentum-resolved probe of chiral and axial multipolar symmetry in solids.

items.title: Bringing coherent closer to compute: coherent-lite multidimensional on-chip interconnect beyond 100 terabits per second
items.summary: The continued scaling of artificial intelligence (AI) demands optical interconnects that deliver higher bandwidth density within stringent electrical-bandwidth and energy budgets. Coherent optics offers a route beyond the per-lane bandwidth constraints of intensity-modulation direct-detection links, yet its receiver complexity and power overhead have largely confined its use to longer reaches. Here we bring coherent optics closer to compute by demonstrating a coherent-lite multidimensional on-chip interconnect that combines wavelength- and mode-division multiplexing with self-homodyne detection. The architecture co-transmits the local oscillator (LO) and parallel data channels within a single silicon waveguide, using polarization-division routing to preserve LO purity and support high-order modulation. Based on this principle, we develop an inverse-designed dual-polarization mode multiplexer that provides over 37 dB inter-polarization isolation across the C band in an $8 \times 6~μ$m$^2$ footprint, enabling millimetre-scale on-chip multimode routing. Without power-intensive digital carrier recovery, the architecture delivers a single-wavelength line rate of 2 Tb s$^{-1}$ and scales to an aggregate line rate of 103.96 Tb s$^{-1}$ across four modes and 100 wavelengths, using formats up to 64-ary quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM). These results extend on-chip coherent interconnects into the hundred-terabit-per-second regime, offering a scalable route to bandwidth-dense optical connectivity for next-generation computing systems.

items.title: Dynamics and Statistical Mechanics of Born-Oppenheimer Auxiliary Velocities
items.summary: In Born-Oppenheimer (BO) dynamics, auxiliary variables such as electron densities, induced polarization and electrode charges follow stationarity conditions, yet their time derivatives, such as currents, are physical observables. Using Mass-Zero constrained dynamics, we interpret these derivatives as explicit dynamical variables and derive the invariant measure giving their equilibrium statistical properties. We illustrate the framework in constant-potential molecular dynamics, where the electrode-charge velocities reproduce BO current fluctuations and the frequency-dependent admittance.

items.title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
items.summary: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

items.title: Band Engineering of Exciton Polaritons in Resonant Polaritonic Metasurfaces
items.summary: Polaritonic metasurfaces provide a versatile platform for engineering hybrid light-matter states through the interplay of optical resonances and excitonic excitations. Yet, predictive models often remain phenomenological and rely on coupled-mode equations. Here, we develop an effective Hamiltonian framework for exciton polaritons in resonant polaritonic metasurfaces, derived from a semiclassical single-pole description of excitonic polarization and a Green's-function description of guided-mode resonances. The resulting non-Hermitian Hamiltonian rigorously incorporates resonant photonic harmonics, multiple excitonic degrees of freedom, and radiative losses. The model establishes selection rules for photonic-excitonic coupling governed by orbital multipole index and polarization and identifies one bright excitonic degree of freedom per retained guided harmonic. We apply the framework to a bulk van der Waals WS$_2$ metasurface patterned into a hexagonal lattice of triangular holes and uncover a new geometry-controlled topological transition driven by dipole-quadrupole band inversion, distinct from the conventional breathing-honeycomb-lattice transition. Full-wave simulations confirm the predicted topological phase diagram and the emergence of photonic and polaritonic edge states at a topological interface. Our results establish a theoretical multimode framework for geometry-controlled bandstructure engineering in polaritonic metasurfaces, with applications in topological, chiral, and quantum integrated photonics.

items.title: Breit interaction in elastic scattering of vortex electron on Hydrogen atomic target
items.summary: The interaction of electron vortex beams with atoms is fundamental to their applications, yet existing studies of elastic scattering have considered only the Coulomb interaction. The role of the Breit interaction, which represents the leading relativistic correction to the Coulomb potential between two electrons, has not been systematically examined. In this paper, we study the elastic scattering of a vortex electron by a hydrogen atomic target, with emphasis on the role of the Breit interaction. Comparisons are made between two situations: the pure Coulomb contribution and the pure Breit contribution. Our results show that the Breit interaction dominates the scattering process when the total angular momentum of the vortex electron is larger than a certain threshold, which challenges the conventional notion that the Breit interaction makes little contribution to electron scattering for low-$Z$ atoms. This phenomenon arises primarily because a vortex electron with large angular momentum possesses a substantial magnetic moment, and the Breit interaction precisely describes the interaction between magnetic moments. The threshold can be adjusted by changing the parameters of the initial vortex electron. Moreover, we further compare the single-atom, mesoscopic, and macroscopic target cases, and show that the target size significantly influences the observability of the Breit-induced effects, with a smaller target size being favorable for observing this phenomenon.

items.title: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) approximations of capillary menisci in polygonal channels
items.summary: A capillary interface must satisfy both its curvature equation and the contact angle at the container walls. We study how strong-form physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) approximate these conditions when the prescribed equilibrium is geometrically incompatible. In zero gravity, the Concus-Finn critical contact angles for spanning graphs in square and equilateral-triangular cross-sections are respectively 45 degrees and 60 degrees. Below these angles, classical subdomain flux balance yields a certified lower bound on the continuous combined interior and wall residual loss, retaining the sampling densities and wall weight. The subdomain bounds and their sums over disjoint regions tend uniformly to zero as the contact angle approaches the threshold from below at fixed wall weight. The computed PINNs return smooth graphs with finite axial extent in the nonexistence regime: small interior residuals coexist with corner wall-flux deficits, where the adjoining contact-angle conditions demand more flux than a finite-slope graph can supply. At the default wall weight, several degrees into this regime, neural losses computed by quadrature are 1.6-1.8 times the bound from one cut per corner, with higher ratios occurring near the critical angle. Polynomial least-squares comparisons support the same geometric interpretation in a second smooth trial family. The bound supplies a physical scale for the residual compromise and explains why residual assessment must include wall flux and continuum compatibility.

items.title: Scaling of the Radial Motion and Size of Filamentary Structures in the Scrape-Off Layer Inferred from 100 kHz Visible Imaging on 294 MAST Discharges
items.summary: Filaments are important carriers of cross-field transport in the scrape-off layer of a tokamak. Analytic models predict that their radial velocity varies with their size. We measured the radial velocity and size of a large population of filaments on MAST, using data recorded from a 100 kHz, 48 x 256 pixel camera in the outboard midplane in the FAIR-MAST archive. Computer vision techniques were used to automate the identification of filaments and tracking of their trajectories, which yielded 86,042 filament tracks over 294 discharges in 4 campaigns. The archive does not contain spatial calibration, so we have obtained a pixel scale by regression of the plasma limb column in the image on the EFIT outboard LCFS radius, with bootstrap intervals. The scale is 2.7-5.2 millimetres per pixel. We find a median velocity of 424 m/s, and median radial width of 3.6 cm. The dependence of velocity on size is mild, with a log-log slope of +0.05 (95% interval +0.03 to +0.07) when the effects of exposure blurring are corrected for. This is because filaments are not in either velocity regime; they span the range $\hat{a}$ = 0.13-1.97 in two-region units, which straddles the maximum velocity predicted by the two-region model, but the normalized velocity $\hat{v}$ is much smaller than the scale of the model, at $\hat{v} \approx 0.06$.

items.title: Phase-field modeling of elastically driven abnormal grain growth
items.summary: Grain-refined metals offer high strength, yet their engineering applications are often constrained by grain coarsening under mechanical loading. Recent experiments have revealed room-temperature abnormal grain growth (AGG) in ultrafine-grained Ni thin films subjected to cyclic loading. This phenomenon occurs in the regime of macroscopic elastic deformation, unlike conventional AGG, which generally requires substantial plastic deformation or high temperatures. The AGG process is characterized by the preferential growth of grains whose in-plane <100> orientations are aligned with the loading direction. Here, we investigate the underlying physical mechanisms by combining phase-field simulations with micromechanical analysis. The results indicate that a reduction in elastic energy provides a thermodynamic driving force for orientation-selective grain growth. Phase-field simulations reveal the kinetic evolution of AGG and demonstrate that local grain geometry and stress state influence grain growth pathways. By applying this framework to materials with varying degrees of elastic anisotropy, we establish a general approach for investigating elastically driven AGG in polycrystalline systems.

items.title: Efficient simulation of the generalized Langevin equation using a basis of dynamically relevant histories for memory and noise
items.summary: The Generalized Langevin Equation (GLE) is a cornerstone for modeling non-Markovian dynamics, but its numerical solution remains challenging due to the history-dependent convolution and the need to generate colored noise with a prescribed correlation function. We introduce a forward construction that addresses both challenges within a single framework. We represent an arbitrary trajectory as sum of relevant and irrelevant parts, where relevant part can be decomposed into a small number of characteristic history patterns that make the main contribution to future dynamics. It allows to reduce numerical cost to \(O(d^2)\) for $d$ chosen patterns instead of full history. The same construction applies to colored noise generation, where the causal filter plays the role of the memory kernel. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the method for several representative kernels, including long-range kernels with power-law tails.

items.title: A Hybrid State Space-Attention Architecture for Forecasting the Trajectories of Battery Degradation
items.summary: Early-life battery degradation trajectory forecasting aims to predict a battery cell's full state-of-health (SOH) trajectory from its initial charge-discharge cycles, potentially reducing cell qualification and evaluation time from months to days. Despite recent advances, accurate forecasting remains challenging for emerging battery chemistries, data-scarce domains, and cells exhibiting degradation behaviors beyond those observed during training. Existing state-of-the-art approaches increasingly rely on model scaling, large language model-derived aging-condition embeddings, and extensive fold-specific hyperparameter tuning, raising concerns about computational efficiency, reproducibility, and generalization. This work introduces DecayFormer, a compact hybrid state-space and attention architecture designed for early-life degradation trajectory forecasting. DecayFormer combines cycle-level selective recurrence, using a single scalar state per channel, with an attention mechanism queried by the recurrent state. It further incorporates state-of-charge (SOC) interval statistics and a master curve head that jointly estimates a scalar lifetime and a monotonically non-increasing SOH profile parameterized by normalized lifetime. We evaluate DecayFormer on the BatteryLife benchmark using all 22 aging-condition-exclusive folds, with a single run per fold and one fixed configuration across all folds, without fold-specific tuning. DecayFormer achieves mean test MAPE values of 2.25% on Li-ion, 2.76% on CALB, 0.95% on Na-ion, and 7.19% on Zn-ion. These results demonstrate the potential of compact sequence models to deliver accurate early-life degradation forecasts across diverse battery chemistries and aging conditions, without relying on extensive model scaling or per-fold optimization.

items.title: Limited-Memory First-Order Methods: Identification, Reconstruction, $H$-Duality and Application to Optimized Methods
items.summary: In general, linear-span first-order methods add at every iteration a combination of all observed gradients to the previous iterate. However, many methods of interest can be implemented in a way that requires storing only a few auxiliary vectors, instead of all past gradients. We call such methods limited-memory first-order methods. A given fixed-coefficient first-order method can be described by a lower triangular coefficient matrix, which expresses each step as a combination of previous gradients. We show that the minimum number of running sums required to implement a method is equal to the minimum rank of a completion of the strict lower triangular part of its coefficient matrix, and propose a reconstruction algorithm. Moreover, taking the $H$-dual of a method, which reflects the coefficient matrix across its anti-diagonal, preserves its memory and translates into a permutation and time-reversal on the coefficients of the running sum recurrences. We apply our results to two optimized first-order methods for smooth strongly convex functions. First, our reconstruction applied to a method numerically designed by Shu and Wang reveals a recurrence with one auxiliary vector, which is related to the Triple Momentum Method (TMM) of Van Scoy, Freeman and Lynch with a particular initialization. We prove that the reconstructed method, called TMM-GD, is minimax optimal at every horizon for the final distance to the minimizer relative to the initial gradient norm. Second, the Information-Theoretic Exact Method (ITEM) of Taylor and Drori, optimal for the final distance relative to the initial one, is known to be memory one. We give an explicit recurrence with one auxiliary vector for its $H$-dual, called ITEM-GG, and prove that ITEM-GG is the unique minimax optimal nonadaptive linear-span method for the final gradient norm relative to the initial one.

items.title: Hyperlyve: Parallelized Enumeration and Exact Lyapunov Stability Certification for Deep ReLU Networks
items.summary: We introduce Hyperlyve (Hyperplane Partitioned Lyapunov Verification and Enumeration), a framework for proving the asymptotic stability of nonlinear dynamical systems, including those with neural network controllers. Hyperlyve learns and formally certifies continuous piecewise-affine (CPA) neural Lyapunov functions within a counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) loop. Hyperlyve's key innovation is a parallel algorithm that enumerates the hyperplane arrangement formed by the ReLU activations of deep networks and certifies that Lyapunov conditions hold within each polyhedral region. We derive sound and complete regional tests to verify the asymptotic stability of the exact smooth dynamics (rather than a piecewise-linear approximation) within a compact domain of interest. Furthermore, we formally characterize the computational complexity of the CPA neural Lyapunov verification problem as co-NP-complete, filling a key gap in the literature. Empirical results demonstrate that Hyperlyve enumerates ReLU networks over 150-times faster than competing tools, which contributes to Hyperlyve proving the asymptotic stability of systems that are currently intractable for state-of-the-art verifiers.

items.title: Exceptional cubics on 7-manifolds
items.summary: A $G_2$-structure $\varphi$ on a $7$-manifold $\mathcal M$ determines a two-dimensional space of invariant totally symmetric cubic forms on each fiber of the rank-$27$ bundle $S^2_0T^*\mathcal M$ of traceless symmetric $2$-tensors. This space is spanned by the trace cubic $C_0$ and a cubic $C_\varphi$ that, up to a constant factor, is the pointwise integrand of the Yukawa coupling on the $G_2$ moduli space. We determine the exact infinitesimal stabilizers over $\mathbb C$ of all nonzero cubics in this family. For $C_0+λC_\varphi$, the stabilizer has dimension $78$ precisely at the two non-real values $λ_\pm=(1\pm i\sqrt7)/8$. Its dimension is $21$ for $C_0$ and $14$ in all other cases. At $λ_\pm$, the stabilizer is simple of type $E_6$, and the corresponding cubic is linearly equivalent to the complex Albert algebra cubic norm. The two cubics at $λ_\pm$, which we call critical, define complex-conjugate $E_6$-reductions of the complexified bundle. At any element with nonzero critical norm, the corresponding cubic determines a complex Albert algebra with basepoint stabilizer $F_4$; a line subbundle of the tangent bundle selects a smooth bundle of these algebras with tensorial operations and a Euclidean real form. The induced Levi-Civita connection preserves either critical cubic exactly when the $G_2$-structure is torsion-free. Its orthogonal projections onto the two exceptional reductions coincide with the connection induced by the minimal $G_2$-connection.

items.title: Adaptive Local Proper Orthogonal Decomposition via Graph Partitioning and Provable Error-Bounded Lossy Compression for Parametric Series in Finite-Dimensional Function Spaces
items.summary: We introduce a spatially adaptive proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) method for error-bounded lossy compression of snapshot data in finite-dimensional function spaces. The method combines hierarchical graph partitioning with independent low-rank approximations on spatial subdomains, allowing the local approximation ranks to adapt to the spatial distribution of information in the data. For partitions that are orthogonal in the discrete inner product, we establish an exact decomposition of the global squared weighted reconstruction error into local contributions and characterize the weighted-norm optimality and coefficient-space quasi-optimality of local POD approximations for fixed partitions and ranks. These results provide a rigorous mechanism for allocating a prescribed global error tolerance among subdomains and selecting the smallest admissible local ranks. We further develop a sufficient error bound for the coefficient-space normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE). A greedy hierarchical refinement algorithm accepts a spatial subdivision only when it reduces the storage required by the local low-rank factors while preserving the prescribed reconstruction-error bound. The method is assessed using synthetic data and snapshot sequences from two- and three-dimensional compressible-flow simulations. The numerical results illustrate how spatially adaptive ranks and partitioning can improve compression relative to global POD and fixed spatial partitions, particularly when the data exhibit spatially heterogeneous dynamics.

items.title: Hyperbolic systems with non-diagonalisable principal part and variable multiplicities, IV: time-dependent characteristics, representation of solutions and regularity
items.summary: We consider first-order linear hyperbolic systems with time-dependent pseudo-differential principal symbols and characteristic roots of variable multiplicity. Building on the time-independent work of Kamotski and the first author, we introduce a finite-type condition along the lifted bicharacteristic flow that accounts for the contact of time-dependent characteristic roots. Under this condition, we construct a representation of solutions using time-dependent Fourier integral operators and a Picard series whose terms become increasingly smooth. This leads to an asymptotic expansion in smoothness and local \(L^p\) regularity estimates with the expected loss of derivatives. We also apply these results to higher-order scalar weakly hyperbolic equations with involutive characteristics and time-dependent principal symbols. Finally, we consider upper triangular systems with possibly non-diagonalisable principal parts and derive a representation formula involving integrated Fourier integral operators. This extends the earlier results of Garetto, Jäh and the first author to time-dependent principal parts.

items.title: Quantum Cohomology and irrationality of Küchle fourfolds
items.summary: We prove that very general Küchle fourfolds of types (c1), (c6), (b8), and (b11) are irrational. The key ingredients are a new rationality criterion, based on the theory of Hodge atoms due to Katzarkov--Kontsevich--Pantev--Yu and its integral extension by Guéré, and a computation of the action of quantum multiplication on the vanishing cohomology of these fourfolds, which uses a version of the Quantum Lefschetz Hyperplane Principle. Quantum multiplication acts as a scalar on the vanishing cohomology, and we give an enumerative interpretation of this scalar.

items.title: The geometry of magnitude for finite metric spaces
items.summary: The main result of this article is a geometric interpretation of magnitude, a real-valued invariant of metric spaces. We introduce a Euclidean embedding of a (suitable) finite metric space $X$ such that the magnitude of $X$ can be expressed in terms of the `circumradius' of its embedding $S$. The circumradius is the radius of the unique sphere that goes through $S$. We give three applications: First, we describe the asymptotic behaviour of the magnitude of $tX$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$, in terms of the circumradius. Second, we develop a matrix theory for magnitude that leads to explicit relations between the magnitude of $X$ and the magnitude of its subspaces. Third, we identify a new regime in the limiting behaviour of $tX$, and use this to show submodularity-type results for magnitude as a function on subspaces.

items.title: Counterexamples to Grad's conjecture of any knot type
items.summary: We construct smooth magnetohydrostatic counterexamples to Grad's conjecture in toroidal domains of arbitrary knot type. The magnetic field is nonvanishing, and nested pressure tori fill the domain outside a nondegenerate magnetic axis. The equilibria have trivial Euclidean symmetry group and occur in smooth families of inequivalent configurations. On each regular pressure torus the magnetic flow is smoothly conjugate to a linear flow with any prescribed positive constant slope. A variation of this argument gives equilibria of arbitrary knot type with twist (that is, nonconstant rotational transform) and any finite regularity. A key ingredient of the proof is a deformation method that creates knot topology from axial symmetry by separating the sheets of a covering immersion into a braid, which may be useful in other deformation problems.

items.title: On strongly pseudoconvex Kähler--Berwald manifolds
items.summary: In this paper, we establish the equivalence between the Kähler--Finsler and Kähler--Berwald conditions for complex Finsler metrics. That is, a Kähler--Finsler metric always satisfies the complex Berwald condition: its Chern--Finsler nonlinear connection reduces to the Chern connection of a Kähler metric. We also provide, for the first time, smooth weakly Kähler--Finsler examples which are not Kähler--Berwald; and propose a condition that is formally stronger than weakly Kähler--Finsler, with equivalence holding in complex dimension two. Then we prove the de Rham decomposition and uniformization theorems for Kähler--Berwald manifolds, and show that every strongly pseudoconvex locally symmetric complex Finsler metric is both Kähler--Berwald and complex Einstein--Finsler. Additionally, we establish several rigidity theorems for the Kobayashi and Carathéodory metrics: $F_K$ is Kähler--Berwald if and only if it is Kähler; if the manifold is simply connected, then $F_C$ is Kähler--Berwald if and only if it is Kähler.

items.title: Fourier Algebras of HLS Groupoids: Lifts, Amenability, and Spectrum
items.summary: We investigate the Fourier algebra of a certain class of groupoids, called the HLS groupoids, within Paterson's continuous framework for locally compact groupoids. We develop the basic harmonic analysis of HLS groupoids by obtaining concrete descriptions of their topology, representations, and Fourier algebra. We then study the restriction maps from the Fourier algebra $A(\mathcal{G})$ of an HLS groupoid $\mathcal{G}$ to the Fourier algebras of its isotropy subgroups, and construct explicit norm-preserving lifts for these restriction maps. As applications, we describe the norm of every element of $A(\mathcal{G})$ in terms of the norms of its restrictions to the isotropy subgroups. We prove an analogue of Leptin's theorem characterizing when $A(\mathcal{G})$ has a bounded approximate identity. We also show that the Gelfand spectrum of $A(\mathcal{G})$ is homeomorphic to $\mathcal{G}$. Finally, using abstract arguments that, unlike our methods for HLS groupoids, do not yield explicit constructions, we show that norm-preserving lifts exist and that the Gelfand spectrum of the Fourier algebra is homeomorphic to the groupoid for every étale groupoid. This generalizes Eymard's theorem and answers a question of Paterson for étale groupoids.

items.title: Trustworthy Numerical Software in the Age of AI: What Would Turing Do?
items.summary: AI coding agents can now produce numerical software faster than human experts can review it, raising serious concerns about usability and reliability. These and other AI tools are already transforming mathematics and software, and they will soon transform mathematical software. These concerns motivated us to assess AI-generated numerical linear algebra (NLA) kernels, which we did through an audit of a recent public GPU QR competition. All five leading kernels passed the competition's accuracy tests, and the winning kernel achieved a 107-fold speedup over the competition's baseline, which calls NVIDIA's QR routine. Yet each failed at least once on new inputs, even those from the competition's generator, under the same checker, while the baseline passed them all. In light of this, we want to develop reusable formalizations of numerical analysis methods, which remain sparsely represented in existing formal libraries. We describe VSCL, our Lean library of mathematical foundations for numerical computing. We also propose VERNA to connect these tasks by using formalized results to guide kernel assessment against explicit specifications. Drawing on Turing's work on rounding-error analysis and program checking, we discuss design principles for developing trustworthy numerical software when direct human checking is impractical.

items.title: Heavy-Light Wall Crossings and Motivic Asymptotics of Moduli Spaces of Curves. Part II: Tameness of Motivic Measures
items.summary: This paper is concerned with the study of the fixed-genus asymptotics of motivic measures of moduli spaces of stable pointed curves and their minimal all-light Hassett compactifications as the number of markings tends to infinity. A motivic wall-crossing argument gives a universal change of variables between the two generating series, depending only on the value of the Lefschetz class. For an arbitrary motivic measure, we use stabilization graphs and support patterns to express the all-light series in terms of universal chain factors and finite residual quotient families. This formal decomposition isolates the rational trivalent contribution without requiring a fixed-locus formula for finite quotients. To pass from formal identities to asymptotics, we formulate analytic hypotheses (the $\mathrm{H}_g$-hypotheses) for scalar realizations with positive real Lefschetz value. We introduce vertex tameness and residual-quotient tameness, whose conjunction, graph tameness, provides geometric sufficient conditions for the $\mathrm{H}_g$-hypotheses. In genus at least two, this yields explicit leading asymptotics in both chambers, depending only on the genus and the Lefschetz value; genera zero and one are treated separately. As an application, we prove graph tameness for Hodge-Deligne evaluations and deduce fixed-product universality and asymptotic concentration of Hodge numbers on the diagonal.

items.title: Peak state transfer in trees and the cost of distance
items.summary: There is peak state transfer between vertices $u$ and $v$ in a graph $G$ if there exists a time $t$ for which $|(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t M})_{u,v}|$ saturates the triangle inequality imposed by its spectral decomposition and $M$ is either the adjacency or Laplacian matrix. We show that peak state transfer at distance $d$ requires $\frac{d^3}{24}(1 + o(1))$ edges in the adjacency case, $Ω(d^2)$ edges in the Laplacian case, and that the leading coefficient in the former is tight. We find a family of graphs with Laplacian peak state transfer at distance $d$ and $Θ(d^5)$ edges, showing that peak state transfer is achievable in a polynomial graph size. In contrast, Laplacian perfect state transfer costs at least $Ω(2^{d/2})$ edges when the distance partition of vertices around one vertex is almost equitable. Finally, we show that Laplacian peak state transfer in trees requires $Ω(d!)$ edges, and we characterize all trees of diameter $\leq 4$ admitting Laplacian peak state transfer, thus answering a pair of questions posed by Coutinho, Guo, and Schmeits.

items.title: Second scaling regime in high-dimensional function approximation and curse of dimensionality
items.summary: High-dimensional function approximation is often subject to the curse of dimensionality, commonly described by a hypercube scaling regime with a large expense of $R^d$ grid points, where $R$ denotes the side length of a hypercube in $d$ dimensions. Here we show that a second scaling regime, which we call the lattice ball scaling regime, also arises and is relevant for practical applications. In this regime, the expense scales as $d^{R^2}/(R^2!)$ and therefore grows polynomially with $d$. This regime arises without additional special assumptions of special types of function spaces or error norms. The lattice ball scaling regime occurs when $R^2\ll d$, due to the discrete nature of counting the expense as the number of lattice points inside a hypersphere. Here we investigate this regime, which arises from the classical problem of approximating high-dimensional functions from common spaces of analytic or $m$-times continuously differentiable functions using orthogonal series (spectral method) such as Fourier, Chebyshev, and Legendre polynomial series. For many applications, the expense in the lattice ball scaling regime can be substantially smaller than that of the hypercube scaling regime, making accurate approximations more accessible. Numerical illustrations include classifying images of handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset and learning the solution operators of partial differential equations, such as Burgers' equation and the radiative transfer equation. The potential for connections with artificial neural networks and other machine learning methods is also discussed.

items.title: Dirac - von Neumann axioms in the setting of Continuous Model Theory
items.summary: We recast the well-known axiom system of quantum mechanics used by physicists (the Dirac calculus) in the language of Continuous Logic. For the basic version of the axiomatic system we prove that along with the canonical continuous model the axioms have approximate finite models of large sizes, in fact the continuous model is isomorphic to an ultraproduct of finite models. We analyse the continuous logic quantifier corresponding to Dirac integration and show that in finite context it has two versions, local and global, which coincide on Gaussian wave-functions.

items.title: Norms of Schneider--Teitelbaum Polynomials in $p$-adic Fourier Theory
items.summary: Let $F$ be the unramified quadratic extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and let $P_n(X)$ denote the Lubin--Tate analogues of the binomial polynomials arising in the $p$-adic Fourier theory of Schneider and Teitelbaum. For a particular choice of Lubin--Tate logarithm, we determine explicitly the norms of the functions $P_n(xΩ)$ on the Banach spaces of locally $F$-analytic functions of fixed order, where $Ω$ is a Lubin--Tate period. Our computation is based on a recent valuation formula of Ardakov and Berger for the values $P_n(Ω)$. As an application, we improve the Bannai--Kobayashi normalization of these polynomials. Each element of the resulting basis has norm one.

items.title: Random compositions of quasiperiodic cocycles
items.summary: We consider the multiplicative process given by random compositions of linear cocycles over toral translations. Under appropriate generic assumptions, we establish effective large deviations estimates as well as the Hölder continuity of the associated Lyapunov exponent of the process. These properties in particular show the regularizing effect of randomness on quasiperiodic dynamics. The novelty of our approach allows for the study of such properties notwithstanding the lack of a spectral gap for the corresponding transition operator.

items.title: Regular subgroups of wreath products and Cayley Cartesian products
items.summary: The Cartesian product of Cayley graphs is again a Cayley graph. For connected graphs, the converse question reduces to Cartesian powers of Cartesian-prime graphs, and consequently to the study of regular subgroups of wreath products in the product action. We prove that, for a transitive permutation group $G$ of degree $2p$ or $4p$, where $p$ is prime, $G\wr S_2$ contains a regular subgroup if and only if $G$ does, and construct counterexamples of degree $8p$ for every prime $p\equiv3\pmod4$. By modifying this construction, we obtain an infinite family of connected non-Cayley graphs whose Cartesian squares are Cayley graphs, giving a negative answer to the converse question. The smallest graph in our family has $120$ vertices and valency $27$. In contrast, we prove that a connected vertex-transitive graph of order $pq$, where $p$ and $q$ are primes, has a Cayley Cartesian power if and only if the graph itself is Cayley.

items.title: Complex Moments of the Derivative of the Riemann Zeta Function
items.summary: We investigate the complex moments of the derivative of the Riemann zeta function through a random Euler product model. For each fixed $σ>1/2$ and every $s\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$, we show, under the Lindelöf hypothesis, that the $2s$-th moment of $|ζ'(σ+\mathrm{i}t)|$ over $t\in[1,T]$ converges, as $T\to\infty$, to the corresponding moment of the derivative of the random Euler product. We then establish, unconditionally, an asymptotic formula for the latter moment as $σ\downarrow 1/2$ throughout the half-plane $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$. For positive real moments, our approach is based on a change-of-measure argument and a Gaussian limit theorem for the logarithmic derivative under a tilted probability measure. For general complex moments, we combine Fourier analysis of weighted complex measures with regularized Riesz distributions. As an application, under the Lindelöf hypothesis, we resolve the conjecture of Simm and Wei [J. Lond. Math. Soc. 113 (2026)] on the complex moments of the derivative of the Riemann zeta function for every $s\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$. We establish the predicted asymptotic formula as $σ\downarrow1/2$, with the leading order $s^2+2s$ and an explicit leading coefficient involving an arithmetic factor and the confluent hypergeometric function of the first kind. The conjecture also holds unconditionally when $\operatorname{Re}(s)\in (0,2)$.

items.title: Axioms for relative entropy
items.summary: For normal states of arbitrary von Neumann algebras, we characterize positive finite multiples of Araki relative entropy among non-degenerate divergences. The axioms are monotonicity under normal unital completely positive maps, tensor additivity, superadditivity for product second states, and separate lower semicontinuity in the predual norm. Alternatively, a conditional-expectation identity replaces the two tensor assumptions. The proof uses order bounds and asymptotic estimates on tensor powers. An appendix proves the known analytic estimates needed here, using standard modular theory and Haagerup L^p spaces. We also obtain the corresponding characterization in the C* algebraic setting.

items.title: Large gaps and the ten martini problem for monotone quasiperiodic Schrödinger operators
items.summary: We prove the ten martini theorem for a large class of monotone potentials. The key strategy is to establish polynomially large gaps for periodic approximations.

items.title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
items.summary: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d.
