items.title: Trajectory Density Ratios under Weak Support: A Survey across the Sciences
items.summary: Many problems across the sciences compare two stochastic processes through the sequences they generate. Reinforcement learning asks what a new policy would return from the trajectories of an old one; molecular simulation asks how much more a ligand binds from samples of the unbound state; climate attribution asks how a heat wave shifted under warming; and language-model post-training asks what a deployed agent will do from logged interactions. In every case, one quantity would answer all these questions at once: the ratio of the two probability laws over their generated sequences, the trajectory density ratio. This ratio exists only under strong conditions. When one process reaches states the other cannot, the ratio does not exist; when their overlap is thin, its variance grows without control with the sequence length; and when they concentrate on different lower-dimensional sets, the ratio is undefined altogether. Weak support of this kind is the norm for sequence data, not a sampling accident, and its price is paid in identifiability rather than in noise alone. This survey organizes the field around a three-level diagnosis of weak support and a map of the nine retreats that methods take when the full ratio is out of reach, from direct estimation and reweighting through staged decomposition, stationarization, and partial-identification bounds to smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional. Each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers and pays for the rest, and each application domain has standardized the retreat its data force. The survey closes with open problems: testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.

items.title: Neural Marked Point Processes for Health Insurance Claims
items.summary: Health insurance claims exhibit temporal dependence, as previous claims may provide information about the timing, type and amount of subsequent claims. Such dependencies are difficult to capture with traditional actuarial models based on aggregated claim counts. We investigate a neural marked point process in which a causal Transformer represents individual claim histories and determines type-specific conditional intensities, allowing for self-excitation and interactions between claim types. The framework also incorporates conditional severity distributions, reporting delays and stochastic medical-cost inflation. We develop a likelihood-based calibration procedure that accounts for incomplete claim reporting and evaluate the model using both simulated and empirical data. A simulation study with 10,000 insurance contracts examines the recovery of known claim dynamics, while an application to MEPS-derived medical-event data assesses predictive performance. The fitted model reproduces the main patterns in claim frequencies and severities, although some discrepancies remain in the tails of the distributions. On the MEPS data, the neural model achieves better predictive performance than two generalized linear model benchmarks in terms of claim-count deviance and expenditure discrimination.

items.title: Measuring price impact and information content of trades in a time-varying setting
items.summary: We propose a non-linear observation-driven version of the Hasbrouck vector auto-regression framework for dynamically estimating trades' market impact and information content. We find that market impact displays an intraday pattern superimposed with large fluctuations. Some of them are exogenous, and, as an example, we investigate market impact dynamics around FOMC announcements. Unlike the vector autoregression results, we reveal that the information content of the trades depends on the local liquidity level and the recent history of prices and trades. Finally, we use the model to estimate the time-varying permanent impact parameter, which allows performing a dynamic transaction cost analysis.

items.title: A Second Order Transport Scheme for Dynamic Portfolio Subspaces under a Varying Risk Metric
items.summary: We analyze the transport of portfolio exposures between moving subspaces under a varying positive definite risk metric. The reference evolution is the induced connection obtained from the ambient connection of minimum norm in fixed asset coordinates. An explicit expansion of risk weighted Procrustes identifies a leading local error that couples metric deformation with covariant motion normal to the subspace. A rank two construction with an exact continuous solution shows that this term can reduce global accuracy to first order even when the metric commutes with its derivative. Geometric mean alignment and a symmetric Procrustes construction cancel the term and yield reversible updates with second order global accuracy. We establish uniform error bounds on nonuniform partitions, characterize the cases in which the Procrustes defect vanishes, and distinguish discretization error from errors in estimated geometry. We also characterize the connection induced by principal square root whitening and its relation to the selected transport. Manufactured examples confirm the predicted defect and convergence rates. A historical geometry stress test then estimates the defect from preceding observations and finds that it predicts the subsequent separation between risk weighted Procrustes and both second order updates, while the two second order schemes remain much closer to each other. Portfolio comparisons separately evaluate target persistence, turnover, and economic implementation.

items.title: Stochastic Modelling of High-frequency (HF) Crypto Limit Order Book (LOB) with General Compound Marked Hawkes Process
items.summary: The paper is devoted to the stochastic modelling of high-frequency crypto Limit Order Book (LOB) with general compound marked Hawkes process (GCMHP). We consider marked Hawkes process in a general form. LLN and FCLTs with stochastic and constant centralization are stated. Numerical example for high-frequency LOB dataset for BTC (bitcoin) based on sources from HF crypto LOB data is presented as well. The novelty of the paper lies in the new LLN and FCLTs for the GCMHP, and in the new application associated with high-frequency (HF) crypto LOB.

items.title: European derivatives pricing via constrained Gaussian process regressions
items.summary: This article develops a Gaussian process method for pricing European derivatives when the underlyings, and the risk factors driving them, follow a multivariate jump-diffusion. A Gaussian process prior on the pricing function is conditioned on the Feynman-Kac partial integro-differential equation at a set of collocation points. The price is returned as a closed-form and differentiable function, allowing the Greeks to be obtained without simulation or finite differences. The jump terms are handled iteratively: the price is computed as the limit of a sequence of boundary value problems. Our main theoretical contribution is a convergence result for this iteration: using Weissinger's fixed-point theorem in the supremum norm, we show that it converges from any starting point, and provide a worst-case number of iterations for a given precision. The method is illustrated with derivatives of two underlyings under the Heston model with Kou double-exponential jumps, a five-dimensional problem, and benchmarked against Monte Carlo simulation.

items.title: Beyond Marginal Risk: ESG and Multidimensional Fragility in Equity Markets
items.summary: Do ESG characteristics provide financial resilience beyond conventional risk, and is that inference stable to the financial state and ESG score being measured? We study a point-in-time panel of nonfinancial S&P 500 constituents from January 2019 through November 2025. Once ex ante return, volatility, and liquidity exposures are modeled explicitly, the broad downside-resilience pattern attenuates and none of the three primary marginal ESG $\times$ Down tests survives Holm adjustment under either conventional or wild-cluster-bootstrap inference. A post-primary exact decomposition then shows that the negative Return+RVOL coefficient is almost entirely allocated to observations that also breach the CHL trading-cost tail, while the mutually exclusive Return+RVOL-only component is essentially zero. Finally, a paired standardized comparison on an identical sample shows that MSCI's downstream Industry Adjusted Score and upstream Weighted Average Key Issue Score imply materially different fitted associations in adverse market states: at a 5% market decline, the difference is about one probability percentage point per score standard deviation. Sector-time, leave- one-month-out, and observed-change timing diagnostics preserve most of this contrast, although the result remains exploratory and inference is sensitive to multiplicity and market-state support. The evidence therefore favors a narrower interpretation of ESG resilience: the apparent association weakens once conventional risk is modeled, while the remaining relation depends on both the adverse state and the MSCI score field used to represent ESG.

items.title: A Convergent Linear Regression Method for Forward-Backward Stochastic Differential Equations with Jumps
items.summary: In this paper, we introduce a large class of convergent numerical methods, based on (linear) basis function regression technique, to approximate the solution to a forward-backward stochastic differential equation with jumps (FBSDEJ hereafter). Numerical experiment shows good applicability of the proposed method.

items.title: Mollification Regularization and Asymptotic Correction for Analytical Expansion of BSDEs with Non-Smooth Terminal Conditions. I. Theory
items.summary: The analytical expansion method for BSDEs of Zhang (2017) breaks down when the terminal condition psi has kinks or discontinuities. We replace psi by psi_epsilon = psi * rho_epsilon and derive a joint error decomposition whose expansion constants explicitly track the derivative blow-up as epsilon tends to 0. For symmetric mollifiers the leading weak bias cancels. The associated balanced rates are conditional on an explicitly stated uniform local-to-global Taylor-propagation assumption: under that assumption the benchmark (l, m, alpha) = (0, 2, 1) gives epsilon* ~ delta_t^{1/3} and weak rate 2/3. Without it, the rigorous additive bound gives no decay when m - 2l = 2; an unconditional positive rate is obtained only for m - 2l > 2. Asymptotic corrections cancel the weak bias through order epsilon^{2J}; their faster exponents are formal targets unless the auxiliary expansion errors and the Picard defect satisfy additional rate conditions, which we state explicitly. For the driver-free fixed-center scheme we identify an n-independent terminal-representation error and show that it depends on the expansion center and on the terminal representative; change-of-basis invariance does not imply centering independence. A Gaussian moment-compression layer combines whitening, a Stein recursion, and knapsack truncation with a jet-conditioned error certificate. This Part I contains the theory, with all proofs self-contained; numerical evidence and implementation measurements are reported separately in the companion paper (Part II).

items.title: SAiFE-gym: Model-based Environments for Automated Market Making with Concentrated Liquidity
items.summary: We present SAiFE_gym, a Python module that provides a collection of simulation environments for studying trading problems in constant product markets (CPMs) with concentrated liquidity (CL). These markets give liquidity providers (LPs) granular control over how their capital is allocated and enable them to adjust their range of liquidity provision dynamically based on market conditions, which in turn determines how they earn fees. We decompose the microstructure of CPMs with CL into interactive components that allow researchers and practitioners to capture various economic settings. We employ a vectorized approach to optimize our environments, making them scalable for high-dimensional reinforcement learning (RL) workflows, suitable for learning dynamic liquidity provision strategies. We demonstrate the benefits of our environments by evaluating the performance of RL agents in CPMs with CL under various market conditions.

items.title: Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Asset-Liability Management
items.summary: This paper proposes a novel approach for Asset-Liability Management (ALM) by employing continuous-time Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a linear-quadratic (LQ) formulation that incorporates both interim and terminal objectives. We develop a model-free, policy gradient-based soft actor-critic algorithm tailored to ALM for dynamically synchronizing assets and liabilities. To ensure an effective balance between exploration and exploitation with minimal tuning, we introduce adaptive exploration for the actor and scheduled exploration for the critic. Our empirical study evaluates this approach against two enhanced traditional financial strategies, a model-based continuous-time RL method, and three state-of-the-art RL algorithms. Evaluated across 200 randomized market scenarios, our method achieves higher average rewards than all alternative strategies, with rapid initial gains and sustained superior performance. The outperformance stems not from complex neural networks or improved parameter estimation, but from directly learning the optimal ALM strategy without learning the environment.

items.title: TAPES: Terminal Adjoint-Propagated Error Scheduling for Financial Diffusion Samplers
items.summary: Financial diffusion samplers are often reused with a small number of function evaluations (NFE) inside scenario and risk pipelines, where numerical time-grid error can distort terminal quantities such as covariances, tails, and drawdown proxies. We study offline grid construction for a frozen probability-flow ODE: the score network, conditioning, Euler solver, report normalization, and deployment NFE remain fixed. TAPES (Terminal Adjoint-Propagated Error Scheduling) estimates signed local defects by Richardson comparisons, transports them through the remaining discrete flow and a terminal-report adjoint, and optimizes the squared norm of their sum before a capped direct refinement. We show that this transported signed sum is the first-order terminal-report error and quantify, under an aligned-defect model, the inefficiency of diagonal criteria. Across six budgets on a regime-switching simulation and chronologically held-out Mag7 contexts, TAPES gives the lowest design- and audit-report errors in all 24 dataset--budget--report rows within the reported five-pipeline panel. Cross-budget mean relative audit-error reductions are about 10--11% on Regime-SV and about 1% on Mag7, with Bonferroni intervals excluding zero; all displayed winners persist under a doubled-resolution reference, and a small Regime-SV Heun probe preserves the TAPES-first audit ordering. TAPES changes only the offline schedule and retains the prescribed deployment NFE; claims concern numerical fidelity to frozen generators.

items.title: Mean--Variance Portfolio Selection by Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms, Regret Analysis, and Empirical Study
items.summary: We study continuous-time mean--variance portfolio selection in markets where stock prices are diffusion processes driven by observable factors that are also diffusion processes, yet the coefficients of these processes are unknown. Based on the recently developed reinforcement learning (RL) theory for diffusion processes, we present a general data-driven RL approach that learns the pre-committed investment strategy directly without attempting to learn or estimate the market coefficients. For multi-stock Black--Scholes markets without factors, we further devise an algorithm and prove its performance guarantee by deriving a sublinear regret bound in terms of the Sharpe ratio. We then carry out an extensive empirical study implementing this algorithm to compare its performance and trading characteristics, evaluated under a host of common metrics, with a large number of widely employed portfolio allocation strategies on S\&P 500 constituents. The results demonstrate that the proposed continuous-time RL strategy is consistently among the best, especially in a volatile bear market, and decisively outperforms the model-based continuous-time counterparts by significant margins.

items.title: EWMA Principal Eigenportfolios of Equity Returns: Market Representation and Beta-Hedging Performance
items.summary: This study examines whether an adaptively estimated principal eigenportfolio improves equity beta hedging relative to capitalisation-weighted and equal-weighted market benchmarks. Using stock returns from a historically changing S&P 500 universe, it constructs a portfolio from the leading principal component of an exponentially weighted second-moment matrix of volatility-standardised returns. The resulting portfolio, EWMA-PC1, is compared with SPY and RSP under a common beta-hedging procedure across randomly generated portfolios of varying sizes and weighting schemes. Evaluation considers variance reduction and average pairwise residual correlation, with paired blockbootstrap inference. EWMA-PC1 exhibits broad market participation and achieves greater mean variance reduction and lower average residual correlation than SPY across all tested configurations. Its incremental advantage over RSP is smaller and mixed. For 50-stock Dirichlet portfolios, mean variance reduction is 92.17% under PC1, compared with 79.03% under SPY and 91.93% under RSP; RSP instead achieves greater mean variance reduction for multistock liquidity-tilted portfolios. Statistical evidence of improvement is more consistent against SPY than against RSP. These findings distinguish the extraction of a market-like component from incremental hedge effectiveness and highlight the importance of benchmark weighting and targetportfolio composition. The results concern gross statistical risk reduction and exclude additional trading, financing, and borrowing costs.

items.title: Re(Visiting) Time Series Foundation Models in Finance
items.summary: Financial time series forecasting is vital for trading, portfolio optimization, and risk management but is challenged by noisy, nonstationary, and heterogeneous data. Time series foundation models (TSFMs), inspired by large language models, aim to learn transferable temporal representations. Whether pre-training on massive, diverse datasets enables similar generalization to finance remains an open question. This study provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation of TSFMs in global financial markets using large-scale daily excess-return data. We assess zero-shot inference, fine-tuning, and pre-training from scratch against strong benchmarks. Off-the-shelf TSFMs generally perform poorly, while finance-native pre-training improves long-window gross portfolio performance. Larger pre-training datasets and synthetic augmentation improve selected specifications, particularly at longer input windows. Configuration changes have mixed effects across forecasting and portfolio metrics, and TSFMs do not consistently outperform strong benchmarks. These findings caution against uncritical AI adoption in finance, where insufficient validation can lead to unreliable forecasts and substantial financial losses.

items.title: Markets for Compute and Inference: Structure, Financing, and Risk Transfer
items.summary: Capacity to run large language models is rented by the accelerator-hour, and their output is sold by the million tokens. Both goods now have published price indices, an over-the-counter forward has traded on one, a perpetual future on one is listed offshore, and CME and ICE have specified futures on rental indices that await the United States regulator. We ask what in these two markets can be hedged, by whom, and at what price. Three findings stand out. First, the price that exchange contracts settle on is not the price that drives operators' revenue. Every contract references the published short-dated rental rate, while most revenue, and with it credit quality, comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed. Second, the token price and the rental rate are linked by an identity through throughput and margin, but they are different exposures, so a hedge on the rental rate does not hedge the cost of inference; at the measured capability of GPT-5 the cheapest list price fell by a factor of 17 in twelve months, and by far less at lower capability. Third, the demand for hedging already sits in credit agreements, as the years by which operators' debt outlives their contracted revenue. Filings cannot measure that gap, because debt is scheduled year by year while contracted revenue rarely is, and the one loan that prices it settles the risk by cash prepayment against a model only the parties see. We design a reverse convertible note through which leveraged operators could buy protection against falling rental rates. Its coupon depends steeply on the annualised volatility of the rental rate, which the two public indices put between about 5% and 89% according to how each is built and the horizon measured; across that range the fair one-year coupon runs from 4.1% to 31.5%.

items.title: Principal component error in high-dimensional factor models
items.summary: In a statistical factor model, principal components (or eigenvectors) of a sample covariance matrix serve as estimates of principal directions, the true drivers of co-movement of a collection of observed variables. We write the often substantial error in these estimates as a sum of two interpretable terms, which we show have almost sure asymptotic limits as the number of variables grows with sample size bounded. This scenario is commonplace in financial economics, genomics, machine learning and signal processing. Out-of-subspace error measures the distance from an estimate to the subspace spanned by population factor exposures. It can be expressed in terms of data, providing an estimable floor for asymptotic error. In-subspace error is driven by a rotation error within that subspace, which arises from the fixed sample size of the latent factor returns and cannot be estimated from data alone. We illustrate our error analysis with a three-factor simulation of the US public equity market, showing the dependence of the magnitude of the error and its components on dimension and sample size. In that simulation, out-of-subspace error dominates. Researchers who rely on principal component analysis to estimate factor models can use our results to quantify errors in model-based predictions and attributions.

items.title: Log-optimal portfolios for market models with regime switching
items.summary: This paper considers market models under regime switching mechanism with $D$ states, and analyses the log-optimal portfolio. It is the portfolio, with finite expected utility, that maximizes the logarithmic utility from terminal wealth. We consider a family $\mathbb{X}=(X^{(i)})_{i=1,...,D}$, of $D$-semimartingale models, among which our agent can switch to-and-from following a switching regime modelled by a continuous-time Markov Chain $α=(α_t)_{t\geq 0}$ with $α_0=1$. Then we define a general switching model $\widehat{X}$ that covers the existing cases, and study the impact of the stochasticity of the regime switching and its intrinsic risks on the optimal portfolio in many aspects. On the one hand, we single out the necessary and sufficient conditions on the pair $(\mathbb{X},α)$, which guarantee the existence of the optimal portfolio for $\widehat{X}$. On the other hand, we quantify the factors that fully affect and determine the increment in maximum expected logarithmic utility from terminal wealth for both models $\widehat{X}$ and $X^{(1)}$.

items.title: CFOs Meet LLMs
items.summary: Business sentiment is closely watched, but measurement is slow and costly: surveys reach a limited number of firms, arrive periodically, and take time to field and compile. We show that large language models hold the potential to address some of these shortcomings. We prompt an LLM to role-play as the CFO of a specific company on a specific date, for every public-company CFO who responded to the Duke--Federal Reserve CFO Survey from 2002- 2025. We find that LLM-generated forecasts reasonably match the cross-section of CFO expectations, with accuracy increasing with the amount of information provided to the LLM.

items.title: AllocFlow: End-to-End Portfolio Trading Action Generation from Raw Market Data
items.summary: Real-world portfolio management requires converting noisy market observations into coordinated, simultaneous allocations across multiple assets under shared capital constraints. Advances in forecasting models and alpha discovery help identify opportunities. However, traditional pipelines often decouple signal forecasting from portfolio construction, potentially misaligning learning with allocation and execution objectives. We present AllocFlow, an end-to-end flow-matching framework that directly generates joint portfolio allocations from raw multi-asset market histories. To capture dependencies among portfolio positions, AllocFlow employs a cross-asset flow Transformer conditioned on temporal market representations to generate continuous, signed position weights across all instruments jointly. To address the sample inefficiency and instability of learning continuous allocation policies from scratch, we establish a two-stage training scheme: strategy-supervised imitation shapes a structured distribution of candidate portfolios, followed by group-relative reinforcement learning (RL) that refines joint decisions using portfolio-level financial rewards and a frozen policy reference. On hourly cryptocurrency perpetual futures, RL refinement raises the annualized net return of the imitation policy from $27.79\%$ to $51.38\%$ and its Calmar ratio from $0.955$ to $4.043$, surpassing the teacher strategy on every metric, and AllocFlow reaches a Calmar ratio of $4.90$ on six further months of unseen 2026 data without retraining.

items.title: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization for Multi-Asset Portfolios
items.summary: Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) insulates asset allocation from Markowitz covariance ill-conditioning. However, classical tree clustering relies on static pairwise Pearson correlation, failing to capture time-varying, asymmetric downside risk contagion across multi-asset markets. We propose a unified deep graph machine learning architecture: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization (ST-GAT-NCO) for multi-asset tactical allocation. The framework extracts temporal momentum and downside risk dynamics via causal dilated 1D-convolutions, then deploys a multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) over dynamic market topologies to learn latent spatial node representations. These learned embeddings define an angular metric distance space that guides two-stage downside NCO optimization under institutional constraints and turnover smoothing. Evaluated over a 73-month non-anticipative walk-forward out-of-sample window (January 2020 to January 2026) across 13 global asset classes net of 10 bps transaction costs, ST-GAT-NCO achieves a 5.32% CAGR and 37.06% cumulative net return, delivering an excess Sharpe ratio of 0.30 and a Sortino ratio of 0.48. This substantially outperforms classical Minimum Variance (3.68% CAGR, 0.08 Sharpe), Hierarchical Risk Parity (2.65% CAGR), and Plain Symmetric NCO (4.11% CAGR, 0.15 Sharpe), while restricting maximum drawdown to -13.07% (versus -19.44% for Equal-Weight and -16.36% for Downside NCO) under a controlled one-way turnover of 15.31%/month. Regime analysis confirms active capital preservation across the 2020 COVID-19 crash, 2022 monetary tightening, and 2023-2026 disinflation rallies.

items.title: Toward an Admissibility Theory of Aharonov--Bohm Arbitrage
items.summary: This note develops a provisional admissibility framework for Aharonov-Bohm type arbitrage. Starting from a categorical filtration $F:\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mic}}^{\mathrm{op}}\to \mathsf{Prob}$ and its distortion on microscopic histories, we ask when a favorable closed microscopic loop can be realized as an executable relative ordinal arbitrage over an open macro-time interval. The history endofunctor $\mathsf{Hist}$ retains the staged decomposition of economic activities, while the twisted-arrow category $\operatorname{Tw}(\mathsf{Hist}(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mic}}))$ represents a microscopic loop as an arrow between distinct histories. An observable clock $Π: \mathsf{Econ} \to \mathcal T_{\mathrm{mac}}$ and a microscopic realization functor $J: \mathsf{Hist}(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mac}}) \to \operatorname{Tw}(\mathsf{Hist}(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mic}}))$ connect economic histories with their microscopic geometry. Executability is treated separately through configuration histories, capacity constraints, observations, and policies. This yields pathwise and almost-sure notions of execution. A finite foreign-exchange model illustrates stochastic execution, capacity failure, terminal settlement, and comparison with a benchmark strategy. A parameterized finite filtration is constructed whose nontrivial statewise distortion agrees exactly with the relative FX settlement multiplier. Hence the resulting filtration--policy model satisfies the bridge $V_*(π^q)=dF(γ)V_*(π^p),$ and, under order compatibility, realizes relative ordinal arbitrage. The remaining problem is to identify the filtration parameters from independent market primitives and to study stability under refinement.

items.title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
items.summary: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

items.title: PIRanNN: Random-Feature Pricing and Calibration under Jump-Diffusion and Stochastic-Volatility Models
items.summary: We study a random-feature method for pricing and calibrating European options under jump-diffusion (Merton, Kou) and stochastic-volatility (Heston, SABR) models. The network has one hidden layer with a probit activation and fixed random inner weights, so fitting it to the pricing equation, the payoff and the boundary conditions is a single regularised least-squares problem, with no iterative training. For Merton and Kou the jump integral of each feature is explicit, so no quadrature is needed. One factorisation of the least-squares matrix gives the price at every state and time, its Greeks, and the exact derivatives of the prices with respect to the model parameters for gradient-based calibration. For the jump models, subtracting the Black-Scholes price removes the payoff kink and reduces the pricing error by about two orders of magnitude. The method is then about as accurate as a standard Crank-Nicolson finite-difference scheme at the same run time, although a finite-difference scheme that also subtracts the Black-Scholes price is about two orders of magnitude more accurate still. On the test problems of a recent physics-informed neural network study, the method matches that network's accuracy in seconds instead of about half an hour. The calibration experiments show that a solver can fit the quotes and still return wrong parameters when its pricing error is not small compared with the effect of the parameters on the prices: without the subtraction the solver misses the jump parameters by up to 50%, and with it they are recovered to within 3%. For Heston and SABR, used as an applicability study with boundary conditions that need no reference prices, pricing errors are about one percent and the calibrated parameters are within about 15% of the true values.

items.title: Affine Pricing Models from Group Quantization and Holonomy
items.summary: The analytic tractability of affine pricing models is usually expressed through two complementary formulations: a coordinate-space pricing operator and an exponential-affine transform representation governed by generalized Riccati equations. We develop \emph{Affine Holonomy Group Quantization} (AHGQ) as a geometric framework in which these two formulations arise from the same underlying structure. The construction separates the affine pricing symbol into a homogeneous quadratic sector and a complementary affine sector. The first generates a finite-dimensional symplectic transport and a centrally extended Lie group, while the second is represented by a multiplicative holonomy carried by a thin-path groupoid. Their combination determines an affine Poincaré--Cartan form. Its characteristic dynamics reduce in momentum variables to the generalized Riccati system and its scalar amplitude, whereas the coordinate representation recovers the standard affine pricing operator. Representative Gaussian and square-root models illustrate the construction. The contribution is structural: AHGQ gives a common geometric origin to the coordinate and transform representations of continuous-path, time-homogeneous affine pricing models.

items.title: AI Governance for Institutional Readiness in Finance
items.summary: Agentic AI is gaining acceptance in asset management, but governance has not kept pace: 88\% of surveyed finance professionals report no operational governance framework for agentic AI, and only 24 of 75 large U.S. money managers disclosing AI use in Form ADV filings report a formal governance policy. We argue this gap is architectural: governance built for static validation does not survive continuously retrained agentic policies. We propose a four-layer framework (Policy, Engineering, Composition, Systemic) grounded in two distinct kinds of evidence, kept explicitly separate: two calibrated synthetic illustrations (a regret-covariance drift monitor; a crowding simulation showing joint drawdown risk rising from 39.2\% to 79.3\%), and three real, documented cases (a deployed LLM-embedding trading strategy, a \$45 billion discretionary fund's forced-deleveraging blowup, and a tribunal ruling holding an airline liable for its chatbot). The synthetic examples demonstrate computability from observable data; the cases demonstrate that the failure modes are not hypothetical. We provide a 90-day implementation sequence spanning trading and payments/customer-facing systems.

items.title: Dynamic portfolio selection under generalized disappointment aversion
items.summary: This paper addresses the continuous-time portfolio selection problem under generalized disappointment aversion (GDA). The implicit definition of the certainty equivalent within GDA preferences introduces time inconsistency to this problem. Within the class of bounded, right-continuous deterministic strategies, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for equilibrium in the form of a fully nonlinear integral equation. Investigating the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the integral equation, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium in this class. Our findings indicate that under disappointment aversion preferences, non-participation in the stock market is the unique equilibrium in this class. The semi-analytical equilibrium strategies obtained under the constant relative risk aversion utility functions reveal that, under GDA preferences, the investment proportion in the stock market consistently remains smaller than the investment proportion under classical expected utility theory. The numerical analysis shows that the equilibrium strategy's monotonicity concerning the two parameters of GDA preference aligns with the monotonicity of the degree of risk aversion. Finally, in a switching-drift market with a random expected return, we prove the existence of a non-deterministic equilibrium.

items.title: Herding or Racing? Decomposing Cross-Account Order-Flow Persistence in On-Chain Markets
items.summary: Most of the autocorrelation in trade signs on decentralized exchanges comes from pairs of trades sent by different wallets. For Uniswap v3, this has been read as herding dominating order splitting -- the reverse of what equity markets show. We show that this herding share mixes two quantities: the probability $p$ that consecutive orders come from the same account, which is small when thousands of wallets are trading, and the ratio $κ$ of cross-account to same-account sign correlation. For any $p$, $κ$ equals one under the public-signal benchmark of Tóth et al. and zero under independent order splitting. On Uniswap v3 USDC-WETH (one week each in 2023 and 2024), the herding share is 0.65-0.86, but $κ$ is only 0.05-0.10. On a fully on-chain EVM limit order book, the herding share is similar (0.61-0.87), but $κ$ is 0.72-0.76; among Uniswap swaps above USD 100k, it is 0.34-0.52. Where $κ$ is high, cross-account co-movement is mostly a race for the price on a centralized exchange. It is concentrated in orders a few blocks apart, and a cross-fitted gradient-boosted filter that sees only Binance data removes about three quarters or more of it. This race flow accounts for most of the losses of liquidity providers. We recommend reporting $κ$ alongside the herding share and modeling on-chain order flow as splitting traders plus arbitrageurs who respond to the centralized-exchange price.

items.title: Corporate Stances on Societal Issues in the US
items.summary: When do firms take public positions on divisive societal issues and why? We assemble a comprehensive dataset on corporate stance-taking in the United States, using large language models to read 52,000 news articles and press releases about 836 companies that belonged to the S&P 500 at any point between 2008 and 2025. We identify 9,917 stances on nine partisan issues such as climate change, abortion, and racial discrimination. We show that stance-taking increased fourfold after 2008 and peaked in 2021. It is overwhelmingly liberal and concentrated among the largest firms. A quarter of stances give no explicit business justification. Stance-taking is only weakly related to lobbying and campaign contributions and, unlike them, does not follow the electoral cycle. Instead, firms tend to speak when media coverage and public interest in an issue peak. Together, these findings suggest that stance-taking can be understood as a contribution to broad policy debates rather than a strategy to shape policies that affect firms' core business. Finally, we investigate whose views corporate stances represent. Consumer-facing firms take more stances, and firms whose consumers lean Democratic take more liberal stances on issues other than climate. Companies with larger shares of Democratic employees, executives, and board members also take more liberal stances. Exploiting within-firm variation, we find that having more Democrats among a company's leadership increases liberal stance-taking, while having more women increases stance-taking on gender-related issues and abortion.

items.title: Financial Resilience Evaluation: From Conditional Expectations to Dynamic Convex Risk Measures
items.summary: Financial resilience concerns whether, and how rapidly, a risky position recovers or deteriorates at a future time $t$, given the information available at time $s\leq t$. As a first step, the resilience rate was introduced as the expected instantaneous rate of change of a price or risk-assessment process. Because this quantity captures only the conditional mean of future increments, it cannot distinguish between positions with the same expected recovery but different conditional risk profiles. We obtain a richer characterization by evaluating such increments through a possibly nonlinear dynamic risk measure $ρ$. For an Itô process $π$ and a normalized, cash-additive $ρ$, we define the resilience evaluation as the $L^1$-limit of $\varepsilon^{-1}ρ_s(π_{t+\varepsilon}-π_t)$, as $\varepsilon\to 0^+$, whenever it exists. For a convex $ρ$ induced by BSDEs with Lipschitz or quadratic drivers, we prove existence and a dual representation: it is the worst-case conditional expectation, over zero-penalty measure changes, of an effective drift that combines the physical drift of $π$ with the risk adjustment assigned by $ρ$ to the volatility of $π$. We establish attainment of the optimal scenario and illustrate the scope of the construction and the role of the required assumptions through examples and counterexamples.

items.title: Risk measures for infinite-server queues driven by a Cox-BESQ process
items.summary: This paper analyses infinite-server queues driven by a Cox process whose stochastic arrival intensity follows a squared Bessel (BESQ) process. Exploiting the affine structure of the model and previously derived transform representations for infinite-server queue variables, we derive the joint moment-generating function (MGF) of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the time integral of the queue length at two or more dates. This enables a detailed analysis of the temporal evolution of infinite-server queues driven by a Cox-BESQ process. The availability of these explicit MGFs enables the development of risk measures for these variables, such as the joint moments of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the integral of the number of customers in the system over a time interval, conditional on one of these variables exceeding a critical threshold. These risk measures can be determined at one or two dates. They rely essentially on the explicit form of the MGF of the state variables and on Fourier representations of the risk measures. Numerical experiments demonstrate the practical implementation of the proposed methodology and highlight the relevance of the theoretical results.

items.title: Optimal Capital Injections in a Microlending Group under External Shocks
items.summary: Motivated by static models of group default in microlending, we study a dynamic problem in which the members of a lending group are exposed to external shocks, such as droughts or floods, and the manager of a common emergency fund decides at each shock how much capital to inject into the members who were hit. Shocks arrive at random times, the set of members that a shock hits may depend on which members the previous shock hit, and the losses may spill over to members who were not hit directly. Between shocks, the members' wealth follows a linear stochastic differential equation in which members support each other, and the fund grows with interest and member contributions up to a cap. The cost balances the members' shortfall below a poverty line, a welfare measure that contains a standard poverty measure as a special case, against the administrative cost of the injections and the benefit of keeping money in the fund. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process embedded at the shock times and prove that the embedded process is Markov with a weakly continuous transition kernel. When the discount rate exceeds a growth rate determined by the wealth dynamics, we show that the expected total cost is finite under every policy, that the finite-horizon optimal values converge to the infinite-horizon one at an explicit rate, and that there exists a stationary optimal injection policy, which can be chosen independent of calendar time.

items.title: Implied volatility models without static arbitrage
items.summary: We investigate the absence of static arbitrage in models describing the stochastic evolution of implied volatility surfaces. For Gaussian factor models, we derive explicit formulas for the probabilities of calendar spread, call spread and butterfly arbitrage, showing that these probabilities are strictly positive under suitable non-degeneracy conditions. We then develop a framework based on bounded stochastic factors and establish deterministic necessary and sufficient conditions for the absence of static arbitrage, together with simpler sufficient conditions. As an application, we construct an arbitrage free modification of the Cont and Vuletić model using Jacobi diffusions, preserving its main empirical features while eliminating static arbitrage.

items.title: Short Windows, Unmodelled Costs, Unknown Cutoffs: A Pre-Registered Evidence Audit of 91 LLM Trading Papers
items.summary: Papers on large-language-model (LLM) trading agents and alpha mining report Sharpe ratios that would be remarkable in any other part of empirical finance. We audit the evidence behind those numbers. Before coding a single paper we pre-registered a population of 91 papers from a curated corpus of LLM trading research, a ten-field coding rubric, an analysis script and five directional hypotheses, and committed all of them to version control. Every code is backed by a verbatim quote that a script checks against the paper's text, and a second, blind coder recoded a random 20%. Of the 75 papers with a trading test, 51% deduct no trading costs and only 9% model costs from data; the median test window is 12 months, and a quarter of windows are six months or shorter. Among the 51 papers whose test window is not known to lie after the model's training cutoff, 98% neither test after the cutoff, nor evaluate live, nor use a chronologically consistent model. Only 9% report a multiplicity-adjusted result, and just five papers combine deducted costs, a leakage control and a reported trial count. Two of the five hypotheses pass (short windows; uncontrolled look-ahead). Three fail: more papers report a trial count than we predicted, though most of those counts are repeated random seeds rather than the number of strategies searched; and the predicted links between headline Sharpe and test-window length, and between headline Sharpe and costs, are not detectable in the 13 papers that state a headline Sharpe in their abstract or conclusion. We release the codes, quotes and script, and propose a six-line reporting minimum.

items.title: Harvesting the Variance Risk Premium in Nuclear and Energy Equities: A Short-Put Portfolio Derisking Strategy
items.summary: We study whether nuclear and energy-adjacent equity options carry a harvestable variance risk premium. Using CRSP and OptionMetrics data for 2000-2024 on a universe of 49 optioned securities under 41 ticker labels, at-the-money implied volatility exceeds the volatility realized over the following 21 trading days in 18 of 25 years, and 29 of 41 tickers show a positive premium on signal days with t-statistics above 2. A fully mechanical cash-secured short-put book sells one put per name per month near 0.25 delta and 45 days to expiry, and exits on the first touch of take-profit at half premium, stop-loss at twice premium, or a 0.50-delta stop, marked daily at validated quote midpoints. Equal-weight and inverse-volatility weightings earn 8.3% and 7.1% a year at Sharpe ratios of 0.98 and 0.99 with maximum drawdowns of 16% and 13%, versus 15.5% a year, a Sharpe ratio of 0.80, and a 46% drawdown for an equal-weight stock book; in 2008 the put book loses 9.5% against the stock book's 37.2%, and the monthly correlation between the two is 0.62. Performance is reported before transaction costs, on a fixed present-day universe.

items.title: Local Stochastic Volatility Iterations
items.summary: We propose a calibration method for local stochastic volatility models that determines the leverage factor by a fixed-point iteration. Each iteration simulates the model with the current leverage factor and approximates the conditional expectation of the stochastic variance given the spot by a single regression in time and state, with a quasi-likelihood loss for positive responses. The resulting leverage factor is a smooth function of time and spot with relatively few parameters, which can in addition be refined directly against option quotes. We recalibrate the leverage factor to S&P 500 index options on the day of an interest rate announcement, keeping the parameters of a two-factor Bergomi model calibrated four weeks earlier. After five iterations, leverage factors with 63 and 143 coefficients reproduce the implied volatility surface fitted to the quotes within a few basis points over the quoted strikes, the smaller one except in the left wing, and further iterations change them little. A few regularized Gauss-Newton steps against the quotes then bring 87% and 95% of the liquid quotes inside their bid-ask intervals.

items.title: Who Should Be on the Panel? Task-Conditioned Persona Selection for LLM Trading Agents
items.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are built by fixing a cast of roles and then designing how the cast coordinates. Which agents should make up the group for a given task is left to the designer, and the same cast is reused for every task. Financial trading makes the cost of that choice visible: stocks trade differently, and the trading styles suited to one need not suit another. We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.

items.title: Incomplete-market CAPM equilibria in continuous time
items.summary: We study continuous-time CAPM equilibria with general mean-variance preferences of the form $U(μ,σ)$, where $U$ is strictly quasiconcave, increasing in the mean $μ$ and decreasing in the volatility $σ$ of terminal wealth. Our framework accommodates both financial and productive assets with nontradeable endowments. We allow for equilibria driven by general semimartingales in the case of linear mean-variance preferences and by continuous semimartingales in the case of general mean-variance preferences. The key insight is a connection between mean-variance efficiency and quadratic utility maximisation. We first characterise quadratic equilibria through an explicit family of equilibrium price processes indexed by the aggregate risk tolerance. We then show that each agent's optimal mean-variance strategy corresponds to a quadratic optimum with an endogenously determined risk tolerance. This correspondence reduces the mean-variance equilibrium problem to a one-dimensional fixed-point problem, whose solvability we establish using fine properties of (dynamic) mean-variance hedging and a novel stability result for quadratic BSDEs with BMO growth at the origin. Finally, examples illustrate how unspanned stochastic-volatility risk interacts with aggregate endowments to affect equilibrium asset prices, and how nonlinear mean-variance preferences influence equilibrium risk tolerance and asset-price comparative statics.

items.title: Mapping NGFS Climate Pathways to GICS Sectors: Application to Portfolio Decarbonization
items.summary: Portfolio climate alignment is limited by the mismatch between asset managers' sector classifications and those of climate scenarios. This article proposes an NGFS-GICS mapping based on the materiality of Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions rather than on semantic similarity. The mapping feeds a Sectoral Decarbonization Approach that down-scales NGFS trajectories into GICS sector pathways at portfolio level, adjusted for regional exposure. Applied to two illustrative ETF indices, it shows how sectoral composition and regional trajectories shape a portfolio's financed emissions pathway. The framework is transparent, asset-class agnostic and usable for internal exercises such as climate stress tests.

items.title: Well-Posedness of Semimartingale Optimal Transport with Partial Marginal Constraints for Model Calibration
items.summary: We study the well-posedness and stability of a semimartingale optimal transport problem with partial marginal constraints at several maturities, motivated by the calibration of financial models to finitely many option prices. We connect its probabilistic and Eulerian formulations within the Benamou--Brenier framework. Under convex-duality assumptions, we establish strong duality for every price vector in the extended-value sense and existence of a primal optimizer whenever the value is finite. Under additional PDE assumptions, we establish dual attainment on the relative interior of the admissible price set, together with uniqueness of the primal optimizer. Under further non-degeneracy assumptions, we show that this price set has nonempty interior, on which the dual optimizer is unique and depends locally Lipschitz continuously on the prices. The analysis combines convex methods with regularity and local strong convexity results for Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman solution maps established in a companion paper. For a fixed deterministic initial state, we also prove continuity of the optimal law on path space in the adapted Wasserstein distance of order two as prices vary within this interior. This stability concerns the optimizer over the full admissible class of semimartingale laws, allowing characteristics that depend on the past. The framework accommodates bounded uniformly continuous payoffs, including European puts in log-price coordinates, without payoff regularization or spatial truncation.

items.title: A Horizon-Specific Attribute-Conditioned Neural Network for Estimating Health-State Transition Probabilities in Irregular Longitudinal Data: The LANTERN Framework
items.summary: Accurate estimation of health-state transition probabilities is essential for long-term care insurance modeling. Conventional actuarial multi-state models provide an interpretable framework but may be restrictive in capturing nonlinear relationships and accumulated health histories from irregular longitudinal observations. This paper proposes LANTERN, a history-dependent neural framework that integrates recurrent health representations, elapsed observation time, and adaptive demographic and socioeconomic attribute conditioning to estimate horizon-specific transition probabilities among Healthy, Mild disability, Severe disability, and Death states. Using longitudinal Health and Retirement Study data, we evaluate our model against a recurrent neural network, multinomial logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees, and an actuarial continuous-time Markov chain across one-, two-, and three-year forecast horizons. At the primary two-year horizon, LANTERN achieves competitive predictive accuracy and calibration, with improvements over selected benchmarks. Its aggregated transition-matrix estimates outperform multinomial logistic regression and are comparable to those of the strongest remaining benchmarks. These findings suggest that history-conditioned neural estimation provides a flexible and competitive approach to estimating horizon-specific health-state transition probabilities, with potential applications in actuarial long-term care modeling.

items.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
items.summary: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

items.title: Price-impact Martingale optimal transport
items.summary: Martingale optimal transport (MOT) provides model-independent bounds for option prices calibrated to vanilla options, assuming frictionless trading in the underlying. In this work, we consider the case where dynamic trading incurs quadratic temporary price impact. First, we prove a duality result for the superhedging price. In particular, the primal of the duality relaxes the strict martingale constraint by penalizing the deviation from a specific martingale. Second, for one asset and one trading period, we interpret this price-impact martingale optimal transport (PIMOT) as a weak optimal transport (WOT) problem, and provide a characterization in the spirit of Wasserstein projection. Finally, we justify that PIMOT is an interpolation between MOT and classical optimal transport (OT), and derive the convergence rate to both sides. Numerical examples with SPX option data show how the price bounds per claim depend on the order size.

items.title: Improving Algorithmic Trading for BESS on Intraday Electricity Markets through Distributional Price Forecasts
items.summary: Grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) are becoming increasingly important in short-term energy markets, where they help balance fluctuations in variable renewable generation. In many countries, the continuous intraday market is the most important wholesale market for BESS to monetize their flexibility. In this paper, we propose an extension to the myopic rolling intrinsic policy that incorporates intraday price forecasts tailored specifically to the BESS trading problem. While a large literature addresses intraday price forecasting, most existing work focuses on volume-weighted prices during the last hours of trading and consequently fails to capture the features most relevant to BESS trading. Our approach addresses this gap by introducing a novel target variable derived from the limit order book and its dynamics. The resulting forecasts are designed to inform the optimization about future profit opportunities while preserving computational efficiency and avoiding the burden of full stochastic optimization. In a realistic high-frequency simulation setting covering 2023 and 2024, our method improves profits by up to 42% over the naive rolling intrinsic formulation. We further analyze the relationship between forecast accuracy, stability, and financial performance, establishing a clear inverse relationship between accuracy and stability. Finally, we find evidence that BESS size and duration jointly influence both overall profitability and the marginal benefit of incorporating forecasts.

items.title: Media Trading with Censored Auction Prices: A Stochastic Control and Reinforcement Learning Approach
items.summary: In real-time bidding, marketing agencies must balance campaign performance, transaction margins and the use of a finite advertising budget. A key difficulty is that market-clearing prices are typically observed only when bids are successful, so the information available for subsequent decisions depends on the bidding policy. We formulate this problem using a continuous-time stochastic control model with a latent price process. To construct a price signal, we consider parallel exploratory subcampaigns in which bids are randomized subject to an upper bound. Under a stylized cross-sectional sampling model, the resulting price estimator is consistent and satisfies a mean-square error bound of order $N^{-1}$, where $N$ is the number of exploratory observations. We then describe a model-based approach combining forward-equation calibration with Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman policy iteration and a physics-informed neural network, alongside an entropy-regularized actor-critic approach based on observable information in a model-free setting. Synthetic experiments illustrate the estimator and the computational procedures. The framework clarifies the decision and information trade-offs faced by the agency, while distinguishing full-information benchmarks and estimated-price policies from the genuinely partially observed control problem.

items.title: Beyond Co-Movement: Locality by Exposures Enables a Joint Factor-Graph Framework for Portfolio Diversification
items.summary: Current portfolio construction methods are either agnostic to the effects of idiosyncratic shocks (standard factor models) or to the latent data structure driving systematic returns (recent graph-based approaches). This presents an opportunity to combine the complementary market aspects captured by the factor and graph domains, allowing asset allocations to operate directly on the underlying market structure, rather than on its observed co-movement or its finite-sample artefacts. In this work, we introduce the Mutually-INformed Graph-Locality and Exposures framework (MINGLE), which mutually regularises the factor and graph domains by redefining graph locality through systematic factor exposure profiles, rather than via observed co-movements. This is formalised through a unified Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) framework that jointly learns a latent factor representation and its induced graph topology directly from market returns. The resulting exposure-similarity graph aligns more closely with established economic sectors than conventional correlation-based graphs. Portfolios constructed from this representation are shown to consistently outperform their correlation-based counterparts across a range of volatility regimes and transaction cost levels. For rigour, paired statistical testing confirms that these gains stem from the reconciliation of the graph and factor domains.

items.title: Deep Learning of Robust Market Making under Regime-Switching Order Flow
items.summary: Classical market-making strategies based on stochastic control, such as the Avellaneda--Stoikov and the Guéant--Lehalle--Fernandez-Tapia (GLFT) extension, provide closed-form quoting approximations, but rest on assumptions that break down at realistic microstructure timescales. One of them is that order flow is stationary, while empirical evidence points to the existence of regimes, possibly associated with algorithmic execution of metaorders. In our experiments, persistent directional flow makes stationary controllers unprofitable. In this paper, we develop a deep reinforcement-learning market maker (RLMM)---a Rainbow-style distributional deep Q-network which is calibrated and tested in a zero-intelligence limit order book. We find that, in the stationary setting, RLMM outperforms GLFT at comparable levels of profit and loss (PnL) dispersion. The stationarily trained RLMM is more robust to flow asymmetry than GLFT, but still suffers inventory saturation and large drawdowns under persistent directional flow. Training a separate RLMM under regime-switching flow, with a Bayesian flow-belief signal and a queue-adjusted quote exposure signal, restores positive mean PnL in our experiments. A final scenario-bandit step prioritizes low-return scenarios and improves performance under varying regime persistence and directional correlation.

items.title: Dynamic Scenario-Based Portfolio Optimization for Multi-Asset ETFs
items.summary: Portfolio outcomes may depend as much on trading restrictions as on how returns are modeled. We compared historical moving-window returns with conditional scenarios from ARMA--GARCH models and a Student-$t$ copula for 30 U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds. Matched mean--variance and conditional value-at-risk portfolios were evaluated under long-only and limited long--short bounds over 946 sessions. Historical portfolios had higher observed reward--risk ratios in most comparisons, but no paired difference remained significant after multiple-testing adjustment. Conditional scenarios did not consistently reduce realized downside risk. We distinguished changes in target weights from trades required to rebalance holdings after market movements. Relaxing the target-adjustment limit changed exposures, turnover, and some returns more than varying scenario count or seed in the examined tests. These findings suggest that assessments of conditional return inputs should consider portfolio constraints and trading requirements.

items.title: Verifiable Settlement and Pricing for Local Energy Markets: Architecture and Deployment on Hyperledger Besu
items.summary: We implement privacy-preserving local electricity exchanges using an automated market maker on the Hyperledger Besu network under QBFT consensus. The proposed protocol operator collects individual electricity positions off-chain and publishes aggregate supply and demand on the blockchain, where smart contracts compute market prices every fifteen minutes. Individual positions remain off-chain; Poseidon2 commitments and UltraHonk zeroknowledge proofs, generated from Noir circuits, verify aggregation, payments, and daily balance updates. The architecture retains community coordination while making financial execution independently auditable. Signed receipts and member-triggered recourse prevent unverified or partial settlement. In a ten-household experiment using simulated US residential profiles, daily settlement uses approximately 19 million gas and produces eight-member proofs in 2.4 seconds. Over four simulated days, local trading covers 34.4% of demand and reduces grid-only costs by 30.5% under assumed tariffs. Numerically computed __-Nash Equilibrium electricity profiles capture 83-88% of the social planner surplus.

items.title: Accuracy Is Not Welfare: Evaluating AI Buyers under Strategic Price Complexity in a Synthetic Duopoly
items.summary: AI buying agents may alter sellers' incentives as well as consumers' decisions. In a synthetic duopoly, we evaluate price-comparison pipelines on a fixed menu and in empirical correlated-equilibrium games. Calculator assistance selects an optimal offer 84.00% of the time, versus 68.57% under verified-total disclosure, yet disclosure has a 20.14-unit higher consumer-worst equilibrium surplus. A frozen-strategy holdout comparison favors disclosure, while re-solving equilibria under scenario resampling produces a range spanning zero. These model-based results show why accuracy, loss severity, seller incentives, and welfare incidence require separate measurement.

items.title: On the continuity of martingale optimal transport in higher dimensions
items.summary: We investigate qualitative and quantitative continuity of martingale optimal transport under perturbations of both marginals in dimensions $d\geq2$. We assume that each pair of marginals admits a reference martingale coupling whose density relative to the product of its marginals is bounded above and away from zero, uniformly along the sequence. If the limiting target measure is not carried by a hyperplane, we prove continuity under $W_1$-convergence for continuous costs of at most linear growth, assuming only finite first moments. For Lipschitz costs, a uniform $p$-moment bound on the targets, $p>1$, yields an explicit stability estimate with exponent $(1-1/p)/2$; uniformly bounded target supports give exponent $1/2$. The proof constructs a correction of couplings with small martingale bias while preserving both marginals. Truncated moment corrections allow the target measure to have unbounded support. The construction also shows that every martingale coupling of the limiting marginals can be approximated in $W_1$ by martingale couplings of the approximating marginals. We also discuss counterexamples showing that neither the uniform density condition nor non-degeneracy of the limiting target measure can be omitted in general.

items.title: Optimal Trading Speed on Blockchain
items.summary: On blockchain-based exchanges, faster blocks weaken the priority-fee competition among arbitrageurs and shift rents from the block producer to them. Equilibrium liquidity peaks at an interior block speed; beyond a threshold, an active liquidity provider cream-skims and passive capital shrinks. Evidence from the Base Flashblocks upgrade, a tenfold block-speed increase, confirms the predictions. Priority-fee bids decrease sharply and arbitrageurs' net profit rises. The active liquidity provider rebalances faster, avoids toxic flow, and earns a higher profit. Pool depth falls and effective spreads widen despite closer tracking of external prices.

items.title: Novel Esscher concepts for informational risks and valuation in market models under random horizon
items.summary: This paper considers the setting constituted by the triplet $(S,\mathbb{F},τ)$. The pair $(S,\mathbb{F})$ is the initial model where $S$ is the discounted price process of risky assets (Stocks) and $\mathbb{F}$ is the ``public" flow of information that is available to all agents over time. $τ$ is an arbitrary random time, which might not be seen through the flow $\mathbb{F}$, and it represents a default time in credit risk and a death time of an insured in life insurance where mortality and/or longevity risks present serious challenges. For simplicity, we suppose $S$ follows a geometric jump-diffusion model with stochastic volatiles and $\mathbb{F}$ is generated by a Brownian motion and Poisson process. In this setting, we address how the Esscher densities and/or measures notions can evolves with the informational risk induced by $τ$. In fact, we introduce the notion of Esscher with degrees-of-freedom associated to the informational risks generated by $τ$. On the one hand, we give various and complete characterizations of these Esscher notions in our informational setting. On the other hand, we fully characterize the Escher-prices bounds, for vulnerable claims (claims built on the occurrence of $τ$), using constrained backward stochastic differential equations (CBSDEs for short hereafter) that appear to be novel as well.

items.title: TradeMech: A Method to Multilaterally Net Trades Without Altering Counterparty Exposure
items.summary: Financial markets such as bond, derivatives, and repo markets form networks of interdependent obligations. Existing multilateral netting methods typically trade off the extent of netting against preservation of counterparty exposure: central clearing reallocates exposure to a central counterparty, while trade compression may alter bilateral counterparty relationships. TradeMech is a mechanism for markets in which one or two homogeneous fungible objects are traded. The mechanism transforms a network of initial bilateral contracts into chains and cycles, nets the designated object multilaterally on those chains and cycles, and replaces initial contracts with multiparty contracts whose assigned trades remain fractions of the original bilateral trades. The construction achieves maximal multilateral netting of the designated object while preserving each agent's contractual profit and preserving the location of counterparty risk. When a party fails to pre-commit a required object, the affected assigned trade is recovered as a bilateral contract between the same original counterparties and the remaining assigned trades are re-netted on residual chains, so no new counterparty exposure is created.

items.title: Convergence rates for truncated and discretised signature expansions
items.summary: Linear expansions in Brownian Stratonovich signatures, which originate in stochastic Taylor expansions, are increasingly used to represent and model processes with memory. Their numerical use requires truncating the signature at a level $M$ and discretising the driving path along $N$ steps. Under a simple growth condition on the coefficients of the linear expansion, we establish strong and weak convergence rates for both approximations, uniformly in time. The strong truncation error decays like $(B^M/(M!)^\varepsilon)^a$ for some constant $B$, uniformly in $N$, where $\varepsilon$ measures the growth of the coefficients and $a$ the regularity of the test function; the weak error does not improve on it. The discretisation error is of order $N^{-a/2}$ in $L^p$, and $N^{-1}$ weakly for polynomial test functions, uniformly in $M$. All these rates are sharp for polynomial test functions, and $M$, $N$ can be chosen independently. We extend the estimates to errors in probability, on distribution functions and on risk measures, and illustrate them on stochastic delay equations, Volterra processes and option pricing in signature volatility models.

items.title: Breaking the Trend: How to Avoid Cherry-Picked Signals
items.summary: Our empirical results show a good fit with the theoretical Sharpe formula of a trend-following strategy depending on the parameter of the signal, which was derived by Grebenkov and Serror (2014). That empirical fit suggests that a mean-reversion process with only one time scale is enough to model the trend-following mechanism at the average scale of CTAs and that, as a consequence, a single simple EMA appears sufficient to capture the trend. Using a complex basket of different sophisticated indicators as signal therefore does not seem to be necessary and exposes to the risk of cherry-picking.

items.title: Portfolio-Size Constraints on Default Correlation: Exact Coherence Tests and Sharp Asymptotic Bounds
items.summary: An absorbing default process imposes joint restrictions on cumulative default distributions across horizons. We characterize these restrictions for finite homogeneous portfolios. For binomial mixtures whose mixing distribution functions cross at most once, stochastic ordering of the entire default count is equivalent to two inequalities: the probability of no defaults must be nonincreasing and the probability of all defaults must be nondecreasing. In the one-factor Gaussian model, these inequalities give an exact interval of admissible later correlations, obtained from two scalar equations. The intervals are nested as portfolio size increases. If the earlier and later default probabilities are $p_0<p_1$ and the earlier latent correlation is $ρ_0\in(0,1)$, both interval boundaries approach $ρ_0$ at rate $(\log n)^{-1/2}$, with common leading magnitude $ρ_0\sqrt{2(1-ρ_0)}[Φ^{-1}(p_1)-Φ^{-1}(p_0)]$. We also give a constructive absorbing coupling, an exact sequential repair, differential conditions for smooth horizon curves, and a finite-size certificate of incompatibility. Log-domain quadrature, bracketed root finding, and deterministic numerical experiments evaluate the intervals and verify the restrictions on the full count distribution. The framework provides a feasibility analysis of prescribed horizon laws.

items.title: Aproximación práctica a los métodos de selección de portafolios de inversión
items.summary: This paper explores the practical approach to portfolio selection methods for investments. The study delves into portfolio theory, discussing concepts such as expected return, variance, asset correlation, and opportunity sets. It also presents the efficient frontier and its application in the Markowitz model, which employs mean-variance optimization techniques. An alternative approach based on the mean-semivariance model is introduced. This model accounts for the skewness and kurtosis of the asset return distribution, providing a more comprehensive view of risk and return. The study also addresses the practical implementation of these models, including the use of genetic algorithms to optimize portfolio selection. Additionally, transaction costs and integer constraints in portfolio optimization are considered, demonstrating the applicability of the Markowitz model. -- Este documento explorar la aproximación práctica a los métodos de selección de portafolios para inversiones. El estudio profundiza en la teoría de los portafolios, discutiendo conceptos como el rendimiento esperado, la varianza, la correlación entre activos y los conjuntos de oportunidades. También presenta la frontera eficiente y su aplicación en el modelo de Markowitz, que utiliza técnicas de optimización media-varianza. Se introduce un enfoque alternativo basado en el modelo media-semivarianza. Este modelo tiene en cuenta la asimetría y la curtosis de la distribución de retornos de los activos, proporcionando una visión más completa de riesgo y rendimiento. El estudio también aborda la implementación práctica de estos modelos, incluyendo el uso de algoritmos genéticos para optimizar la selección de portafolios. Además, se consideran los costos de transacción y las restricciones enteras en la optimización del portafolio.
