We further provide an analogous algorithm for the submodular utility case. Finally, beyond forest communication hierarchies, we rule out an FPTAS for the sender's optimal utility even in the symmetric utility case, unless P=NP.

items.title: Coal Mining, Women's Work, and Local Demographic Change: Evidence from Interwar Japan
items.summary: This paper examines how coal mining shaped local demographic change in interwar Japan, focusing on the role of women's work. Coal mines initially employed married couples as underground teams, offering women wages well above those in textile mills. The mechanization of haulage and the subsequent revision of labor regulations, enforced in 1933, removed most women from the pits. Linking mine locations with municipal-level census and vital statistics, I find that coal mining substantially increased local populations, mainly through the inflow of workers, whereas marriage and fertility rates in mining areas were lower than in surrounding areas. After women were removed from the pits, these gaps narrowed. Early-life mortality was higher in mining areas and increased with the number of female miners, consistent with occupational hazards to pregnant women, whereas there is little evidence of pollution channels.

items.title: Truthful compromise and insurance on a sphere
items.summary: Can public choice without transfers insure conflicting interests when action intensity is fixed? We require truthful reporting for every increasing-concave evaluation of alignment with private ideals. On a sphere, efficiency at profiles with at most three ideal directions forces fixed-weight random dictatorship; weaker tests suffice in two and three dimensions. From four dimensions, binary efficiency permits committees to insure members by placing outcome risk orthogonally to their reports. We identify restrictions shared by all mechanisms with these incentives and binary efficiency: binary winning probabilities determine mean outcomes at every profile and individual alignment distributions at planar three-camp profiles. When these probabilities depend only on camp size, complete insurance at balanced equilateral disagreement requires dimension proportional to population. In contrast, committees reduce each participant's welfare loss relative to certain zero alignment to any prescribed positive fraction of the equal-weight random-dictatorship loss in a population-independent dimension.

items.title: Random Utility Models in the Consumption-Budget Setting: Vertex and Network-Flow Characterizations
items.summary: This note supplements our paper \textit{Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations} and serves two purposes: 1. We clarify the conceptual distinctions between two classes of random utility models (RUM): those in the consumption-budget setting \citep{kitamura2019nonparametric} (hereafter KS) and those in the finite-alternative setting (e.g., Chapter~7 of \cite{chambers2016revealed}). In particular, we show (Theorem 1) that each rational type, as defined in KS, can be obtained as a coordinate projection of the deterministic choice vector induced by a strict preference ranking that satisfies what we call a patch-monotonicity condition. 2. We generalize the network-flow characterization for finite-alternative RUM in \cite{fiorini2004short} to the consumption-budget setting (Theorem 2). Specifically, we show that a vector of choice probabilities in the consumption-budget setting is rationalizable in the KS sense if and only if it is the image of a unit flow on a multi-arc powerset digraph under a fixed linear map. The key distinction is that our digraph allows multiple arcs between the same pair of nodes, whereas the digraph in Fiorini has at most one arc between any pair of nodes.

items.title: Post-Selection Inference for Partially Identified Parameters
items.summary: Partial identification of parameters such as average treatment effects, average partial effects and welfare is particularly common when using observational data and experimental data with imperfect compliance due to the endogeneity of individuals' treatment uptake. In this setting, the researcher is typically interested in a treatment or policy that is either selected from the estimated set of best-performers or arises from a data-dependent selection rule. In this paper, we develop new inference tools for partially-identified parameters chosen via these forms of selection. We develop three types of confidence intervals for data-dependent and partially-identified parameters, discuss how they apply to several examples of interest and prove their uniform asymptotic validity under weak assumptions.

items.title: Benefits and Costs of Adaptive Sampling
items.summary: Multi-armed bandits are widely used for sequential experimentation in clinical trials, public policy treatment, recommendation systems, and online platforms. While regret minimization and valid inference from adaptively collected data have each been studied individually, one question remains: when does adaptivity \emph{improve estimation precision} relative to uniform designs, and how should inference be balanced against the online cost of experimentation? We first study arm-level mean estimation under mean-squared-error (MSE) objectives. We characterize when an adaptive Neyman allocation, which allocates samples according to arm variance, yields strict MSE improvements over uniform sampling in finite samples. When there is variance heterogeneity across arms, these improvements arise at modest sample sizes, clarifying that adaptivity can be preferable for inference not only asymptotically, but also in finite-sample settings. We then study a joint inference--regret objective that accounts for the cost of assigning units to inferior arms during experimentation. We propose three policies: the Plug-in Oracle Rate Policy, Static-Allocation Rate Policy, and Neyman-Adaptive Rate Policy, all of which attain the oracle-optimal asymptotic rate. The latter two offer computationally efficient and easy-to-implement alternatives by combining existing regret-minimizing algorithms with inference-oriented sampling through closed-form mixing rules, avoiding repeated numerical optimization while being managerially interpretable. We compare their finite-sample statistical performance through simulations and empirically calibrated applications. The results highlight the relative strengths of our policies across instances and their tradeoffs between joint inference--regret performance and computational cost.

items.title: Approximating an Ideal Experiment with Induced Order Statistics
items.summary: Many economic questions concern the conditional distribution of an outcome at a fixed covariate value. We refer to observing i.i.d.\ draws from this distribution as an \emph{ideal experiment}, under which many statistical procedures admit exact, finite-sample guarantees. When the covariate is continuously distributed, however, this ideal experiment is unavailable. We provide a general method for approximating this ideal experiment using \emph{induced order statistics}, the outcomes attached to the nearest observed covariates. We derive explicit bounds on the approximation error in Hellinger and total variation distances. These bounds quantify how local approximation errors accumulate as the nearest-neighbor sample grows and provide a unified way to transfer rejection and coverage guarantees across statistical procedures. Under quadratic mean differentiability and local regularity of the covariate distribution, the bounds apply to both interior and boundary conditioning points and give explicit conditions on the growth of the nearest-neighbor sample. We illustrate the approach in four distinct applications: covariate balance testing in regression discontinuity designs, conditional quantile inference, conformal prediction at a fixed covariate value, and policy-irrelevance testing under network interference.

items.title: Orthogonal Scores and Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Possibly Misspecified GMM
items.summary: We develop Neyman orthogonal scores for GMM models that remain valid when the moment conditions may fail to hold. Existing score constructions typically require the moment conditions to hold exactly, which may fail in over-identified models, where the number of moment functions exceeds the number of parameters. We construct \emph{misspecification-robust} orthogonal score that has a closed form; it is the conventional orthogonal score plus adjustment terms, for the estimation of the Jacobian and of the weighting matrix, which are proportional to the population moment and vanish under correct specification. The moment functions may depend on nonparametric or machine learning first steps, and we show that double/debiased machine learning (DML) combined with the proposed scores and cross-fitting provides uniformly valid inference for a low-dimensional GMM estimand, while the conventional DML standard errors are inconsistent when the moment conditions fail. We illustrate the results in the partially linear instrumental variables (PLIV) model and in the local average treatment effects (LATE) model with multiple instruments.

items.title: AI and the Two Margins of Work: Why Job Losses Show Up Before Job Creation
items.summary: Technological change acts on labor demand at two margins: adjustment within established activities and the creation of additional activities, often by new firms. Payroll statistics record the first promptly and the second late. In the computing era, firms that entered in 1978 or later held 42 percent of payroll by 1998 and entering cohorts kept about 80 percent of their payroll after five years; in the industries most exposed to automation, incumbents contracted before entrants accumulated, a sequence that is precise early in the period and suggestive by its end. We develop a model in which one AI capability lowers the full cost of acceptable output in existing production and makes additional projects worth attempting, with founder effort separate from hired hours. If operating products re-scale instantly, automation displaces no aggregate hours; if they take time, hours fall first and recover as incumbents re-expand and new products arrive, with the long-run sign set by income effects. Establishment job flows through the first quarter of 2026 show no gradient on language-model exposure on either margin, which is what the model predicts under the observed adoption path and also what no effect on payroll would look like; studies with founding-task exposure find entry rising 10 to 20 percent. We propose a net reinstatement ratio and show that statistics which record new work late overstate displacement for years.

items.title: Dynamic Pooling and Regional Participation in Deceased-Donor Organ Allocation
items.summary: Moving from geographically fragmented to pooled waiting lists in deceased-donor organ transplantation can improve efficiency, but it raises concerns about regional fairness and participation incentives. This paper studies Pareto gains from such transitions in a multiclass queueing model with impatient agents, perishable items, and a tractable homogeneous compatibility friction. In contrast to standard approaches that emphasize static match quality or overlook regional incentives in dynamic contexts, this analysis identifies dynamic risk pooling as the primary source of Pareto improvements for regions. Pooling reduces organ waste resulting from stochastic supply-demand fluctuations, temporal mismatches, and random compatibility outcomes. Although this dynamic surplus theoretically enables Pareto improvements, a purely utilitarian policy that treats all patients equally across regions often fails to achieve these improvements when regions are asymmetric. In these situations, utilitarian redistribution removes an excessive number of organs from high-supply regions and violates their participation constraints. To address this conflict, it is demonstrated that the set of achievable utilities can be represented by mixtures of static priority index policies. Building on this structure, the Constrained Pareto Frontier Search (CPFS) is proposed as a polynomial-time procedure that computes an approximately optimal allocation policy with arbitrarily small participation-constraint violations, implemented as a single priority list with a lottery at registration. The results indicate that, by adjusting priority indices to ensure redistribution remains within the gains from pooled supply, demand, and compatibility risk, policymakers can achieve global efficiency while maintaining local participation incentives.

items.title: Setting Optimal Reserve Prices using Fine-Tuned Language Models
items.summary: Online auction houses must set reserve prices for highly differentiated products whose unstructured descriptions contain valuable demand information. Existing approaches generally require managers to specify product attributes in advance. We ask whether a language model can instead learn from listing descriptions and historical bids to set item-specific reserve prices before bidding begins. We fine-tune a pretrained text embedding language model using the structural likelihood of auction bids as its training objective. This directs representation learning toward the valuation distribution that determines the reserve decision. We show that consecutive upper bids identify the tail information needed to set an optimal reserve without observing or modeling the number of potential bidders. A split-sample estimator learns the representation on one half of the data and conducts structural estimation and inference conditional on that representation on the other. We apply the method to approximately 65,800 online used-vehicle auctions. With seller values calibrated to match the sale rate among listings, the model implies a counterfactual net increase of $165.8 million, representing a 14.6% increase above the incumbent reserve policy. The framework translates a listing description and a seller's value into an item-specific reserve recommendation without constructing a product taxonomy or requiring a bid history for the item being priced. It provides an approach to adapting language models for operational decisions in marketplaces where products are heterogeneous and demand-relevant information is recorded in text.

items.title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Bellman Tournaments
items.summary: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because estimation errors in fitted $Q$-functions and occupancy ratios cannot be directly evaluated using held-out transition data. Existing Bellman-residual-based validation methods often require auxiliary regressions, while many minimax-based methods require optimization over separate critic classes. We propose pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a family of penalized Bellman tournament methods that reduces validation to computing held-out sample averages. PBV constructs critics from pairwise candidate differences, on the log scale for occupancy ratios, and selects the candidate with the smallest worst-case penalized score. This construction approximates oracle critics given by $Q$-function errors and log ratios of candidate to true occupancy ratios, whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. Critic penalties account for approximation error under candidate-class misspecification. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. For $Q$-function selection, unweighted PBV avoids importance weighting but requires a coercivity condition on a quadratic form induced by the Bellman operator. Importance-weighted PBV (IW-PBV) uses marginalized importance weighting to exploit Bellman contraction under the target-policy occupancy measure, avoiding this condition. For occupancy-ratio selection, adjoint PBV (A-PBV) exploits KL contraction of the adjoint Bellman operator to obtain oracle guarantees under the offline data law. On Hopper and DeepOPE, unweighted PBV is competitive with LSTD-Tournament, often achieving higher accuracy on Hopper, while importance weighting can further improve performance under controlled overlap.

items.title: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression
items.summary: Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: at least 50% of the observational causal studies we review in leading journals state or imply it, while 7% describe an imputation model. We develop a framework for when complete-case regression consistently estimates the population average treatment effect (ATE). With a constant unit-level treatment effect, two checks suffice: whether covariates and the missingness indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools within-covariate comparisons appropriately, possibly using inverse propensity weighting. A collider--mediator illustration highlights the first check: the same missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism can require different adjustment choices. With heterogeneous effects, conditional effects must be transportable to the population and be reweighted to its population distribution. These formal results provide practical checks for applied researchers to run complete case regressions, recover existing guidance as special cases, and are illustrated with applications across fields.

items.title: Maximum score and non-smooth M-estimators with multiway dependence
items.summary: Under i.i.d. sampling, the maximum score estimator of Manski (1975) converges at the cube-root rate to a non-Gaussian limit, and under median independence alone no regular estimator attains the parametric rate Chamberlain (1986). We show that, under multiway dependence and low-level conditions, the estimator is asymptotically normal at a parametric rate in the smallest number of clusters and, when the cluster-level variance is non-degenerate, as fast as regular estimators such as probit. The result rests on a general theory for non-smooth M-estimators, under which a modified bootstrap is first-order valid given a consistent Hessian estimate. With two-way clustering a cube-root term can remain. We then develop two-scale non-standard asymptotics, in which the limit is a Gaussian vector plus an independent Chernoff-type vector and either term may dominate, along sequences of laws from a non-degenerate cluster-level variance to the degenerate case. Under high-level conditions, the symmetric bootstrap intervals for suitable scalar parameters control size uniformly over such classes of laws, asymptotically exactly where the Gaussian term dominates and conservatively otherwise.

items.title: Choice via Dual Ownership
items.summary: When there are multiple agents (or rationales), an ownership rule assigns the choice for each menu to one of them. We study choice under dual ownership, where decision control alternates between two preferences. The main contribution is the behavioral characterization of a rule that endogenously decides ownership to maximize consensus. We also axiomatize two simpler exogenous rules. Identification results are provided for each rule.

items.title: Contractual Structure and Obvious Manipulation in Many-to-Many Matching
items.summary: We study how contractual structure affects worst-case and best-case obvious manipulation in many-to-many matching with substitutable preferences. Efficient individually rational mechanisms rule out best-case obvious manipulations on both the full substitutable domain and the unitary domain. Under simple and economically natural conditions on hospitals' choices, every stable mechanism on the full domain admits obvious manipulations in both cases; hospital-proposing deferred acceptance can admit both types even under unitary doctors' preferences. A further sufficient condition makes efficient stable-dominating mechanisms obviously manipulable in the worst case. On the unitary domain, doctor-proposing deferred acceptance is not obviously manipulable. If each doctor--hospital pair has at most one feasible contract, this positive conclusion extends to every stable-dominating mechanism.

items.title: Doubly robust estimation of direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
items.summary: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. Under certain identifying assumptions, both components may be identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, even in the absence of an uncontaminated comparison group. Under a no-anticipation assumption, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time-series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment, provided that the model used for the extrapolation is correctly specified. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for possibly high-dimensional covariates by machine learning. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ consistent behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors under specific regularity conditions. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.

items.title: Improving control over unobservables with network data
items.summary: This paper develops a method to conduct causal inference in the presence of unobserved confounders by leveraging networks with homophily, a frequently observed tendency to form edges with similar nodes. I introduce a concept of asymptotic homophily, according to which individuals' selectivity scales with the size of the potential connection pool. The resulting network formation model accommodates common empirical features such as homophily, degree heterogeneity, sparsity, and clustering, and provides a framework to obtain consistent estimators of treatment effects that are robust to selection on unobservables. In an application, I recover an estimate of the effect of parental involvement on students' test scores that is greater than that of OLS, arguably due to the estimator's ability to account for unobserved ability.

items.title: Unequal Rewards and the Direction of Scientific Work: Evidence from U.S. Public Universities
items.summary: Research on pay dispersion has long asked whether unequal rewards increase or depress performance. Tournament theory expects stronger effort, while social comparison accounts expect withdrawal. Both perspectives, however, treat performance as a single scale on which workers can be ranked. Scientific work often resists such ordering. Some contributions extend recognized lines of inquiry and can be evaluated against prevailing standards; others revise the frames through which value is judged and become legible only later. We argue that intellectual tournaments more readily reward the first kind of contribution than the second. Pay dispersion may therefore be associated not only with how much scholars produce but also with what kinds of intellectual exploration are encouraged. We test this argument with administrative payroll records for 105,050 tenure-line faculty in 4,839 departments at 93 U.S. public universities from 2004 to 2026, linked to publication histories in OpenAlex. For each department, we estimate a separate pay equation using rank, contract basis, and seniority, then measure the Gini of the salary variation this local ladder cannot explain. Scholars in departments with greater unexplained pay dispersion publish more papers and receive more citations, but their work is less disruptive, less novel, and more conventional. Additional analyses show that compensation premiums above the ladder go disproportionately to scholars with broad collaborations and topical breadth. Although the design cannot fully separate treatment from selection, the evidence shows that inequality is not only a distributional outcome but also an evaluative structure, shaping which forms of knowledge are recognized, rewarded, and reproduced within organizations and communities.

items.title: AI Search as an Information Intermediary: Clickstream Evidence on Web Traffic
items.summary: AI search retrieves web information to ground generated answers. We study this new information intermediary using U.S. desktop clickstream data observing use alongside referrals during ChatGPT Search's rollout. Referrals accompany 5.4% of ChatGPT sessions versus 31.1% of Google queries. Ad-supported sites receive a smaller share of ChatGPT than Google referrals, while reference and technical sites receive larger shares. Conventional searches (Google, Bing, Yahoo) decline after ChatGPT adoption, sooner when adoption follows ChatGPT Search's expansion to users without accounts. Among existing users, that expansion raises ChatGPT use; conventional searches show no detectable overall change but fall among households with lower prior search activity. These findings suggest AI search can reshape open-web traffic through its own referrals and changes in conventional search.

items.title: Price co-movement and price information diverge across Nordic electricity zones after the energy crisis
items.summary: After the 2021-2022 energy crisis, day-ahead prices in Nordic bidding zones no longer move together. We ask whether this divergence also changes the information carried by prices. The answer matters for integrating variable renewable energy (VRE), because it can help identify where wind and solar forecasts are worth producing, publishing, and using. We measured the co-movement of each Norwegian and Swedish zone with Germany-Luxembourg (DE-LU) in 2018-2025. We then used a single model, selected on 2024 data, to forecast 2025 prices at 11:00 on the previous day and tested which inputs improved accuracy in each zone. The zones moved alike until 2019, but co-movement diverged in Sweden in 2020 and in Norway in 2021, and the split has persisted. In 2024, four southern zones co-moved strongly with DE-LU (intraday correlations of 0.54-0.71), while four northern zones co-moved weakly (0.25-0.30). Yet price information did not follow this split. Previous-day neighbouring prices reduced mean absolute error by at most 2.2% in any zone, equally in coupled and isolated zones. Removing the transmission system operators' wind and solar forecasts increased mean absolute error by at most 6% in Norway, 8-16% in Sweden, and 31% in DE-LU, and the ordering held in 2024. Within Norway, the value of these forecasts showed no detectable dependence on reservoir filling. The divergence in co-movement was therefore not matched by a divergence in price information, which differed mainly between national generation systems. Thus, a zone's coupling to the continent does not indicate the value of VRE forecasts there.

items.title: Uniform Inference for Two-Way Clustered Data
items.summary: We establish uniformly asymptotically exact inference for the population mean of two-way clustered data, allowing the data-generating process to vary with sample size. This finding does not contradict the well-known impossibility result of Menzel (2021), which places a fundamental limit on uniform estimation of the asymptotic distribution of the normalized full-array mean. We estimate the same population mean by averaging the sample means from random matchings. A closed-form standard error makes the resulting confidence interval straightforward to implement. The variance estimator is positive semidefinite and the studentized matching estimator is uniformly asymptotically standard normal. The cost of uniform validity is a slower convergence rate under degeneracy. We extend the result to smooth functions of GMM parameters, allowing the different moment components to exhibit different dependence regimes. In simulations, the proposed confidence intervals achieve coverage close to the nominal level across the dependence regimes considered.

items.title: Ramping Procurement and Bid-Cost Recovery in Real-Time Market
items.summary: We study ramping procurement co-optimized with economic dispatch under net-demand uncertainty. We examine two flexible ramp product designs implemented by grid operators: single-interval and multi-interval co-optimization. Both rely on rolling-window stochastic optimization with binding and advisory interval decisions. We develop analytical frameworks to evaluate generator profits, consumer payments, bid cost recovery (BCR), and operational efficiency. In particular, net-demand uncertainty may lead to generator under-compensation, requiring discriminatory BCR. While operational efficiency is invariant to energy and ramp prices, producer profits and consumer payments depend critically on pricing. We examine locational marginal pricing (LMP) and two uniform pricing: maximum dispatch cost pricing (MDCP) and maximum temporal locational marginal pricing (MTLMP). With out-of-market BCR, LMP yields discriminatory energy prices, whereas MDCP eliminates BCR and MTLMP does so in most cases. This property enables us to establish truthful bidding incentives for price-taking generators under MDCP. Our analysis highlights trade-offs between single- and multi-interval co-optimization and pricing designs: multi-interval energy-ramp co-optimization outperforms single-interval co-optimization when ramping forecasts are accurate and ramping needs are tight, but its advantage diminishes under large forecast errors and moderate ramping needs. Empirical results on CAISO and ERCOT data show that MDCP and MTLMP increase producer profits with negligible BCR, albeit at the expense of higher consumer payments relative to LMP.

items.title: Localizing Mean Shifts in High-Dimensional Vector Autoregressive Models
items.summary: We study the localization of mean changes in high-dimensional vector autoregressions (VARs) when the autoregressive dynamics remain common across regimes. We develop a three-step procedure that first obtains preliminary change-point estimates from the raw series ignoring the dependence structure, then estimates a common sparse VAR using observations away from the estimated changes, and finally filters the series to refine the change point locations. For a single change point, we show that the preliminary localization rate depends directly on the strength of temporal dependence, whereas filtering removes this dependence penalty from the oracle rate. With an estimated filter, the refined rate additionally reflects the error in estimating the VAR dynamics and the relation between the change in the stationary mean and the corresponding change in the VAR intercept. We characterize these rates explicitly and establish conditions under which filtering improves localization. Because filtering near a change point uses lags from adjacent regimes, it also creates a short-lived distortion in the filtered mean; we characterize when this boundary effect is innocuous and develop a transition-corrected alternative. We extend the procedure to an unknown number of change points. Overlapping local windows are used to generate candidate locations, an information criterion removes redundant and spurious candidates and estimates the number of changes, and the retained locations are subsequently refined using the estimated VAR filter. We establish consistency for the estimated number of changes and simultaneous localization rates for their locations. Numerical experiments corroborate the localization gains and show robustness to moderate departures from common VAR dynamics. An application to a large panel of U.S. macroeconomic indicators identifies economically interpretable changes.

items.title: On the modelling and prediction of high-dimensional functional time series
items.summary: We propose a two-step procedure to model and predict high-dimensional functional time series, where the number of function-valued time series $p$ is large in relation to the length of time series $n$. Our first step performs an eigenanalysis of a positive definite matrix, which leads to a one-to-one linear transformation for the original high-dimensional functional time series, and the transformed curve series can be segmented into several groups such that any two subseries from any two different groups are uncorrelated both contemporaneously and serially. Consequently in our second step those groups are handled separately without the information loss on the overall linear dynamic structure. The second step is devoted to establishing a finite-dimensional dynamical structure for all the transformed functional time series within each group. Furthermore the finite-dimensional structure is represented by that of a vector time series. Modelling and forecasting for the original high-dimensional functional time series are realized via those for the vector time series in all the groups. We investigate the theoretical properties of our proposed methods, and illustrate the finite-sample performance through both extensive simulation and two real datasets.

items.title: Observable Self-Restraint in Repeated Cheap Talk
items.summary: A long-lived sender seeks to persuade short-lived receivers to take his preferred action. Receivers observe his past advice but cannot verify its accuracy. Restrictions on recommendation histories alone can support a partially informative equilibrium. Under rolling quotas, which cap favorable recommendations within a fixed memory window, favorable advice is more costly when past favorable recommendations are more numerous or more recent. In an informative equilibrium, a violation can itself convey enough information about the current state for the receiver to follow the recommendation. After some sequences of states, the sender therefore breaks his own restriction, ending informative communication on the equilibrium path. As the sender becomes patient, suitable rolling quotas approach his normalized equilibrium payoff ceiling.

items.title: Double Machine Learning for Panel Data: Identification, Specification, and a Bank Regulation Effect
items.summary: This paper examines robustness and causal interpretation of panel estimates using double/debiased machine learning. The prototype treatment setup is the 2018 US banking regulation. Under common treatment timing, we characterize identification and nuisance restrictions and derive exact bank-level representations of specified "within" and "first-difference" scores. Simulations assess panel model transformation-induced specification bias and inference under weaker overlap. Empirically, estimates vary with asset-size classification and prior growth. Prior-growth adjustment reduces overlap-weighted estimates across four Machine Learners (ML); doubly robust estimates depend on the fitted propensity and concentrated weights. Both bank groups received relief, so we estimate differential exposure effects. The findings highlight specification issues and the relation between functional-form robustness and causal identification.

items.title: Bayesian Machine Learning Methods For Large Scale Demand Estimation
items.summary: This work studies how Bayesian machine learning methods can be used for large-scale demand estimation with many product categories. I compare two model classes, a latent factorization model and a mixed logit model and two Bayesian estimation approaches, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and Variational Inference (VI). The analysis combines a simulation study with an application to supermarket scanner data. The results show that the latent factorization model benefits from information across categories and improves its predictive performance as the dimensionality of the choice environment increases, whereas the mixed logit model does not exhibit the same pattern. MCMC delivers the highest predictive accuracy but is computationally intensive. VI achieves slightly lower predictive performance while substantially reducing runtime. In the empirical application, VI also outperforms the mixed logit benchmark. These findings highlight a trade-off between accuracy and computational feasibility in multi-category demand estimation.

items.title: Tractable Estimation of the Money Pump Index
items.summary: The Money Pump Index (MPI) of Echenique et al. (2011) measures the severity of consumer irrationality, but computing the exact mean and median MPI over all revealed preference cycles is NP-hard (Smeulders et al., 2013). Existing solutions rely on heuristic proxies, such as evaluating only shorter cycles or bounding the MPI. By framing revealed preferences as a directed graph, this paper projects choice violations onto fundamental cycle bases, which are minimal sets of linearly independent cycles that span the graph's entire cycle space. This yields computationally tractable estimators for the mean and median MPI that are asymptotically equivalent to the original MPI. Applying this methodology to the scanner dataset analyzed by Echenique et al. (2011) and Smeulders et al., (2013), the proposed estimators compute quickly and with negligible small-sample bias.

items.title: Inference for High-Dimensional Regression with a Possible Threshold
items.summary: This paper develops uniform inference for slope coefficients in high-dimensional threshold regressions without pretesting for a threshold effect. Confidence intervals based on a debiased threshold Lasso estimator are uniformly asymptotically valid, allowing for heteroskedasticity and non-sub-Gaussian covariates and errors. We also propose a threshold-effect test and extend inference to stationary time series. Applying the method to racial tipping in U.S. neighborhoods, we find that the relationships between white population change and residential turnover, housing age, commuting schedules, and utility payments differ across minority-share regimes. Threshold effects are detected in fewer metropolitan areas in 2000--2010 than in 1990--2000.

items.title: One-Sided Randomization in Two-Sided Platform Experiments: Which Side Should be Randomized?
items.summary: Two-sided marketplace platforms often use randomized experiments to evaluate new features, raising the question of whether to randomize customers or listings. Randomizing the smaller (\emph{short}) side can reduce interference bias due to weaker competition, while randomizing the larger (\emph{long}) side provides a larger nominal sample, potentially reducing variance. On the surface, these competing considerations suggest a bias-variance trade-off in choosing which side to randomize. We investigate this trade-off in a two-sided marketplace with first-come, first-served (FCFS) booking and heterogeneous customer preferences, studying the bias and variance of difference-in-means estimators of the global average treatment effect. Our findings suggest that rather than a bias-variance tradeoff, in fact short-side randomization is generally preferable on {\em both} dimensions. We prove these results in an asymptotic regime where market imbalance increases. We establish conditions under which (1) short-side randomization eliminates first-order interference bias, while long-side randomization retains it; and (2) short-side randomization also achieves a variance rate of no larger asymptotic order than long-side randomization. The key insight is that although the long side contains more participants, the number of matches is constrained by the population on the short side, limiting the apparent variance advantage of randomizing a larger sample. Our conditions accommodate heterogeneous preferences and treatment effects and are satisfied by familiar logit models of customer choice. Together, these findings support randomizing on the short side, despite the larger sample size available on the long side.

items.title: Self-Equivalent Voting Rules
items.summary: In this paper, I introduce a novel stability axiom for stochastic voting rules, called self-equivalence, by which a voting rule must be able to induce$\unicode{x2014}$whenever applied to a suitable finite set of voting rules$\unicode{x2014}$a convex combination of voting rules that coincides with itself. I then show that the unique anonymous, efficient, neutral, and self-equivalent voting rule assigns to every voter equal probability of being a dictator (i.e., uniform random dictatorship). Since randomly choosing a dictator might be considered undesirable, this paper suggests one reason for democratic societies not to decide whether to replace their voting rule by applying it to arbitrary finite sets of voting rules if they also desire stability.

items.title: Hedging out the HEDGE Bias: Identifying Dynamic Partial-Equilibrium Effects with Panel LP-IV
items.summary: Cross-sectional designs are widely used to estimate dynamic partial-equilibrium effects of an aggregate treatment. We show analytically that these estimates are biased when exposures to the treatment and to aggregate confounders are correlated or the confounders feed back into the treatment. This paper develops the heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV) framework, which compares units while holding the confounder path fixed by instrumenting the treatment and this path with exposure-weighted shock proxies. We prove that HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect. We further extend the framework, with the corresponding inference, to multiple exposure margins and confounders, forward-looking outcomes, and cumulative multipliers. Finally, we apply HELP-IV to state fiscal multipliers and regional stock-wealth effects, where it yields partial-equilibrium effects that are smaller than conventional estimates and deliver different implications when ported to macroeconomic models.

items.title: A Sensitivity Framework for Assessing External Validity
items.summary: Assessing the external validity of experimental results is a pervasive challenge in causal inference as internally valid findings need not generalize beyond sites in which the experiments were conducted. Since the number of sites is often smaller than the number of site-level variables that moderate causal effects, we develop a partial identification framework that lets practitioners assess external validity under a wide range of assumptions that allow extrapolation across site-level variables. Our optimization-driven approach can accommodate any affine family of parameter restrictions, such as interaction terms being dominated by direct effects (the "effect hierarchy principle"). Since standard estimating-equation arguments do not apply in our setting---underspecified parameter directions responsible for partial identification make the covariance matrix singular---we develop a novel debiasing approach for estimands given by constrained optimization problems, giving rise to semiparametrically efficient estimators for our flexible partial identification bounds. We illustrate our approach on multi-site microcredit experiments harmonized by Meager (2019), whose lending environments differ widely in interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion. Holding out one country at a time, we construct external-validity intervals for the held-out country from the remaining source sites and show how our framework connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.

items.title: Core nonemptiness for $2/3$-convex games
items.summary: We study the core of $2/3$-convex games, a class of transferable-utility (TU) games that generalizes convex games, which requires at least two of any three distinct coalitions satisfy the supermodular inequality. We show that every $2/3$-convex game admits a marginal worth vector in the core, and hence has a nonempty core. Our proof is constructive and yields a linear-time algorithm for finding such a core allocation. We also show that $2/3$-convexity does not imply permutational convexity in general, while the implication holds under an additional superadditivity condition on pairs of singletons. As an application, we introduce a TU model motivated by the OSCE's consensus-minus-two procedure and show that the resulting game is $2/3$-convex but need not be convex.

items.title: How does online shopping affect offline price sensitivity?
items.summary: The rapid rise of e-commerce has transformed consumer behavior, prompting questions about how online adoption influences offline shopping. We examine whether consumers who adopt a retailer's online shopping channels become more price-sensitive in their subsequent offline purchases with that retailer. Using transaction-level data from a large Brazilian pet supplies retailer operating both online and offline, we compare "adopters" -- customers who began shopping online after a period of offline-only purchasing -- with "non-adopters" who remained offline-only. We estimate a discrete choice logit model with individual-level heterogeneity, based on an algorithm that can handle both high-dimensional fixed effects and price endogeneity. We then apply a staggered difference-in-differences approach to the estimated price elasticities and obtain the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT). We find that offline price sensitivity increases significantly after online adoption in three out of four product categories. Our results underscore the importance of recognizing cross-channel effects in consumer behavior and contribute to the literature on pricing and multichannel retailing by identifying online adoption as a key driver of offline price sensitivity.

items.title: Testing Density Discontinuity Using Spacings
items.summary: In the regression discontinuity design, researchers assess the credibility of assumptions by testing the running variable's density for a discontinuity at the cutoff. This paper proposes a novel such test. The test uses q spacings on each side of the cutoff, where spacings are the widths between ordered observations. Spacings yield a continuous statistic that behaves well under weak assumptions. I study its properties in two asymptotic frameworks: one where q is fixed as the sample size increases and one where q slowly diverges to infinity. With q fixed, the test achieves exact asymptotic size control without user randomization. When q increases slowly, the test becomes consistent without sacrificing exact asymptotic size. Compared to the preferred version of Bugni and Canay's (2021) test, the only other test with comparably weak assumptions, this test reduces sensitivity to the tuning parameter and performs similarly when theirs is well-chosen.

items.title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Just Classification and a Few Regressions
items.summary: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to recover a reward function from observed behavior, but rewards are typically only partially identified: many reward--value pairs can induce the same behavior policy. We study this problem in the maximum-entropy, or Gumbel-shock, model under a broad class of statewise affine normalization constraints, with anchor-action constraints as a special case. This leads to Generalized Policy-to-$Q$-to-Reward (GenPQR), a modular approach to normalized reward recovery based on policy estimation and $Q$-evaluation via the Bellman equation; both components can be instantiated with off-the-shelf classification and regression methods. We establish modular finite-sample guarantees under general function approximation, with separate terms for policy-estimation and $Q$-function estimation error. We also give explicit bounds for GenPQR with fitted $Q$-evaluation. In experiments, GenPQR improves on DeepPQR in reward recovery. Our guarantees extend beyond anchor actions, accommodate large action spaces, and are not tied to a specific neural-network architecture or training procedure.

items.title: China's Local Government Debt, Strategic Competition, and Bitcoin Demand: A Conditional Transmission Framework
items.summary: How might the resolution of China's local-government debt affect strategic competition and Bitcoin demand? This paper develops a conditional framework connecting debt accounting, bank balance-sheet adjustment, public spending priorities, and constrained portfolio substitution. A debt swap can increase recognized government debt without increasing consolidated principal, while its effect on credit capacity depends on capital relief, loss recognition, and recapitalization. A protected strategic-spending floor can preserve current effort while shifting adjustment toward civilian productive services. In the asset block, stronger relative preference for Bitcoin does not ensure greater effective demand: access constraints and global funding conditions can reverse the sign. We derive a finite-shock threshold and deterministic sign bounds, and distinguish Bitcoin demand from demand for dollar stablecoins. Reproducible numerical illustrations and channel-removal exercises show that opposite outcomes are compatible with the same assumed fiscal stress. The analysis uses dated primary sources to establish institutional context, but estimates neither a debt-to-Bitcoin causal coefficient nor a price-impact scale. Its contribution is a compact set of conditions and measurement distinctions for evaluating transmission claims, rather than an unconditional price forecast or an inference about conflict probabilities.

items.title: RepoMech: A Method to Reduce the Balance-Sheet Impact of Repo Intermediation
items.summary: A repo trade involves the sale of a security coupled with a contract to repurchase at a later time. Following the 2008 financial crisis, accounting standards were updated to require repo intermediaries, who are mostly banks, to increase recorded assets at the time of the first transaction. Concurrently, US bank regulators implemented a supplementary leverage ratio constraint that reduces the volume of assets a bank is allowed record. The interaction of the new accounting rules and bank regulations limits the volume of repo trades that banks can intermediate. To reduce the balance-sheet impact of repo, the SEC has mandated banks to centrally clear all Treasuries trades. This achieves multilateral netting but shifts counterparty risk onto the clearinghouse, which can distort monitoring incentives and raise trading cost through the imposition of fees. We present RepoMech, a method that avoids these pitfalls by multilaterally netting repo trades without altering counterparty risk.

items.title: Data-center growth impacts household electricity costs more through wholesale prices than through grid reinforcement
items.summary: Rapid data-center expansion is raising concerns about electricity affordability, yet how the costs of serving these large new loads reach residential customers remains poorly understood. Here, we quantify the potential impact of 371 announced Texas data-center projects, totaling 38.9 GW by 2030, on residential electricity costs by linking power system expansion, wholesale electricity markets, transmission reinforcement, and retail cost allocation. We find that accommodating this demand increases modeled residential electricity costs in one representative case by 1.64 cents/kWh, with 68% arising from higher wholesale electricity prices and 32% from regulated transmission charges. Allowing new gas generation near data centers reduces the 2023 residential cost increase to 0.92 cents/kWh, whereas excluding data centers from the transmission cost-sharing base raises it to 1.87 cents/kWh. These findings reveal that the residential cost burden of data-center growth is driven primarily by wholesale electricity price increases, rather than direct transmission investment costs, and depends critically on generation siting, infrastructure planning, and cost allocation.

items.title: Human Capital in Context: What Employment Survival Reveals About Worker-Firm Match
items.summary: There is no best worker in general, only a best worker for a particular firm. We develop a measure of worker-firm match quality that treats fit as a property of the pair, learned from the survival of employment relationships. A two-tower neural network embeds workers, from their career histories and current positions, and firms, from their characteristics and business descriptions, into a common space, and match quality is the cosine similarity of the two vectors. The measure takes its functional form from the skill-weights model of firm-specific human capital, and its only estimated objective, a separation hazard, from the view of the job match as an experience good. Estimated on more than a billion person-periods covering 101 million workers and 8.4 million firms, a 0.1 increase in match quality lowers the odds of separation by 48%. About a quarter of the variance of match quality is specific to the worker-firm pair, which worker-, firm-, and occupation-level measures set to zero by construction. Workers earn more when better matched, especially early in a relationship, and firms whose workforces score higher grow faster, become more profitable, and are issued more, and more valuable, patents over the next five years than their industry peers. Because it scores pairs that never formed, the measure also predicts where movers go, and acquirers record a larger share of the price as goodwill when the target's workers would fit the acquirer better than they fit the target.

items.title: Delegating Authorization to Misaligned Agents: Coalitional Alignment and Safe Control
items.summary: Long-running AI agents create a control problem: each action they take changes the state, which in turn affects the trajectory of future actions. If the agent is not fully aligned, then guaranteeing safety requires approving consequential actions before allowing them to be executed. But requiring human approval at every step makes attention a bottleneck. Delegating review to other AI agents raises the same alignment problem: the reviewers may themselves be misaligned. We identify a condition on a reviewing panel that is weaker than individual alignment yet necessary and sufficient for a guarantee that the principal fares at least as well in expectation as under a designated baseline policy. Each reviewer agent reports whether an action proposal made by a proposer agent improves its own utility relative to the baseline. We show that a threshold rule tolerating $k$ disapprovals is safe exactly when, after any $k$ reviewers are removed, the principal's utility can be written as a nonnegative combination of the remaining reviewers' utilities, plus a term that is nonnegative on every feasible proposal. We call this property $k$-robust coalitional alignment. The characterization lifts to sequential control: in a discounted MDP with an arbitrary proposer agent, safety at every state is both necessary and sufficient for the induced policy to match or improve on the baseline. When reviewers vote strategically, full-panel coverage in reward-function space guarantees that every Nash equilibrium is safe under the unanimous approval rule; in contrast, more permissive thresholds can admit unsafe equilibria even when reviewers are individually aligned. Experiments with existing reviewer models show that collective review can remain sound without an aligned individual, even when some disapprovals are tolerated.

items.title: Perceived Social Norms and Information Disclosure
items.summary: Social-information messages are widely used to influence norm perceptions and norm-relevant behavior, but their effects may depend on what they report and how they are disclosed. This paper develops a belief-based framework connecting personal values and perceived social norms through inference about a latent appropriateness standard. The framework shows how messages affect perceived social norms, with potential implications for subsequent behavior, through two mechanisms: First, personal-value and perceived-norm statistics encode previous participants' private information differently because perceived-norm reports also incorporate an inference about others' assessments. Second, relative to private disclosure, public disclosure also affects recipients' beliefs about others' assessments, as they expect other group members to update using the same statistic. These mechanisms imply that, for equally sized changes on the same scale, perceived-norm statistics induce larger shifts in current perceived norms than personal-value statistics, and that public disclosure induces larger marginal responses than private disclosure. Thus, the effect of a norm-relevant message can depend not only on the value it reports, but also on how the reported statistic is constructed and who is known to observe it.

items.title: Empirical Bayes Estimation in Heterogeneous Coefficient Panel Models
items.summary: We develop an empirical Bayes (EB) G-modeling framework for short-panel linear models with nonparametric prior for the random intercepts, slopes, dynamics, and non-spherical error variances. We establish identification and consistency of the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) under general conditions, and provide low-level sufficient conditions for several models of empirical interest. Conditions for regret consistency of the EB estimators are also established. The NPMLE is computed using a Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao gradient flow algorithm adapted to panel regressions. Using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, we find that the slope coefficient for potential experience is substantially heterogeneous and negatively correlated with the random intercept, and that error variances and autoregressive coefficients vary considerably across individuals. The EB estimates reduce mean squared prediction errors relative to individual maximum likelihood estimates.

items.title: When is p-hacking detectable?
items.summary: We show that some forms of p-hacking and publication bias cannot be detected by examining the histogram of t-statistics or their p-values. Even when p-hacking is detectable, standard tests may lack power against some alternatives. We propose a novel test that is consistent against every form of selective reporting that is detectable from the distribution of reported t-statistics. Our test statistic is the distance between the smoothed empirical t-curve and the set of possible honest distributions. Unlike existing tests which target roughness or incorrect derivatives in the t-curve and p-curve, the projection test is much less sensitive to rounding and derounding of the printed t-scores and we provide a novel deterministic derounding procedure that preserves its validity. In an empirical application to economics articles we show that the projection test rejects more often than any of seven tests from Elliott et al. (2022) and Simonsohn et al. (2014, 2015). Moreover, the projection test certifies that detection was not driven by rounding or derounding. In a simulation exercise that resamples actual medical trials we show that there are simple p-hacking techniques that the projection test detects but the others do not.

items.title: Degrading the Grade: Grading Variance as Evidence of Shirking
items.summary: Variation in grading standards across instructors who teach the same students is evidence of a moral hazard problem, whether or not grades are inflated. The optimal standard is the same for every section of a course, yet grades vary widely across sections. We present a principal-agent model in which instructors who know the optimal standard still depart from it, leniently or harshly, depending on their incentives. Penalizing deviations from the department average leaves the average unchanged but compresses grading variance, which raises student welfare. Disclosing the same information to students instead increases grading variance.

items.title: Introducing and Repealing an EV Subsidy: Evidence from New Zealand's Clean Car Discount
items.summary: New Zealand's Clean Car Discount (CCD) was a feebate scheme that offered rebates for low-emission vehicles from July 2021, added fees for high-emission vehicles from April 2022, and was abolished at the end of December 2023. Shortly afterwards, road user charges were introduced for electric vehicles (EVs). We study how EV adoption responded to the introduction and the abrupt repeal of the scheme, using monthly vehicle registration data from 2014 to 2024. A structural break analysis following Bai and Perron, combined with a regression discontinuity in time, shows that breaks in the registrations of battery electric, plug-in hybrid and conventional vehicles coincide with the policy dates. To estimate causal effects, we apply a difference-in-differences approach with Queensland, Australia, as a comparison region and Newey-West standard errors. Because the New Zealand market was about four times larger, the analysis uses log-transformed registrations, so that parallel trends refer to equal growth rates. The results are asymmetric. After the introduction of the rebates, EV registrations in New Zealand rose strongly, but by a similar proportion as in Queensland, and the average effect relative to Queensland is not statistically significant. A specification allowing for a change in slope suggests a gradual acceleration of EV uptake. After the repeal, EV registrations fell by about 72% relative to Queensland, and the decline persisted in 2025. Both policy dates were preceded by a rush of purchases. The average CO2 emissions of newly registered vehicles fell markedly during the scheme and rebounded after its end. The results suggest that an abrupt end of EV purchase incentives can cause a large and lasting drop in EV uptake, and that a gradual, pre-announced phase-out may be preferable.

items.title: Quantile restrictions, revealed rankings, and the limits of multinomial choice
items.summary: This paper analyzes when choice probabilities reveal rankings of deterministic utility indices in semiparametric discrete choice models. It begins with binary choice, showing that quantile thresholds can arise from behavioral departures from utility maximization under exchangeable unobservables, or from non-exchangeable unobservables under utility maximization. These behavioral and distributional routes are then extended to multinomial choice. Under limited attention, balance restrictions on attention probabilities give linear separators whose strict signs reveal rankings uniformly over admissible unobservable distributions and parameter values. Beyond these restrictions, opposite rankings can generate overlapping probability images. Under non-exchangeable unobservables, a common ranking partition across distributions need not exist. Under a common location-scale structure, both extensions admit an injective, generally nonlinear probability map that permits ranking recovery on its attainable image. The results distinguish distribution-robust ranking rules from recovery under specific structural restrictions, clarifying the limits of extending binary quantile restrictions to multinomial choice.

items.title: Inference After Model Refutation: Uniform Post-Relaxation Inference for Partially Identified Models
items.summary: When data reject an econometric model, the researcher must decide which identifying assumptions to give up. If several equally preferred repairs restore compatibility, the repair itself is unknown, and inference under any one of them can exclude structural values supported by the others, even when that inference is exact. I propose Post-Relaxation Projection (PR), which carries one simultaneous confidence event through every repair that may be minimal. With repair-by-repair primitive bounds, PR equals the union of all post-relaxation targets compatible with the band, so no smaller band-based set has the same guarantee. I derive limits on learning the repair, the exact perturbation radius of the minimal-repair correspondence, oracle-equivalent adaptation, and a reduced-form version valid at zero first stages. In cross-country data on institutions and income, the data do not settle which historical instrument should be dropped, yet every admissible minimum repair implies a positive effect of institutions.

items.title: Not Strassen's theorem
items.summary: Suppose there is an uncertain state of the world, drawn from a CDF G. It is well known that the random posterior mean induced (via Bayes's rule) by a signal must have a distribution F that is a mean-preserving contraction of G, and conversely that any mean-preserving contraction is induced by some signal. This is not Strassen's (1965) theorem! It is a distinct result, versions of which were stated (or at least alluded to) by Hardy, Littlewood and Polya (1929), Blackwell (1951) and Kolotilin (2014). I give a precise statement and a complete proof.

items.title: Social choice with transfers
items.summary: We consider the problem of social choice when transfers between agents are possible. This includes several canonical applications: public-good provision, management of a common resource, settlement of debts, and division of goods. The question of interest is, given a set of possible alternatives, which should be chosen and what transfers, if any, should be made? We show that the Shapley value of the stand-alone game is the only solution to satisfy certain desirable properties.

items.title: Factors Influencing Rural Female Workforce Participation in India, 2017- 2025: An Econometric Analysis Using District-Level Panel Data
items.summary: Rural female workforce participation rate (RFWPR) in India declined between 1993-94 and 2017-18. After 2017-18, the trend reversed, and RFWPR rose from 23.7% in 2017-18 to 44.9% in 2025. Using district-level panel data for about 500 districts for nine years, 2017-18 to 2025, the paper analyzes econometrically some key determinants of RFWPR in India in the recent period. We find that the presence of young children in the family tends to reduce RFWPR, consistent with findings from several previous studies. Our econometric model results indicate that an increase in household real income, proxied by the monthly per capita consumption expenditure deflated by the consumer price index, tends to reduce RFWPR. Increases in the real wage rate of casual workers in rural areas, likely reflecting a shortage of such labour, particularly in agriculture, tend to raise RFWPR. However, the positive effect of wage hikes on RFWPR continues only until real rural wages reach a particular level. Beyond that wage rate, the positive effect of wages on RFWPR diminishes or could even turn negative, i.e., rural wage hikes tending to reduce RFWPR.

items.title: The amplifier effect of artificial agents in social contagion
items.summary: Individuals and organizations increasingly consider delegating decision-making to AI agents, which may significantly alter social contagion dynamics. We ask whether artificial agents exhibit different adoption thresholds from those of human subjects when making decisions and, if so, how such differences may affect the spread of social contagions. To answer these questions, we conduct two choice experiments - recently administered to human participants - with artificial agents powered by large language models (LLMs). Across two domains and five LLMs, artificial agents exhibit systematically lower adoption thresholds than human subjects. Simulations of diffusion calibrated with the experimental findings show that, holding network structure fixed, even a modest share of artificial agents leads to higher total adoption. Our findings suggest that the presence of artificial agents in social networks can alter diffusion.

items.title: From the firm- to the application-level: A new typology of AI use in organisations
items.summary: Artificial intelligence is applied in organisations in many different ways. However, the firm-level literature on AI lacks a conceptual framework able to describe that variety. Empirical studies typically examine one dimension of AI use at a time. This paper argues that the difficulty follows from the unit of analysis: a firm may hold many AI applications at once, each with its own novelty, sourcing mode, objective and technology type. These dimensions are defined at the level of the application rather than of the firm. We therefore propose shifting the unit of analysis from the firm to the individual AI application, and develop a typology combining these four conceptual dimensions. The new framework locates any application in a common space, and it points out in particular two types that the prevailing adoption-innovation distinction neglects: co-invention, novel uses of technology the firm did not develop, and internalisation, in-house building of AI that could have been bought instead. Documented use cases illustrate the framework, which is then used to discuss implications for firms strategies and the diffusion of AI in economic systems.

items.title: Measuring Information Burden: From Coalition-Based Reasoning to the Price System
items.summary: The price system is often said to economize on what individuals need to know. This paper measures a particular informational burden associated with decentralized reasoning in its absence: the coalition-feasibility information required for individual rejection decisions to recover the core. We develop a proof-theoretic framework in which information is represented by economically meaningful sentences and reasoning by derivations in Gentzen's sequent calculus. An agent rejects a proposed payoff vector only when she can establish the existence of a profitable coalitional deviation; failure to reject may instead reflect ignorance. For each transferable-utility game, the main theorem characterizes the informational distributions under which the set of unopposed payoff vectors coincides with the core: every noncore payoff vector must have a blocking coalition known to at least one of its members. This yields a game-specific measure of minimum informational burden. We extend the characterization to pure-exchange economies through a first-order framework that preserves finite informational premises. Applying the result to Shapley's (1975) replica economy, within the core-convergence tradition of Debreu and Scarf (1963), we show that the minimum average coalition-level informational burden grows as $Θ(4^k/k^{3/2})$, exponentially with replication. The result quantifies an informational requirement of direct decentralized coalitional reasoning that price-mediated coordination can spare agents, without claiming to measure the total informational savings of prices.

items.title: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents
items.summary: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. We show what the shift in perspective buys with a simulation in which one technical act, copying an agent's competence, is institutionalized as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity that creates no new participant, and as the splitting of one economic position into successors that inherit some obligations and not others. In a paired task, all three produce an identical technical trace despite differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated, and who gets paid. We close with a research program: building a principled chart of institution space, mapping how its implementable region shifts with agent capacities, and revising the chart wherever engineered agents expose distinctions it cannot express.

items.title: A Practical Guide to Instrumental Variables Methods with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
items.summary: Instrumental variables (IV) methods are central to applied microeconomics. While classical approaches assume linear models with constant effects, recent literature has shifted toward the local average treatment effect (LATE) framework to accommodate heterogeneous treatment effects. This paper provides a practical guide to aligning empirical practice with recent theory. We first examine how different specifications with covariates lead to distinct weighted averages of covariate-specific LATEs. We then discuss how parametric misspecification can undermine the causal interpretation of these estimands and suggest flexible specifications as essential robustness checks. Finally, we review formal tests for LATE assumptions and methods robust to monotonicity violations. We provide a guide to software implementations to help researchers apply the methods in practice.

items.title: Prediction Sets and Conformal Inference with Interval Outcomes
items.summary: Given data on a random variable $Y$, a prediction set with miscoverage level $α\in (0,1)$ is a set that contains a new draw of $Y$ with probability at least $1-α$. Among all prediction sets satisfying this coverage property, the oracle prediction set is the one with minimal volume. The oracle prediction set offers a complementary view of the distribution of $Y$, beyond point estimators such as the mean and quantiles, and has attracted considerable interest recently. This paper develops methods for estimating such prediction sets conditional on observed covariates when $Y$ censored or interval-valued. We characterise the oracle prediction set under partial identification induced by interval censoring and propose consistent estimators for both oracle prediction intervals and more general oracle prediction sets consisting of multiple disjoint intervals. In addition, we apply conformal inference to construct finite-sample valid prediction sets for interval outcomes that remain consistent as the sample size grows, using a conformity score tailored to interval data. The proposed procedure accounts for irreducible prediction uncertainty due to the stochastic nature of outcomes, modelling uncertainty arising from partial identification, and sampling uncertainty that vanishes as sample size increases. We conduct Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications using UK job postings data and the US Current Population Survey. The results demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of the proposed methods.

items.title: The Cherry-Picking Trap
items.summary: When a better-informed proposer puts forward a policy proposal, the responder should not take the proposal at face value but ask why it was chosen. We model how this inference can undermine trust even when interests are broadly aligned. A proposer privately observes a "basket" of viable policies and proposes one; a responder decides whether to approve the proposal but may lack the expertise to evaluate it. A larger basket makes a Pareto improvement more likely to be available but also gives the proposer greater scope to cherry-pick a policy that favors him at the responder's expense. In the unique equilibrium, Pareto improvements are often proposed and yet rationally rejected. Flexibility that should enable agreement instead breeds distrust.

items.title: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence
items.summary: Curiosity, the drive to close the gap between what one knows and what one wants to know, pulls consumers beyond their familiar content, sustains engagement, and breaks them out of the filter bubbles of repetitive, relevance-only recommendations. Despite its importance, curiosity is hardly incorporated into modern recommender systems for lack of a formal measure. The information-gap theory of curiosity provides no formal quantitative model that a recommender system can operate on, and existing proxy metrics do not accurately measure the curiosity that a recommended item evokes. To fill this research gap, we formalize the information-gap theory into five axioms of curiosity and construct the canonical formulation of a computational measure of the curiosity that a recommended item evokes in a consumer. We validate our curiosity measure through a survey-based study, in which it matches consumers' self-reported curiosity and outperforms alternative proxy metrics. We subsequently build a curiosity-aware recommender system that incorporates this measure into the utility function design, and we show through offline experiments on three real-world datasets that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale online controlled experiment at a major video-streaming platform in Asia, where we show that our method significantly increases click-through rate, video views, and time spent over the latest production system, leading to tangible economic impact for the company. Our method has since been deployed on the platform and remains in operation. Our findings establish consumer curiosity as a measurable and actionable objective for recommender systems, with important managerial implications for digital platforms to recommend what consumers wonder about.

items.title: Sharp Fréchet--Hoeffding Bounds under Selectively Incomplete Observation
items.summary: Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fréchet--Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. I establish an exact reduction of the identification problem to finite-dimensional optimization, yielding computable characterizations of both bounds. Illustrations involving income mobility, potential outcomes, and split questionnaires demonstrate how incomplete records can improve identification relative to the classical bounds.

items.title: The Price of Anarchy in Markets for Lemons
items.summary: We study the worst-case equilibrium gains from trade in simple bilateral trade mechanisms with interdependent valuations.
